src/data/tutorials.js: , guide:
s Arts, Items, Guard (halve the damage and act sooner) or Flee.
Don't feel like fighting this one? *Auto* lets the party fight on its own ({key:info} turns it on and off), and *Skip* plays the whole battle out at once and shows the results.
Random Battles
Auto-Battle & Skipping
Out in the wilds, the *orb* in the lower left warms from green to red as a random battle draws near.

Settings can change how they go: *Encounter Rate* halves them or turns them off (story battles still happen), *Auto-Battle* starts them on auto, and *Skip Random Battles* resolves them at once. You still earn the EXP, gold and drops.
Poise & Breaks
Each foe has a *Poise* shield: the number under it. Hit its weaknesses to chip it away.
At zero it *Breaks*: it loses its next turn and takes 50% more damage until it recovers. Weaknesses start hidden, so try everything.
The party shares the *Afterglow* gauge. It fills when you strike weaknesses, Break foes, land criticals and take hits.
In the command menu, press {key:pageLeft} / {key:pageRight} to *Surge*: spend it to strengthen the action you pick.
Big Attacks
A foe that is *Charging* (⚡) or *Winding Up* (⚠) will unleash something big on its next turn.
Guard to halve it. Better: Break the foe before it acts, and the attack is lost.
*Link Arts* are combination techniques between friends. When enough Afterglow is stored and the partners are free to act, pick *Link Arts* in the command menu.
A Link Art spends the Afterglow shown beside it and pushes the partners\' next turns back a little.
How Foes Fight
Foes think. A *healer* mends the most hurt of its side, so put it down first. A pack piles onto whoever its leader has *Marked*: Guard, or keep that friend healed.
A *thief* steals gold and runs; fell it before it goes and you get the gold back. And once a status bounces off someone, foes stop trying it on them.
Crests & Supports
In the menu ({key:menu}), *Crests* sets each character's *Primary* Crest (stats, weapons, Arts) and *Secondary* Crest (its Arts too). Crests rank up with CP from battle.
Each rank teaches an Art or a *Support*, a passive that stays yours whatever you wear. Equip Supports under *Supports*. Two Crests at rank 5 braid into a Tier II Crest.
Mastery & Ascension
A Crest at rank 10 is *mastered*: it leaves a *Legacy*, a bonus that stays with that character whatever Crest they wear.
Its CP keeps flowing into five *Ascension* stars: more stats and stronger Arts, and two *Mastery Arts* to learn. Read every Art in detail under *Arts* in the menu.
Only the first four in your *Formation* fight. Change the order on the menu\'s Formation screen.
In battle, *Swap* brings a reserve member in for the one whose turn it is.
New gear! Open *Equipment* in the menu ({key:menu}) to put it on. What each character can wear depends on their primary Crest.
Press {key:info} there to *Optimize*: the best you own, all at once.
*Hearthstones* restore the party and let you save. You can also save from the menu almost anywhere.
The game *autosaves* too, into three rotating slots. On the Save or Load screen, {key:info} exports a save to a file or imports one.
The World Map
Pick a place and go. The marker shows where your objective lies, and blue ones mark side quests.
Towns and the Hearthstones you have touched can be reached at once with *Travel* in the menu.
Side Quests
A *side quest*: optional, and kept in the *Journal* in the menu.
Blue *◆* markers show where side quests lead: over people and places, on the minimap and on the world map. Settings → Side Quest Markers turns them off.
Riding Kindle
*Kindle* the Emberhart carries you on open roads and in the wilds. Press {key:ride} to ride, and again to get down.
Kindle runs faster than you can, and nothing from the Gloam catches you while you ride: no random battles. Towns, buildings and dungeons are on foot.
The Compendium
*The Compendium* is in the menu ({key:menu}). It records every creature you meet, chapter by chapter, with *???* where something is still out there.
It fills in as you learn: weaknesses you strike or Scan, resistances you run into, moves you see. Fell three of a kind to learn its tactics. {key:pageLeft} / {key:pageRight} turn the sections.
A *mark*: a named rare beast on Greer\'s Ledger. It hits hard, can\'t be fled, and winds up for a big move.
Hunt it now, or leave it be and come back stronger. Tell Greer when you fell one: she pays for every mark.
Lost Callings
A *Lost Calling*: a Crest the Choir struck from its rolls. Its quest leads to a slab of crest-glass where a guardian waits.
Win, and the Crest is yours to wear like any other. The Crests screen shows a rumor of where each lost one begins.

src/story/ch1.js: The Kindling
Lanternfall has been up since before dawn: bunting on every line, the Choir\'s white boats rocking in the harbor, the Lantern swept and shining.
The girl from the rocks — Nana has her. I should see if she\'s awake.
I\'m Wren. That\'s Ilse, and the big loud one is Bram.
What\'s your name?
You don\'t remember it?
Then... Sable. Your hair — it\'s like a sable\'s coat. There\'s a picture in my atlas.
On the back of Sable\'s left hand, a mark like a closed eye. Black as the inside of a shell.
That\'s a Crest. But she can\'t be older than us, and she\'s never been Kindled— has she?
The Hierophant\'s here. If anyone can tell us what that is, he can.
And the Kindling is at noon. He\'ll be there. Sable — will you come?
The Lantern\'s light is warm. Warmer than sunlight. It goes all the way through you, like you are made of glass.
Wren\'s Crest awakens — *Vanguard*! Crest Arts are now usable in battle.
Ilse\'s Crest awakens — *Mender*!
When the light returns, the black mark on Sable\'s hand is open. An eye. Looking back.
The Hierophant has gone white as his robes. He is looking at Sable\'s face, not her hand.
Who\'s Lysa?
You don\'t sleep. You lie listening to the sea until the window goes gray, and then gold.
Aurenne. I\'m really going.
Late in the night, voices. They carry down the hill from the Lantern: your mother\'s, sharp as a gull\'s — and the Hierophant\'s.
Home. Mom\'s still up at the Lantern with the Hierophant.
I feel like I\'ve been awake for a week.

And I know what my mother told me about the night Aurenne went dark. About the Keeper\'s choice. About your sister.
I\'m afraid you\'ve heard two grown-ups being tiresome. Your mother is a remarkable Keeper. And remarkably stubborn.
Your friend. Sable. She needs answers I can\'t give her on an island. The Choir\'s archives in Aurenne might hold them.

I\'m sixteen. I have a Crest. The Hierophant asked me himself. You can\'t stop me.
Dad\'s compass.
Mom gave me Dad\'s compass. It points west, always. She said: come back to me, little bird.
Strait\'s calm as a millpond. Too calm, if you ask me.
I\'ve been on a ship before. Several. I am not seasick. This is my normal color.
Hold on! There\'s something under the hull!
Thirty years! Thirty years and I\'ve never— you kids. You _kids!_
All in a day\'s work for the Dawnguard.
There — Port Gale. The mainland. Your mother\'s whole world ends at that coast, Wren. Yours starts there.

ll keep her circling! If you\'re not back by the Long Bell I\'m coming in after you, and I WILL scratch the paint!
She means it about the paint.
Always wanted to see the sun up close. Thought it\'d be bigger.
It\'s the *biggest piece*.
Like I said.
It\'s warm. The ground is warm. Nothing\'s been warm for a year.
It\'s like standing on a stove that loves you.
And above it all, the Spire: white and gold, too tall and too clean. Around its top hangs a circle of blue sky, like a halo — the only blue sky left anywhere in the world.
She\'s in there.
Halfway up the shard there are tents. Dozens of people sit among them, waiting, every face turned toward the Spire like flowers toward a window.
So\'s everybody else, looks like.
Climb the shard to the Noon Spire and find a way inside.
The Noon Spire. The ground is warm. Around the top of the tower the sky is blue — the only blue sky left anywhere. Sable is inside. So are a lot of people\'s dead, they say.
_(down the rope)_ Supply line\'s open! Shout what you want and I\'ll lower it. Prices are Odessa\'s. I learned from the best.
Vesper Lift-Warden
Halt. The Spire receives no visitors. The gate will open when the Hierophant\'s work is done, and not one Bell sooner.
We\'re not visitors. We\'re the garbage. Every fortress has a back door, sparrow — usually it\'s where they take the garbage out.
The supply lift waits on its chain, a wooden cage stacked with crates of honey, linen and paper lanterns.
Ride the supply lift into the Spire.
Inside, the Spire is cool and white and full of clocks. Clocks on every wall, in every niche, ten thousand faces. Every one of them has stopped at noon.
Somebody really likes noon.
Under the silence, faint, from three directions at once: tick. Tick. Tick.
Three of them are still going. West, east, and up in the gallery.
And the big door at the end won\'t open. Let me guess.
To get to her, we stop the last three clocks. We help him stop time.
Find the three clocks that still tick (west wing, east wing, north-west gallery) and stop them at noon.
The Spire is full of clocks, all stopped at noon. Three are still ticking: west, east, and up in the gallery. To reach Sable, we have to stop them ourselves.
Both hands point straight up. The clock is silent.
A great clock, taller than Bram, its face painted with a summer sky. Its hands are moving — and as you watch, the painted sky dissolves, and the face becomes a window.
Stop the hands at noon?
Stop them
Not yet
You push the hands up until they meet. The clock stops. Somewhere far above, something settles, like a held breath getting easier to hold.
All three clocks are still. At the end of the nave, the seal on the dais stairs melts away like frost — and something on the dais stirs.
The dais is open. Approach the Noon Gate.
Young Cassian
Father! Lysa\'s still outside — she went to the bridge to see the fireworks, she\'s still *out there*—
Keeper Lorne
The Lantern first, Cassian. If the light fails tonight, the whole city goes dark.
Then let it! Let it go dark! She\'s *out there*!
One child. Or ten thousand. You will understand one day. I pray you never have to.
She isn\'t *one child*. She\'s *Lysa*.
The window goes dark. The clock ticks on.
His father chose the Lantern.
And Cassian\'s been choosing her ever since.
A younger man, already gray at the temples, at a desk heaped with music. Night outside. A single candle.
Forward, the Dawnsong calls the sun up. Backward...
Backward, it might hold it still. Just one afternoon. Just one.
He writes. Crosses it out. Writes again.
Forgive me, Father. I am going to save the wrong thing too.
He knew. Even then.
Knowing doesn\'t stop anybody. Believe me.
An old man at a reading-table, a letter in his hands. He reads it twice. He reads it a third time, smiling.
"Dear Hierophant. I\'m sorry to write again. Mom says I shouldn\'t bother you. But you said I could ask you anything, so: do you think a person can be more than one thing?"
"Ilse says the light always knows best. I think the light might not have met me yet. — Wren Halloway, Lanternfall. (The westernmost one.)"
_(softly)_ A restless heart. Like mine.
I\'m fine. I\'m okay.
You always say "okay" when you aren\'t.
On the dais, a figure of gold rises from its knees: a winged statue with a clock where its face should be. All twelve numerals are blank but one.
Don\'t tell me. It counts to twelve.
And then it\'s noon.
And then we\'re dead?
Don\'t be there at twelve. Got it. Excellent plan.
The Hour-Warden folds its wings over its blank face and is still. Behind it, the Noon Gate swings open on warm air, birdsong, and the smell of honey.
Pass through the Noon Gate into Evernoon.
We stopped the last three clocks. One of them showed me Cassian reading my letters. He smiled. I don\'t know what to do with that, so I\'m writing it down.
White. Then gold. Then — a city.
Aurenne. Not the ruin Ilse patched together in the Ember Ward — Aurenne whole, Aurenne young, on a summer afternoon with bunting on every line and the smell of honey-buns in the air.
Somewhere, a band is about to start playing. It has been about to start for forty years.
Everyone\'s smiling.
Everyone\'s *always* smiling. Look at \'em. Nobody\'s blinked since we walked in.
I don\'t like it. I don\'t like it, I don\'t like it, I don\'t like it.
Stay close. She\'s here somewhere.
If he rebuilt the day his sister disappeared... she\'d be at home. The Keeper\'s house — next to the Lantern.
Search Evernoon for Sable. (The Keeper\'s house stands in the north-east, beside the Lantern.)
Evernoon. It\'s beautiful. Everyone smiles and says the same thing over and over, forever. Pip hasn\'t stopped holding my sleeve.
A girl\'s room. Paper stars on the ceiling. A ribbon on the bedpost. Jars of festival flowers on every surface, none of them wilting.
At the vanity sits a girl in white and gold, brushing her black hair in long, slow strokes. In the mirror her face comes and goes, like a candle in a draft.
Dusk. Why doesn\'t it ever get dark?
Wren, you came. I asked them— I asked every—
Who are you? Are you Cassian\'s friends? He never brings friends home.
Sable, it\'s us. It\'s Ilse. I\'m the one who made you eat the soup.
The soup was warm.
Mama makes soup. I don\'t like soup. I like honey-buns.
She\'s slipping. Wren, she\'s *slipping*—
Don\'t wake her. She\'s sleeping so beautifully.
Hello again, little Keeper. I am so glad you came. She asked for you every day. Every day was the same day, of course. But she asked.
Let her go.
Go? Go *where*, child? Out there? To ash, and hunger, and a sky with seven holes in it? I have seen your world. I walked out of it.
In here, no one is hungry. No one is sick. Nobody in the Undercroft coughs blood into their hands. Every child has a honey-bun, and it is always warm.
And none of them ever grow up.
Why would they want to? You did. Look at you. Look what it cost.
Lady, I\'ve met a lot of people selling a lot of things. You\'re the first one selling *nothing* this hard.
Ring, bells. It is noon. It is always noon.
It doesn\'t... matter. He\'s coming. He\'s always coming. It\'s always...
Sister Mercy walks out into the festival, still smiling, into the brightest part of the light — and then she is not there anymore.
Someone is coming. My— his—
Cassian\'s home!
Sable, wait!
Follow Sable to the festival square.
By the fountain, where the water hangs glittering at the top of its arc, a tall man in white is holding a little girl\'s hand. Except the girl is sixteen. Except the girl is Sable.
You came. I hoped you would. You must be so tired.
Oh, Wren. Cassian. You always wrote "Your Grace" and then crossed it out. I could see it through the paper.
I am not going to fight you. I never wanted to fight anyone. I only wanted the afternoon to last.
Tonight the Lantern fails. My sister walks out onto the bridge to watch the fireworks, and the dark comes up off the river and takes her, and my father holds the light steady and lets it.
But tonight never comes. Not here. Here it is always the afternoon, and she is always ten, and she is always just upstairs.
And there is room. There is room for all of you. Every good day you ever had. Every face you ever lost.
Wren! Little bird — come here, you\'ve got ash in your hair.
There\'s my girl. Look how tall.
Ana Marrow
Ilse, sweetheart. Come and help me with the rosemary.
I don\'t— I don\'t even remember her voice. I was two.
That\'s not fair. That isn\'t *fair*, that he\'d know it and I wouldn\'t.
Sir Aldous
Bram, lad! There you are. Come and have an ale — your old knight\'s buying, for once.
Sir... you\'re not... you\'re not the Penitent.
Penitent? What have I got to be penitent about? Come here, boy. You did fine. You did *fine*.
Pipkin Tallow. You come here this instant and let me wash that face.
Corvin Ashe. You\'re late. You\'re *always* late.
No. No, no, no. Not you. Not *you*, Hal.
And you, Lysa. Mother is waiting. I am here. You never have to be cold again.
I was cold.
In the sea. Before I had a name. It was cold, and it was full, like a crowd.
Then Wren gave me a name.
A name for a coat. From a picture in a book.
Yes. It was the first thing anyone ever gave me.
Lysa was ten. Here she is always ten. She will be ten forever.
I am sixteen. I think. I would like to be seventeen.
And then eighteen. And then old, with white hair, like yours. I want to find out what I am like when I am old.
Lysa — you would *die*.
That is why the bread is warm.
The honey-buns here have been warm for forty years, and nobody eats them. Bread is only warm because it does not last.
She reaches up and unties the ribbon from her hair, and holds it out to him.
This is hers. I am not her.
My name is Sable.
The white and the gold drain out of the festival dress like light out of an evening sky. What is left is plain, and dark, and hers.
Please. I can\'t.
Then I will keep it. For her. Not as her.
Mom told me to grow up well.
I can\'t do that here.
Goodbye, Mom.
I\'ll remember your voice wrong for the rest of my life. That\'s *mine*. He doesn\'t get to fix it.
My knight died saving a coward. The coward\'s going to make it worth it.
So — no. Thank you. No.
Corvin\'s hand comes down on Pip\'s shoulder, and stays there.
Hal would\'ve shot you for this, Hierophant. I\'m thinking it over.
She was the key. A memory wearing a face, to open the door from the inside. Without her, I must open it from the outside: all seven pieces of the sun.
It will take longer. It will cost more. I am so sorry, Wren. I would have given you every good day there ever was.
I know. That is why it was a cage.
The dead stop mid-word. Their smiles stay where they are.
Across the square the honey-buns go cold. Every falling petal hits the ground at once. The bandleader says "and-a-THREE" — and the music, finally, horribly, begins, and tears like paper.
Uh. Sparrow? The sky\'s coming apart.
She was holding it together. Without her it\'s all—
Here. Your coat. I\'ve been carrying it for a year. Don\'t ask.
I will not ask. I will just wear it.
Thank you for my name. I would like to keep it.
It\'s yours. It was always yours.
Great. Lovely. Can we RUN now?
Escape! Back through the Noon Gate (south) and out of the Spire before Evernoon comes apart.

Sable chose her name. She gave Lysa\'s ribbon back and he couldn\'t take it, so she kept it — "for her, not as her." Cassian says he\'ll need all seven Shards now. Evernoon is coming apart. We\'re running.
Evernoon is unraveling. Where the sky was, there are seams of violet dark. The puppets stand frozen mid-sentence, and the Gloam is coming in through the gaps between their words.
The gate. South. The way you came in.
The two festival guards at the gate turn to face you. Their faces are gone. Behind them, where the gate was, the light is pouring out like water from a cracked jar.
Fellas. We were just leaving.
Gate\'s clear! Go, go, go!
The Spire shakes. Cracks of violet light run up through the white marble, and every one of the ten thousand clocks begins, all at once, to tick.
The lift! Back to the lift—
Lift shaft\'s full of light, kid. We\'d come out the bottom as a smell.
East side. Mags always comes round the east side; she says the light\'s better. There — that door\'s blown open. There\'ll be a balcony.
Reach the Sky Balcony on the east side of the Spire — Mags will bring the Halcyon.
The corridor is filling with things that were almost people — puppets with their strings cut, stitched together out of unfinished sentences.

On the balcony, the leftover pieces of Evernoon are pulling themselves together: every "lovely day," every "any moment now," every "ask me" that was never answered — knotted into one shape, the size of a house, with a hundred smiling mouths.
It is everything they never finished saying.
Then let\'s finish it for them.
Out of the bruised dark, engines howling, comes the Halcyon — listing, scorched, trailing smoke, and beautiful.
DID SOMEBODY ORDER A SHIP?
MAGS! You magnificent wrench!
I scratched the paint! I\'m putting it on your tab!
I don\'t *have* a tab anymore!
YOU DO NOW!
Everybody — jump!
Wren. I have never jumped before.
Me neither. Not like this.
Wren holds out her hand. Sable looks at it for a moment, as if it were bread. Then she takes it.
They jump.
For one long moment there is nothing under them at all —
— and then there is a deck, and Bram landing on Corvin, and Pip landing on Bram, and Ilse landing on her feet because of course she does.
Behind them the Noon Spire stands, white and untouched. The circle of blue sky at its top dims, slightly. Then it steadies.
The sky is the wrong color.
It\'s been the wrong color for a year.
I know. I like it. It is the color of _after_.
What was it like? In there?
Warm. All the time. Like a hand on your forehead when you are sick.
I do not want to be held like that. I want to be let go of. A little at a time.
Seven Shards. He\'s going after every piece of the sun.
Then we get there first.
All seven.
We got Sable back. She chose her own name, and then she jumped. Cassian is going after the seven Shards. So are we.

src/story/ch10_side.js: She has stopped mid-word, still smiling. Nothing behind the smile is moving anymore.
Old Bess
Oh! Oh, there it is. My Tomas always gets the mint in. Every time.
She drinks. Something in her face changes — the smile goes soft at the edges, the way a real smile does.
It\'s warm. Lemonade\'s never warm. How long have I been sitting here, dears?
Then I think I\'ll go home. My feet hurt. Isn\'t that wonderful? They haven\'t hurt in ever so long.
She stands up, and turns into a scatter of golden motes, and the motes drift up and away, and do not come down.
On the bench where she sat lies a charm on a faded ribbon.
Sit, sit. My Tomas will be back with the lemonade any moment.
How long has he been gone?
Any moment, dear. Any moment.
Any Moment Now
Old Bess on the river bench has been waiting forty years for Tomas to come back with the lemonade.
Any moment now. He knows I like it with mint.
Tomas has stopped mid-stride. Both cups are empty now.
Bess? ...Bess went home. Good. Good. Then so can I.
Two lemonades. Mint in one. I\'m going, I\'m going, I\'m nearly there.
Go on. She\'s on the bench by the river. She always is.
Two lemonades. Mint in one. I\'m going, I\'m going...
He is mid-stride, one foot lifted, a cup in each hand. He has been mid-stride for forty years.
They stand frozen on the bridge, his hand halfway to his pocket. The question will never be asked now.
Ask me.
Ask you what?
You know what.
Ask Me
Two lovers on the river bridge have been one question away from the rest of their lives for forty years.
He\'s got a ring in his coat. Left pocket. I can see the box from here.
He\'s been reaching for it for forty years.
Oh, for— *fine*.
Pip walks up behind Rafe and, with the deftness of a boy who has picked a thousand pockets, lifts the ring box from his coat and puts it *into* his hand.
He looks down at the box. He goes down on one knee — it creaks, forty years of creak — and he opens it.
Della. Will you—
Yes. Gods, *yes*. What took you so long?
They laugh, and hold each other, and are gone — two drifts of gold, rising together. On the bridge rail, something glints.
Smooth, kid.
Somebody had to. Adults are *useless*.

// Party members stand at their posts aboard, in whatever they
The Halcyon runs dark above the Ruin, every lamp shuttered,
until the Noon Spire is only a white needle far behind — and then not even that.
Right. Nobody\'s following us. Or they\'re following very politely.
Is it over? Tell me it\'s over. I want to lie down on something that isn\'t moving.
It isn\'t over. Three things. One: he let us leave. Two: he let us leave because he doesn\'t need us. Three—
Three: he needs the Shards.
He said it to me in the white room. "Then I will need all seven." He was not threatening. He was making a list.
Seven Shards. The sun broke into seven. So... they fell somewhere?
They fell home. Each one to its own Lantern. I can hear them. Like seven people humming in other rooms.
The Lanterns are ruins. The Keepers are—
Not all the way gone. Something is holding each Shard. What a Keeper was, wound around the light so tight it cannot let go.
Like the Penitent was Sir Aldous.
Yes. Remnants.
So Cassian sends his people to pry the Shards out of whatever\'s left of Tamsin. And Halvard. And Osk.
Or somebody gets there first. Somebody with a fast ship and a deeply irresponsible captain.
Off the stern, far out in the west, a single light burns on the edge of the dark.
Been there all year. Sailors call it the Widow\'s Lamp. Only Lantern in the world still burning.
One of the seven voices is there, Wren.
I know whose voice it is.
Not yet. We start somewhere else. Okay? Somewhere else.
And when we\'ve got all seven? What then?
Then we go to Evernoon and we— I don\'t know yet. Something better than what he\'s doing.
That is not a plan.
It\'s a Wren plan. They work out. Mostly. Eventually. With screaming.

Here\'s the actual plan. I fly. You lot do the heroic bits. Come find me at the helm when you\'ve picked a heading — and get some sleep first. All of you. That\'s an order from the only adult on this boat.
I\'m nineteen.
Like I said.
The Halcyon is your home in Act III. Talk to *Corvin* at the helm to fly anywhere in the Ruin. Rest in the bunks below decks, trade with *Mags* on deck, and save at the Hearthstone on the forecastle.
Your companions will have things to say between voyages — and some of them may ask something of you.
Recover the seven Sun Shards from the Remnants of the Keepers before Cassian does.

We got away from the Noon Spire. Cassian needs seven Sun Shards to finish Evernoon. Each one is held by what\'s left of a Keeper. We\'re going to get there first. (There\'s a light in the west. I\'m not ready.)
Pick a heading, sparrow. She\'ll get you there. Probably in one piece.
You\'re making Cassian nervous. I can tell. The sky\'s got that tight look.
The Ruin\'s big, and the Halcyon\'s small. I like those odds. Nobody can find us.
West, then. I\'ll take her in slow.
Where to?
Set a course
Fly into the Stormwall
Not yet
Behind me. All of you, behind me—
Please put the sword down, Bram. I\'m not really here. Neither, in a sense, are you. Nothing is anywhere very solid anymore.
Get off my boat.
Corvin. You look well. You look _sober_, which is new.
Wren. Three Shards. I felt each one go out, the way you feel a tooth come loose.
They were Keepers. They were stuck in the worst moment of their lives, and they were _hurting_.
Yes. And you ended them. In Evernoon they would have had their best day instead, every day, forever. I want you to understand the trade you are making on their behalf.
They didn\'t want your forever. Not one of them asked for it.
No one asks for the sun to rise either.
You are not trying to stop the world from hurting. You are trying to stop _you_ from hurting.
I am not Lysa.
No. I\'m told you were very clear about that.
The ward on the Grand Lantern has fallen, now that three of its sisters are dark. Garrick holds it. I would ask you not to hurt him. He has only ever done what I asked of him.
That\'s the whole problem with him.
And Wren.
The light in the west. You know whose hands it is in.
She has held it for a year so that you could reach the boat. Will you take that from her too?
Well. I hate him a completely normal amount.
Wren. Look at me. He says the true thing in the worst way on purpose. It\'s what he does.
I\'m okay.
You said "okay."
The *Grand Lantern* of Aurenne can now be reached from the helm.

Cassian came aboard — not really, a reflection made of Gloam. He says every Shard we take ends what\'s left of a Keeper. He says Mom has held the light for a year. The Grand Lantern is open. Garrick is waiting.
Six Shards hum together in the hold. Off the stern, the light in the west burns, steady as a held breath.
Six. The seventh is singing very quietly. I think it is trying not to wake someone.
I kept saying "not yet." Like if I didn\'t go, she\'d just... keep being there.
I know.
I\'m not ready, Ilse.
You don\'t have to be ready. You just have to go. You taught me that. I hated it.
Heading west, sparrow. I\'ll take her in slow.
*Lanternfall* can now be reached from the helm. Once the seventh Shard is taken, Evernoon will not wait long — finish anything you have left undone first.
Six Shards. The last one is at home, in Mom\'s Lantern. I told Corvin to head west. I\'m not ready. Ilse says that isn\'t the point.
For the first time in a year there is no light in the west.
In the hold, seven Shards lie together in a crate stuffed with Pip\'s spare socks. They are singing.
Far in the east, Evernoon burns white — a noon with no evening, waiting.
Seven. We actually did it. I want that on a plaque. "Pip Was Here, And Also Some Other People."
I\'d go on that plaque.
In small letters.
Wren. How are you?
Not okay.
But better than okay, kind of? Is that a thing? She said goodbye. I got to say it back. Most people don\'t.
It is a thing. I think it is most of what grown-ups are.
The light\'s still here. Look.
In Wren\'s open hand, a small warm light. It does not need a Lantern.
What do we do with them? The Shards. When we get there.
They want to be together. Cassian wants to make them into one moment. I do not think they want to be a moment.
Then we\'ll ask them what they want to be.
Evernoon whenever you\'re ready, sparrow. Not before. Come find me at the helm.
Seven Shards. The light in the west is out — it\'s in my hand now. Evernoon is waiting in the east. Corvin says we go when I say.
Evernoon. Last chance to turn around and become goat farmers.
Fly to Evernoon (there is no coming back)
Set a course elsewhere
Take your time. The end of the world\'s been waiting a year. It can wait an afternoon.
Everybody hold on to something that isn\'t me.
Three things. One: we come back. Two: we all come back. Three—
Three: if I die, you\'re telling my mother.
Too soon?
Way too soon. Three: you don\'t get to die. That\'s three.
For the record, I am terrified.
Me too. Is that allowed? I\'m doing it anyway.
I am also afraid. It is a very crowded feeling.
Corvin. Let\'s go end a perfect day.
We turned east. Everyone said they were scared. Everyone came anyway.
Enter Evernoon. Stop the Vespersong.
Sir Bram Kestrel. I keep saying it under my breath. Pip caught me. It was humiliating.
Garrick walked out of the Grand Lantern on his own feet. I let him. I think Aldous would have, too.
Sir Bram Kestrel. I keep saying it under my breath.
Garrick is at the Grand Lantern. I\'m still scared of him. That\'s alright. I\'m scared of lots of things. I go anyway now.
I beat him. Garrick. On my own, with my own hands, and they were shaking the whole time.
I think that\'s the trick. Nobody tells you your hands shake the whole time.
The Grand Lantern. Garrick. I\'ve been dreaming about his voice for a year.
Don\'t let me do anything stupid. Or do. I haven\'t decided.
I stand up here at the bow because it\'s the first place anything will hit us. Very knightly.
Also the wind is nice. Don\'t tell anyone the second part.
Scrapfall. Tilly. Corvin knows the way.
I\'m fine. I\'m fine. I\'m completely fine, stop looking at me like that.
Tamsin said "go be little." Like it\'s a thing you just do.
How do you do it? Do you just... sit there? Being little? I don\'t remember how.
I climbed the mast. Corvin said not to. That\'s how I knew it\'d be good up there.
You can see the whole Ruin. It looks like somebody dropped a plate.
I tied the ribbon in my hair. Then I untied it and tied it on my wrist. Then my hair again.
Ilse says this is called "fussing." I like fussing.
Elowen said the girl is waiting under her roots. In the Thornwood, past the crystal trees.
I want to go, Wren. I am frightened of her. I want to go anyway. Pip says that means it is important.
The voice in the west is singing very quietly now.
It is a lullaby, I think. I do not know the words. You might.
Your mother looked at me as if I were already someone.
Not Lysa. Not a Remembrance. Someone. I did not know a look could do that.
I watch the west because you will not, yet.
Someone should. It is a very lonely light.
I slept nine hours last night. Nine. Bram checked on me twice. He thought I was dead.
I\'m going to do it again tonight. Out of spite.
The infirmary in Mirefen. The east island, past the boardwalk. The red cord on the door.
I\'ll cut it myself.
I turned the galley into an infirmary. Corvin objected. Then he cut his hand on a sardine tin and stopped objecting.
Osk kept her patients alive for a year after they should have gone. I keep thinking about that. I keep thinking I\'d have done the same.
Eat something. That\'s not advice, that\'s a diagnosis.
Back again, duckling? Mags\'s Drift Market: everything here fell off something else.
Margery Pennywhistle, purveyor of things that fell off other things. Call me Mags. Your captain owes me money, so I tied my barge to his boat. Now he can\'t run off.
Best arrangement I\'ve had in years. Buy something. Help him pay me back.
Fine goods
Ship\'s stores
If it\'s broken, I can fix it. If it isn\'t broken, give me an hour.
Those Sun Shards in the hold run hot enough to forge a star. Bring me anything that needs a second life.
Nothing to forge on, though. The furnace wants something hotter than coal.
Nell. Engineer. Don\'t touch the red lever, don\'t touch the blue lever, don\'t touch the lever that isn\'t painted.
The Halcyon\'s held together with spite and copper wire. Mostly spite. Mine.
Six bunks, three hammocks, one of them Pip\'s. Someone has left a sock on every pillow, possibly as a system.
the Halcyon\'s bunks
The west is dark now. It is only the west.
The light in the west. Close enough now to see that it flickers, the way a hand trembles when it has held something too long.
Far out in the west, a single light. You look at it for exactly one second, then look somewhere else.

Saltglass. Used to be the hottest place in Solmere. Now it\'s the hottest place in the sky. Same sand, more falling.
Tamsin\'s up there.
She gave me my Crest. Way too early. She said, "I\'ll catch hell for this, little thief, and it\'ll be worth every minute."
Faintly, from the top of the glass steps: a choir, holding one note. It does not breathe. It does not stop.
Climb the Glass Steps to the Lantern of Saltglass.
The glass bell hums faintly, still remembering its hour.
A bright, clean note, like the first gull of the day.
A round, full note that hangs in the air and refuses to fall.
A low note that leans toward the west, the way a tired person leans on a door.
Strike the bell?
The bells clash. The whole garden shrieks like a struck window, and the choir in the glass answers.
Wrong order. The stone said "as the sun walks." So — where does the sun start?
Tamsin taught me that. "The sun walks, little thief. You only have to listen to where it\'s going."
She taught you about bells?
She taught me about everything. In about a week. Like she knew she didn\'t have long.
The glass wall is broken. Go up to the Lantern.
Before the dead Lantern stand three figures with their eyes bound in white cloth. One note pours out of them. It has been pouring out for a year.
Who walks in my Lantern?
I know those feet. Light on the heel, heavy on the toe, always ready to run. Little thief. You\'ve grown.
I gave you a Crest you weren\'t old enough to carry. I heard you grow up too fast, all the way from here. Every step.
I\'m fine. I\'m— I\'m _fine_.
Liar. You always were a lovely liar.
Stay. Sing with us. If you sing loud enough, you cannot hear the world end. I have not heard it once.
She is singing so she will not have to listen.
Tamsin— it already ended. We heard it. We\'re still here.
Then I will sing louder.
The note breaks. In the silence after it, the blindfolds slip, one by one, to the glass.
Ah. It\'s quiet. I had forgotten quiet.
Little thief. Come here.
Go be little a while longer. That is an order from a Keeper. It is the last one I have, so you had better obey it.
I don\'t— I don\'t know how anymore.
Nobody does. Practice.
You alright, kid?
No. Shut up. Yes. Give me a minute.
Take two.
Saltglass. Tamsin was a choir, singing so she wouldn\'t hear the end of the world. She told Pip to go be little. He didn\'t say anything for a long time after.
This is where he— the avalanche. Right up there.
We saw him go under. He was smiling.
Monks. Always smiling at the worst possible moment. It\'s the vow of silence. All the jokes back up.
He is still up there. He is very cold, and he is apologizing.
Climb Frosthollow\'s frozen terraces to the Lantern on the peak.
The brazier burns steadily. Somewhere below, meltwater runs.
A monastery brazier, packed with oil-black kindling that was never lit. Frost covers it like lace.
Light the brazier?
The snowbank beside the brazier stands up.
Allow me. Fire\'s the one thing I\'m reliably good at starting.
Heat rolls up the cliff. On the ramp above, the wall of ice sags, weeps, and slides away.
The way to the frozen lake is open. Keep climbing.
The way to the peak is open.
At the Lantern\'s foot, a monk kneels in the snow. Frost has grown over him like a second robe. He does not look up.
I should have said it on the first day. "This fork is wrong." Four words.
I waited to be certain. Certainty is a luxury for people with time.
Brother Halvard— you saved us. The avalanche. We\'d all be dead.
I buried a mountain on top of my own foolishness. That is not saving. That is _tidying_.
Kneel with me, young knight. Penance is warm, once you stop fighting the cold.
That isn\'t penance. That\'s freezing to death very slowly and calling it a virtue.
Nothing. I\'m fine. Let\'s get him up.
The ice splits down the middle with a sound like a held breath let go.
Ah. The young knight.
You carry the same frost, I think. Guilt keeps a man very still. Always looking back over his shoulder at the thing he did not do.
Look forward, boy. It is the only direction that thaws.
Look forward.
You alright?
There\'s a place near here. In the Greyspine. I... I\'ll tell you on the ship.
Frosthollow. Brother Halvard was kneeling in the snow, saying sorry for being too slow. He told Bram to look forward. Bram wants to tell us something.
Gloam-rot. I can smell it already.
Smells like a sock died.
That is exactly what it smells like. Don\'t touch anything. Don\'t touch _me_.
Someone is singing a lullaby. Very badly. Very tenderly.
Find a way through the rot to the Lantern of Mirefen.
Osk\'s herb-shed. The cauldron is cold. Bundles of bitterleaf hang like sleeping bats.
Osk\'s herb-shed: a cold cauldron, bundles of bitterleaf, and a dented brass censer hanging from a hook marked, in neat letters, FOR ROT.
Bitterleaf smoke. Mirefen healers burned it to keep the rot off the wards. It doesn\'t cure anything. It buys time.
Time\'s good.
Time is the only medicine there is. Everything else is a way of buying more of it.
Burn the rot-blooms off the boardwalks with Osk\'s Censer.
Gloam-rot blooms have grown across the boardwalk in a hedge of violet crystal. They pulse, slowly, like something breathing in its sleep.
Don\'t touch it. I mean it, Pip. There\'ll be something in Osk\'s herb-shed for this — every healer keeps rot-smoke.
Ilse lights the censer and swings it, low and steady, the way you would rock a cradle.
The blooms shriek as they shrivel — and the things nesting in them come boiling out.
The blooms curl and crumble to gray ash.
The Lantern of Mirefen lies ahead.
Something rises from the swamp before the Lantern: huge, swollen with black water, cradling shapes in its arms the way you hold a sick child.
Hush, hush. Mother\'s here. Nobody dies in Mirefen. Nobody. Not while I\'m awake.
Those are— Wren, those are _patients_.
Mender. Oh, thank the light. You have the hands. Help me. They need their medicine every hour, and the hours never end.
Since the sun broke. Someone must be.
I know.
I _know_, Wren. Let\'s let her sleep.
The black water runs out of her like a fever breaking. What is left is a small, stooped woman in a healer\'s hood, looking at her empty arms.
Oh. Oh, they\'re sleeping. Look at them. All of them, finally sleeping.
Thank you, child. I couldn\'t— a Mender can\'t be the one to stop. You understand.
I understand.
You have the look. Ward-tired. Listen to an old woman who got it wrong.
The sick will always be there tomorrow. _You_ must be there too. That means sleeping. That means wanting things. A healer who wants nothing has nothing left to heal with.
My staff is in the infirmary, on the east island. Red cord on the door. Take it. It never did me any good on a hook.
You should take it.
I\'ll think about it.

Mirefen. Mother Osk had kept her patients alive for a year after they should have gone. Ilse let her sleep. Osk left Ilse her staff, in the infirmary on the east island. Ilse says she\'ll think about it. (She wants it.)
This is where Elowen told us about Lysa. The trees were green then.
Is it me, or are the trees... sad?
It isn\'t you. They\'re dying. Trees do sad very well. They\'ve had practice.
Find a way through the thorns to the Lantern of Thornwood.
The statue\'s hands are closed now, around nothing, very gently.
A statue of a woman with leaves for hair, hands cupped in front of her. In her palms, a seed that glows like a coal and is not burning.
As you lift the Ember out, the statue\'s stone fingers close — slowly, slowly — around the space where it was.
Elowen left it for whoever came. I think she knew the thorns would grow.
Burn a path through the thorn walls with Elowen\'s Ember.
A wall of black thorns, each as long as a finger. As you reach toward it, the nearest thorns turn, very slightly, to follow your hand.
Nope. No. Absolutely not. There\'s got to be another way, or a very big knife.
The Ember flares in Wren\'s palm. The thorns remember fire, and draw back from it like a hand from a hot stove.
A fairy ring of glowing mushrooms. The old stories say: stand in it, and make a wish.
Stand back. I\'m doing it.
What did you wish for?
Don\'t tell him. If you tell, it doesn\'t come true.
It wasn\'t gonna come true anyway.
Then you may as well tell us.
Nice try.

In the Lantern court grows a flower the size of a house, petals the color of an old bruise. At its heart stands a tall woman with leaves for hair. The flower turns toward you, the way a face turns toward the sun.
Child. Lysa\'s face.
No. Not Lysa. You stand differently. Like someone who means to keep standing.
My name is Sable.
I knew a girl once who never got to choose a name for herself. She was ten. I have lived ten thousand summers in this wood, and I would give every one of them to give her one more.
Every flower fades. I would not. I drank the forest to stay in bloom. And now I am so very thirsty.
She\'s draining the whole wood.
She is doing what Cassian does. Holding on to summer with both hands. Let us help her let go.
The great flower folds in on itself, petal by petal, and what is left is a seed the size of a fist, and an old, old woman sitting very tired beside it.
There. That is how it is supposed to go. Bloom, fade, seed. I had forgotten the last part.
Sable. Lysa is not wholly gone. The Gloam keeps what is loved too hard to let go.
There is a hollow under my roots, past the crystal trees, where it gathers. If you would meet the girl whose face you wear, she waits there. She has been waiting a long time to give something away.
Give what away?
Ask her. It is hers to give.
Sable\'s Rite: The Girl Under the Roots
Elowen said Lysa waits in the hollow under Thornwood\'s roots, past the crystal trees in the north-west.
Thornwood. Elowen had drunk the whole forest to keep from fading. When she let go, she told Sable that Lysa is waiting under the roots. Sable wants to go. She\'s scared. She wants to go anyway.
A hollow under the roots of the oldest tree, full of a cold violet dark that moves like water.
This is the place.
Not yet. Something down there is asleep. We should not wake it for no reason.
Stormcrown. Vasha\'s lot used to fly drakes through this for fun.
For _fun_?
Very strange people. I liked them enormously. They fined me forty crowns once for flying drunk.
Were you drunk?
I was _celebrating_. There\'s a difference and I will die on that hill.
There\'s a — ward? Over the bridge to the top. Like a wall made of lightning.
Storm-ward. Vasha\'s riders grounded it with rods. Ground the rods, drop the ward.
Ground Skyreach\'s three lightning rods to drop the storm-ward.
The rod hums, earthed and quiet. Rain runs off it in a thin silver line.
A lightning rod of black iron, taller than Bram. Its grounding chain has snapped and lies coiled at its foot like a sleeping snake.
Reconnect the grounding chain?
The chain snaps taut — and the lightning comes down the rod, and something comes down with it.
Across the sky, the storm-ward over the crown bridge sputters, flickers, and goes out.
The storm-ward is down. Climb to the crown.
A woman in a rider\'s coat stands before the dead Lantern with her arms raised to the storm, and the storm comes down to her like a hound to a whistle.
HEAR ME! The Hierophant brings the endless noon! Give him your light, as I gave mine! I gave it— I gave mine—
I gave it to him. I gave it. I _gave_—
Ardent. You look terrible.
You ran from the Stormwall. Everyone saw the Kingfisher burn, and everyone saw you turn tail.
Later, kid.
The storm lets go of her all at once, and she sits down on the wet marble like someone who has been standing for a year.
I gave it to him. He held my hands and thanked me, and I have never been so certain of anything in my life.
So did I. I gave him ours. I took it out of my mother\'s Lantern with my own hands.
Then we are a pair of fools, girl. Better a fool who stops than a fool who keeps shouting.
Ashe. Hal Merrow\'s ship is still up there. In the Stormwall, where you left her. No one has dared fly the wall since.
Least of all me.
Least of all you.
Corvin\'s Rite: The Stormwall
The wreck of the Kingfisher is still inside the Stormwall. Corvin hasn\'t said he\'ll go. Ask him at the helm.
Corvin. Who\'s Hal?
Ask me at the helm sometime. When I\'ve had a drink. Or when I haven\'t. One of those.
Skyreach. Ardent Vasha gave Cassian her light because he asked so kindly. So did I. She told Corvin a ship called the Kingfisher is still inside the Stormwall. Corvin says ask him later.
Aurenne. The Cathedral\'s still standing. Mostly.
Garrick\'s in there.
I know. I can smell the boot polish from here.
Bram. Your hands.
Shaking. Yes. They do that. Ignore them, they\'re very dramatic.
Find a way into the Grand Lantern\'s tower.
Captain Brask
Go on. The Lord-Commander\'s at the top. He\'s always at the top.
Halt! Who goes— ...Kestrel? Squire Kestrel? The one who froze?
Yes. Hello, Captain Brask.
Ha! The Lord-Commander will laugh himself sick.
He never laughs. It\'s one of the worst things about him.
Dawnguard! Form up!
I\'ve polished this breastplate every morning for a year, because nobody told me to stop. Tell him I stopped.
Use the Commander\'s Seal on the lock-lever in the nave.
The lock-lever stands thrown. The choir-screen gate is open.
A Dawnguard lock-lever, chained to a signet plate. Without the Commander\'s Seal, it will not move.
The Commander\'s Seal fits the plate. The lever drops with a clang that rolls up the empty nave and out through the missing roof.
Climb the Grand Lantern. Garrick is waiting at the top.
The Grand Lantern\'s gallery. The Great Lamp is dark. A man in black plate stands before it, leaning on a greatsword, as if he has been waiting there a long time and could wait a long time more.
Kestrel. And the Halloway girl who rang the end of the world.
Don\'t look so wounded. I\'d have done the same at sixteen, if a saint asked me nicely.
Stand aside, Garrick.
There\'s no Dawnguard anymore. There\'s no _dawn_.
There will be a noon. Forever. Cassian will freeze this world, and frozen is better than broken. I have seen broken, boy. I\'m standing in it.
You don\'t believe in Evernoon.
I believe in holding a line. Somebody has to, while the rest of you have feelings about it.
Garrick goes down on one knee. His men do not get up. After a moment, he laughs, low and ugly.
Six against one. Aldous would be proud.
No. Venn would be _ashamed_. Face me alone, boy. Finish your knighting trial. The one you ran from.
Absolutely not.
If I don\'t, he\'s right about me. Forever. And I am so tired of forever, Wren.
Garrick: That blade. That\'s Venn\'s. Where did you—
Bram: Where we buried him.
Bram goes down hard. The gallery is very quiet.
Down again. Blood in his mouth. The floor is cold.
There it is. Stay down, Kestrel. You always do.
Stay. Down.
Bram gets up.
No. I— no. Again.
Garrick\'s greatsword rings across the marble and spins to a stop at the foot of the dark Lamp. Bram stands over him, breathing like a bellows. His sword hand is shaking so hard the blade chatters.
Well? Finish it. That\'s what knights do.
Knights stand between. That\'s all it ever was. Aldous didn\'t die for me because I was worth it. He died because that\'s what you _do_. You stand between.
I\'m not standing between you and anything. So I\'m done.
I\'m still afraid.
Then he was right after all. Damn him.
Above you, the Great Lamp cracks. From the heart of it, something falls into Garrick\'s cupped, empty hands: a piece of the sun.
Take it. I held the line. The line moved.
The tower\'s coming down! Everybody out — that includes you, Lord-Commander.
I\'ll walk. I\'ll not be carried out of my own Lantern by a squire.
Bram: Knight. Sir Bram Kestrel.
Garrick: Hm. And who dubbed you?
Bram: A deserter.
Garrick: Ha. Of course he did.
Bram: Then walk.

The Grand Lantern. Bram fought Garrick alone. He went down twice and got up twice. He didn\'t kill him. Garrick gave us the Shard and walked out on his own. Bram\'s hands didn\'t stop shaking for an hour. He says that\'s the trick.
Pressed between two volumes of liturgy: a child\'s drawing. Two stick figures under an enormous yellow sun. The tall one is labeled CASS. The small one is labeled ME.
Underneath, in a grown man\'s careful hand: _Lysa, age 7._
Everybody draws the sun too big when they\'re seven.

A Choir ledger. Columns of names from the Undercroft, each with a date and a single word beside it: _Offered._ At the foot of every page, the same initials, in the same careful hand as the drawing: C.L.
He knew. About Mercy. About the Undercroft. He signed every page.
He dismissed her in front of the whole city.
He\'s always very kind in front of people.

s compass, and told you to go.
That was not her. That was the island remembering her.
The whole island is doing it. Look. The square. The well.
The Lantern\'s still burning. Up on the bluff.
She\'s up there.
Then we walk up. Nobody\'s in a hurry, sparrow. Not here.
Walk through Lanternfall. The memories here are blocking the way to the Lantern.
Lanternfall. The dock hangs over nothing. The island is remembering things. It remembered Mom saying "come back to me." I did. A year late.
Up on the bluff, the light in the Lantern\'s doorway thins, like a held breath let out.
The Lantern is open. Climb the bluff.
The village well. WREN + ILSE + THE SEA. The W is backwards. It always was.
Little Ilse
You did the W backwards.
Little Wren
It\'s _stylish_. When I\'m famous everyone\'ll do their W\'s like this.
You\'re not going to be famous. You\'re going to be a Keeper like your mum.
I\'m going to sail to the end of the world and come back with a sea monster.
Obviously. Somebody has to carry the bandages.
We were seven.
I did come back with a sea monster. Sort of. Brinefang counts.
It doesn\'t count, you didn\'t bring it back.
The memory sours at the edges, the way milk turns — and the well vomits up black water, and the water has hands.
For the record, I still have the bandages.
Home. The east wall is gone; the sky looks in. Everything else is exactly where it was. Two plates on the table.
Because the last Halloway who sailed east never came back!
Your father would have gone _with_ you.
I left the table. I didn\'t even finish supper. That was the last supper we ever had, and I didn\'t finish it.
Outside, something is scratching at the door. Something that came up out of the sea on a stormy night, a long time ago, and never really left.
Two plates. She kept setting two plates. For seven years. Even after Dad.
No. Not for Dad. For me. One for her and one for me.
Your mother\'s herb garden. Rosemary gone to ash. Thyme gone to ash.
And the sea-lavender — the one that never flowered in all the years you knew it — is covered in small purple flowers.
Perhaps it was waiting for someone to come home and see.
The lamp room of Lanternfall. The light is everywhere — in the walls, in the floor, in the air like warm water.
At the heart of it, with her back to you and her hands lifted to the lamp, a woman in a Keeper\'s robe. Her braid has come undone. The light pours out of her hands and does not stop.
Wren. You\'re late for supper.
Come inside, little bird. It\'s getting dark. It\'s been getting dark for such a long time.
Mom, you can let go now. The boat got away. We made it. I made it. It\'s been a whole year.
If I let go, the dark comes in.
If I let go, you\'ll leave. You always wanted to leave. You used to toddle to the end of the dock and just _look_.
In Wren\'s pack, the little brass lantern her mother gave her flares, as if it has recognized someone.
Stay. I\'ll keep the light on. Nothing will take you. Not the sea. Not the Hierophant. Not _time_. You\'ll be sixteen forever, and I will never have to watch you go.
Wren. That is what he wants. That is Evernoon.
But it isn\'t her. My mom never once asked me to stay. Not even at the dock. She wanted to, I _saw_ her want to. She gave me Dad\'s compass and she let me go.
That\'s who you are, Mom. Not this. I\'m going to get you back to who you are.
Then I will make you stay.
The light gutters. The shadow that was wound around her peels away like wet paper, and burns, and is gone.
What is left is a tired woman kneeling on a stone floor, holding a lamp that is still, somehow, alight.
Oh. Look at you. You\'ve grown. You— your _hair_. You cut it yourself, didn\'t you. It\'s terrible.
_(laughing, and not laughing)_ Ilse did the back.
I did my best, Keeper. She wouldn\'t hold still.
She never would.
How long?
A year.
A year. I meant to hold it for a minute. Just until the boat was clear.
Something took hold of me afterwards. It kept saying, _not yet. Not yet. Keep her safe._ I think it was me. I\'m sorry. I think it was only ever me.
I\'m sorry. I\'m sorry I took the Dawnstone. I\'m sorry about what I said at supper. I\'m sorry I left. I\'m sorry I didn\'t come home sooner—
Wren. Little bird. Breathe.

I knew you would leave from the day you could walk. I wasn\'t angry that you wanted to go. I was angry that I was so afraid of it. Those aren\'t the same thing. It took me sixteen years and the end of the world to see it.
You went out after Dad. That night. I found your hand-lamp, tied to the Gull\'s Return.

I left the Lantern dark for two hours. The only two hours in two hundred years. I looked for him until the oil ran out. Then I rowed home, because you were asleep in the house, and someone had to keep the light on for you.
You never told me. I thought for seven years you didn\'t even try.
I know. I let you think it. It was easier to be the villain than to be the one who wasn\'t enough.
I always thought you could have saved Dad. I thought it for seven years.
I know you did. I tried, Wren. Some day you might find out how hard. Don\'t hate me for not telling you.
I never hated you. I was just— sixteen.
I remember sixteen. It\'s dreadful. I wouldn\'t do it twice for all the light in the world.
Ilse. You kept her alive. I can see you did.
Squire Kestrel. Late again.
Sorry, Keeper.
Don\'t be. You came.
And you have a name now, I think. A real one.
Sable. Wren gave it to me. I kept it.
Good. Keep it. Keep it the way you\'d keep a promise.
I\'m Pip. I\'m— a friend. Of hers. I steal things.
Then you\'re welcome in my house, Pip. Don\'t steal the spoons. They were my mother\'s.
Bring them home.
They\'re not mine to bring.
They are now.
Now. The light.
She holds out the lamp. Inside the brass, where the Dawnstone used to sleep, a piece of the broken sun.
A Keeper\'s light can\'t go out while the Keeper holds it. So I\'m going to stop holding it. And you\'re going to carry it instead.
I don\'t know how to be a Keeper. I never learned the Lantern. I left before you could teach me.
Oh, Wren. A Keeper isn\'t a lighthouse. A Keeper is someone who keeps a light going for the people still out in the dark. You\'ve been doing it all year. I watched.
Not here. Not this island. Wherever you go.
Wren carries the Lanternkeeper\'s light. The *Lanternkeeper* Crest can now be equipped.
There. Oh, that\'s better. My hands were so tired.
Mom. Don\'t—
I have to, little bird. That\'s the whole point. That\'s what I was too afraid to learn.
Grow up well, my little bird.
I\'m trying.
I know. I can tell.
And for the first time in a year, the Lantern of Lanternfall goes out.
For a moment there is nothing at all.
Then, in Wren\'s open hand, a small warm light. It does not need a Lantern.
She was terrible. She was the best.
Both. She was both.
Yeah. Both is allowed.

I said goodbye to Mom. A real one, this time. She said a Keeper is someone who keeps a light going for people out in the dark. Then she let go, and the Lantern went out, and the light was in my hand. Grow up well, she said. I\'m trying.
The Lantern log of Lanternfall, open on its stand, two hundred years of weather and oil in neat columns. One page is creased, as if it has been opened to many times.
_14th of Harvest. Keeper absent from the lamp, second bell to fourth. Keeper at sea in search of the fishing boat Gull\'s Return, lost with one aboard. — Y.H._
And below it, in a hand that is not quite steady: _Lamp relit at fourth bell. Wren asleep. Did not find him. Do not tell her._
