s hand goes to her pocket without her meaning it to. Dad\'s compass. It points west. It has always pointed west, wherever she was.
That\'s not right.
The needle swings, shivers, and points _down_ — through the deck, through the cloud, to somewhere south and west and very far below.
There are Shards in the hold now. Their light is very loud. Perhaps it woke something in the compass.

South-west and down. That\'s the Drowned Reef. When the sea fell upward, the sea floor came with it. Every ship that ever sank off the Westmost Isle is out there, hanging in the dark. Sailors don\'t go.
Dad\'s boat went down off Lanternfall.
Wren\'s Rite: The Drowned Light
Dad\'s compass is pointing at the Drowned Reef, where the old sea floor floats. The Gull\'s Return went down off Lanternfall.
The *Drowned Reef* can now be reached from the helm.
Dad\'s compass stopped pointing west. It\'s pointing down, at the Drowned Reef, where all the ships the sea ever took are floating now. His boat went down off Lanternfall.
The bottom of the Western Sea, hanging in the sky. Gray coral. Bones of fish the size of houses. Ships of every age lying on their sides in the sand, as if they had only lain down for a moment.
Fish bones. Big fish bones. Unreasonably big fish bones.
Wren. Are you alright?
The needle\'s pointing north. To the big wrecks. He\'s— it\'s up there.
Follow the compass across the Drowned Reef.
The Gull\'s Return, lying in the gray sand where the sea set her down.
A fishing boat lies on its side in the gray sand, its paint long gone. On the bow, under the barnacles, letters you have known your whole life: _GULL\'S RETURN._
It\'s his. It\'s Dad\'s boat.
He painted the name himself. He said the gull was me. Because I always came back.
Under the thwart, wrapped in oilskin the way he wrapped everything: his cutlass.
And lashed to the mast-step, tied with a knot only the Keepers of Lanternfall are taught — a small brass signal lamp.
That\'s Mom\'s. That\'s Mom\'s knot.
She was here. That night. She found the boat. She tied her lamp to it so if he was still in the water, he\'d see the light and swim to it.
She never told me. She told me the sea took him, and that was all. I thought she didn\'t even— I thought she just stayed in the Lantern.
Perhaps she did not want you to know she had been too late.
Or she didn\'t want you to know she\'d left the Lantern dark to do it. That\'s the one thing Keepers never do. Every sailor knows it.
She did it anyway.
The sky-water around the reef draws back all at once, the way the sea drew back on the night of the storm.
Something\'s coming up. Something big. Everyone behind me!
The Undertow sinks away into the dark below the reef, and does not come back.
Dad oiled this every Sunday. He\'d hate it rusty.
Nell can fix it. Nell can fix anything, if you don\'t mind the shouting.
Found the Gull\'s Return, Dad\'s cutlass, and Mom\'s hand-lamp tied to the mast. Take the cutlass to Nell\'s forge below decks on the Halcyon.
Take Edrin\'s Cutlass to Nell, below decks on the Halcyon.

We found the Gull\'s Return. Dad\'s cutlass was under the thwart. Mom\'s hand-lamp was tied to the mast with a Keeper\'s knot. She went out after him. She left the Lantern dark and went out after him, and she never told me.
Now that\'s a blade. Rust\'s only skin-deep. Whose was it?
My dad\'s. He was a fisherman. It was for cutting nets, mostly.
Then it\'s cut more knots than throats. Best kind of sword there is. Hand it here.
Sun Shard heat, Halcyon steel, and your old man\'s edge. It\'ll cut anything now. It\'ll still cut nets too, if you ask it nicely.
Nell reforged Dad\'s cutlass in Sun Shard fire. Edrin\'s Blade. It\'s light in my hand. I said hi to it. Nobody laughed.
Something comes out of the clouds, tumbling, and lands on the deck in a heap of sailcloth and string: a kite, painted with a lopsided sun.
That\'s one of ours. That\'s a Kiteholm kite.
Tied to the spar, a letter in crayon. Mostly capital letters.

_PIP. TILLY RAN OFF. SHE SAID SHE WAS GOING TO FIND THE LUCKY SHIV FROM YOUR STORY SO YOU WOULD NEVER LOSE AGAIN. SHE TOOK THE BIG KITE. SHE WENT DOWN TO SCRAPFALL. WE ARE SORRY. WE DIDNT STOP HER. — JUNIPER (AND EVERYONE)_
That idiot. That stupid, stupid little—
I MADE that story up. There\'s no Lucky Shiv. There\'s no Magpie King. I made it up so they\'d go to sleep!
Corvin. Scrapfall. Now.
Scrapfall it is.
Pip\'s Rite: The Lucky Shiv
Tilly, one of the Kiteholm kids, has flown down to Scrapfall to find the "Lucky Shiv" from one of Pip\'s bedtime stories.
*Scrapfall* can now be reached from the helm.
A kite landed on the deck. Tilly — one of Pip\'s kids — has gone to Scrapfall looking for a magic knife from a story Pip made up. Pip went very quiet and very grown-up. I don\'t like it.
Tilly\'s small, red hair, never shuts up. If you see a kite, that\'s her. If you see a giant bird, that\'s not her. Hit it.
Pip, she\'ll be alright—
You don\'t know that. Nobody knows that. That\'s the whole problem with everything.
Find Tilly somewhere on Scrapfall.
Tilly! Are you— what were you THINKING, you—
I found it! The Lucky Shiv! The Rook Queen had it in her nest and I stole it right out from under her, and she was SO mad—
The sky over Scrapfall goes dark with wings. Something enormous lands on the junk-heap, and every shiny thing on the island leans toward it.
Oh no, she\'s back.
The Rook Queen flaps away over the edge, shrieking, trailing buttons.
Do you know how dangerous— you could\'ve— there were BIRDS, Tilly, there were—
SO scary.
Yeah. Me too.
You get scared?
All the time. Don\'t tell anyone.
Here. It\'s the real one. I know it is. It was in the Queen\'s nest, and she\'s the best thief in the whole sky, so it has to be the best knife.
It is a kitchen knife. It is very rusty. Someone has wrapped the handle in a strip of red ribbon.
Come on, short stuff. We\'ll fly you home.
Can I fly my kite off the back of your ship?
Ask the captain.
You\'re the captain!
Then yes.
Found Tilly, and the "Lucky Shiv" — a rusty kitchen knife. Pip says it is the real one. Maybe Nell can help it look the part.
Take Tilly home. Show Nell the Lucky Shiv.
We found Tilly at Scrapfall with a rusty kitchen knife she\'d stolen from a giant bird. Pip started to shout at her and then he didn\'t. He asked if she was scared. He said he was too.
Off the stern of the Halcyon, a kite with a lopsided sun climbs into the bruised sky.
Pip holds the string. Tilly holds Pip\'s sleeve. Neither of them says anything for a long while.
It\'s as high as it goes!
Make it go HIGHER, you\'re the BEST at everything—
I\'m not the best at everything! I\'m twelve!
He says it like it is a surprise to him.
Let me try. I\'m nineteen. That\'s seven more years of kite.
You\'ll break it.
I will absolutely break it.
Pip and Tilly flew a kite off the stern. Bram broke it. Everyone laughed, including Pip. We dropped Tilly home at Kiteholm after.
This is a kitchen knife.
It\'s the Lucky Shiv.
It\'s a kitchen knife with rust on it and a hair ribbon round the handle.
It\'s the LUCKY SHIV. It was in the Rook Queen\'s nest. Stolen from the best.
Kept the ribbon. Didn\'t seem right to take it off.
Pip\'s Lucky Shiv. Stolen from the best.
Nell turned Tilly\'s rusty knife into Pip\'s Lucky Shiv. She kept the ribbon on. Pip says it was stolen from the best. He means Tilly.
Tilly says when she grows up she\'s going to be a sky-pirate. I told her it\'s a terrible job.
She asked if she could be one with me. I said only if she finishes growing up first. All the way. No skipping bits.
Halvard said look forward. I\'ve been trying. It\'s very hard to do on purpose.
There\'s a place in the Greyspine. The Vigil Hall. Squires stand the night there before they\'re knighted. You kneel on the stone until dawn. You don\'t move. You don\'t sleep.
That\'s where I froze. Something came out of the dark, and I froze, and Aldous stepped in front of it.
I want to go back. I want to stand the vigil. Properly. All night.
We\'ll come.
It\'s supposed to be alone.
It\'s supposed to be a lot of things. Most of them stupid.
And you\'ll need a knight to dub you, after. I might know one. Deserted. Disgraced. Technically never stripped of his spurs, because he ran before they could take them off him.
Don\'t make it weird.
Bram\'s Rite: The Vigil
Bram wants to stand the knight\'s vigil at the Vigil Hall in the Greyspine, where he froze on the night Sir Aldous died.
The *Vigil Hall* can now be reached from the helm.
Bram wants to go back to the Vigil Hall and stand the vigil he never finished. Corvin says he\'ll knight him after. Bram cried a bit. Corvin told him not to make it weird.
It looks smaller.
Places do that, I am told. When you come back to them bigger.
Kneel on the vigil stone in the Vigil Hall.
The vigil stone. Worn in two shallow dips where a great many knees have been.
Begin the vigil? (Bram will kneel until dawn.)
Bram kneels on the vigil stone. The torches burn down. The hall gets very cold, and very quiet.
Near midnight, the stone knights along the walls turn their heads.
Don\'t— don\'t move for me. I\'m fine. Keep them off, and I\'ll keep kneeling.
Still here.
The small hours. The cold gets into your teeth. The knights come again, slower, heavier, testing.
Still— still here.
The hour before dawn. At the far end of the hall the dark thickens, and gets up, and comes toward the stone. You knew it would. It was here the first time.
I know you. You\'re what I saw. You\'re the thing I froze in front of.
The Dread
_You will freeze again._
Probably! I\'m terrified! Look at my _hands_!
But I didn\'t come here to stop being scared. I came here to stay. That\'s all the vigil is. I finally get it. You don\'t have to be brave. You just have to _stay_.
And through the high windows of the Vigil Hall, gray and thin and absolutely ordinary: dawn. Or the nearest thing the broken sky still has to one.
Sir Aldous Venn. He stood between.
The Penitent carried a sword the Gloam made. The real one\'s here. We buried it with him.
Bram takes the greatsword from the cairn. It comes out of the stones easily, as if it has been waiting to be asked.
Kneel, you great lump.
By the authority vested in me by the Dawnguard, which is dead; and the sky-wing, which is ash; and by me, who is mostly sober—
Arise, Sir Bram Kestrel.
That was beautiful.
I\'ve been practicing in the mirror for eighteen years.
You were going to knight _yourself_?
Tell anyone and I\'ll leave you on a rock.
Bram stood the vigil. He shook the whole night and didn\'t move. At dawn he took Sir Aldous\'s sword from the cairn and Corvin knighted him. Sir Bram Kestrel. He keeps saying it under his breath.
Osk\'s staff.
It\'s stupid.
It\'s not stupid.
Three reasons it\'s stupid. One: I have a staff. Two: it\'s a dead woman\'s staff. Three—
Ilse. Do you want it?
Then that\'s one reason it isn\'t.
That isn\'t how lists work.
It is now.
Ilse\'s Rite: Small Mercies
Mother Osk left her staff to Ilse, in the drowned infirmary on Mirefen\'s east island. Ilse wants it. She has said so out loud.
Ilse wants Osk\'s staff. She said so. Out loud. With her mouth. I\'m writing it down in case she denies it later.
Ilse cuts the red cord herself. Inside: the smell of bitterleaf and old linen, and rows of beds, every one made with hospital corners.
She kept it so clean. A year with no one to see it, and she kept it so clean.
Find Osk\'s staff in the infirmary.
Osk\'s ward ledger. Every patient, every hour, every dose. The last forty pages are the same eleven names, over and over, and beside every one the same word: _comfortable._
She never wrote "died." Not once.
On a stand at the head of the ward: a healer\'s staff of black willow, worn pale where a hand held it. Tied to it with string, a card: _For whoever comes next. — O._
For whoever comes next.
Put that down.
The Matron
Mender. You don\'t get to _want_ things. You get to work. Who will change the dressings while you\'re off wanting things? Who will hold the line?
One Crest. One life. Yours is _this_. Every night, every ward, forever.
She sounds like you on a bad day.
Every day is a bad day, Wren. That\'s what a ward _is_.
Then let\'s have a better one.
The Matron comes apart like wet ash and settles on the clean floor. Ilse stands still for a long moment.
I want to study. Properly. In a real hospital with clean sheets and nobody bleeding on me before breakfast.
I want to sleep until noon. I want to grow lavender, badly, on a windowsill. I want—
Go on.
I want my best friend back. Not the one who rang the end of the world. Not the one I stitched up in the Ember Ward and wouldn\'t speak to. Just you. Stupid, too-honest you.
You never lost her. She just went somewhere really dumb for a while.
I forgave you, you know. A long time ago. I just never said it out loud, because I wanted to hold on to being angry a little longer. It was warm.
And now?
Now I want something else more.
She takes the staff from its stand.
The Staff of Small Mercies. That\'s what Osk called it, in the ledger. Because the big mercies were never hers to give. Only the small ones. Every scratch matters.

Ilse took Osk\'s staff. Before she did, she told me everything she wants. It was a long list. I was on it. She says she forgave me a long time ago and just liked being angry. That\'s the most Ilse thing anyone has ever said.
Alright. Alright. Everybody who isn\'t strapped to something, strap yourself to something.
The Stormwall is a cliff of black cloud a hundred miles high, lit from inside. The Halcyon goes into it like a moth into a lamp.
Captain! Starboard prop\'s taking water! We lose it in this and we _drop_!
I know. Hold her together, Nell.
With _what_?
Spite. You\'ve got loads.
Off the stern rail, the lifeboat swings on its davits. It would be the easiest thing in the world.
Eighteen years ago I got in the lifeboat.
Hal was my captain. Hal Merrow. The Kingfisher, Dawnguard sky-wing. I would have followed her into the sun, and she told me to get in the boat, so I got in the boat.
Everybody tells it like I ran. I let them. It was easier than saying she sent me away.
Why\'d she send you away?
Never found out. Never came back up to ask.
Something vast moves in the cloud below the hull — and rises, and opens a mouth full of lightning.
Not now, you overgrown weather—! Wren! Get them off my deck!
You\'re not coming?
I\'m staying at the helm. Somebody has to.
The Squall King tears away into the storm, shrieking. And then — all at once — quiet.
The eye. A bowl of still air, a mile wide, with a pale sky at the top of it. And hanging in the middle of the stillness: a broken gunship, her colors still flying.
Corvin flew into the Stormwall and stayed at the helm. The wreck of the Kingfisher hangs in the eye of the storm.
The Kingfisher. Gunship, Dawnguard sky-wing. Fastest thing in the air, for about a week, eighteen years ago.
There are people at the guns.
Yeah. There would be. Hal never let anyone leave a post.
Except me.
Reach Captain Hal\'s cabin at the Kingfisher\'s stern.
The gunners turn from their guns, very slowly. Their coats are Dawnguard blue. Their faces are rain.
Stand down, lads. Battle\'s over. It\'s been over a long time.
They do not stand down.
Rest easy. All of you. I\'ll tell her you held.
Hal\'s cabin. The chart table, the bunk, the empty peg where a coat used to hang.
Not yet. The lads at the guns first. They were always first.
Hal Merrow\'s cabin. The door is gone; the chart table is bolted down, and on it, held flat under a brass weight, the ship\'s log.
"Kingfisher. Last entry. Starboard engine gone, fire in the magazine."
"Sent Ashe to the boat. He\'ll hate me for it. He\'ll think I didn\'t trust him to stay."
"It\'s the opposite, you great idiot. Somebody has to live long enough to be brave about something else. Go and be brave about something else, Corvin. — H."
Corvin, are you crying?
It\'s raining, Pip.
It stopped raining.
It\'s raining on me specifically.
On the bunk, wrapped in a sky-wing flag: a long silver pistol with a star set into the grip.
The Star. Hal\'s. She called it that because stars are the only lights in the sky that don\'t need anybody to keep them.
Named my ship after her. Now the gun after the ship. I\'m not a very imaginative man.
I think it\'s lovely.
Something else to be brave about. Huh.
Turns out it\'s you lot.
Right. That\'s enough feelings for one decade. Everybody back on the ship.

Corvin flew into the Stormwall and didn\'t get in the lifeboat. Hal Merrow\'s last log said she sent him away so he\'d live to be brave about something else. He says it turns out to be us. He said it was raining on him specifically.
It is cold here. It is like being inside a closed eye.
Stay close. All of you. I don\'t like how quiet it is.
It is not quiet. Listen.
Follow the echoes to the bottom of the Gloam Rift.
_Cass? Cass, the lamp\'s gone out. It\'s so dark._
That is her voice. My voice. Hers.
_Don\'t let go of my hand. Don\'t let go. Cass, you\'re hurting—_
He was holding on very tightly.
_FATHER! Father, Lysa\'s still out there! Leave the lamp! FATHER!_
That is him. He was twelve.
_...Cass? I can\'t see you. It\'s alright. I\'ll wait. I\'m good at waiting._
She has been waiting for forty years.
A bedroom, made of memory. A small bed. A shelf of wooden animals. A girl of ten in a white dress, sitting on the end of the bed swinging her feet.
Oh! You have my face.
Yes. I am sorry. I did not choose it.
It looks good on you. You\'re older. I always wanted to be older.
I am sixteen. Or I appear so.
I was going to be sixteen. I had plans. I was going to be a sky-pilot. And a baker. Both.
Both is allowed. I am learning that.
Is Cass sad?
Yes. Very. He is trying to bring you back. He has built a whole noon for you to live in.
I know. I can hear him. He sings all the time. It\'s very loud. It\'s always the same song.
Will you tell him something for me?
Tell him I\'m not in the noon. I\'m not anywhere. I\'m just a memory he\'s holding too tight. Memories don\'t grow up. People do.
And tell him he was a good brother. Tell him the lamp going out wasn\'t his fault. He always thinks everything\'s his fault.
I will tell him.
Lysa pulls the ribbon out of her hair and holds it out.
Here. For you. Not because you\'re me. Because I want somebody to wear it somewhere I never got to go.
Will you get old? Properly old? With wrinkles and everything?
I would like that very much.
Good. Do it for both of us.
The dark at the edges of the room thickens. Everything the Gloam has ever kept, every forgotten thing, leaning in — wanting one thing more.
_You are made of us. Come home. Be no one again._
No. I have a name. And now I have a present. You cannot have either.
I am keeping it. Not as Lysa. As someone who was given a present.
It suits you.
I know. I have decided to be a little vain about it. Pip says it is good for me.

Under Thornwood\'s roots we met Lysa — what\'s left of her. She gave Sable her ribbon and asked her to get old, properly old, for both of them. She gave her a message for Cassian. Sable says she\'ll deliver it.
Visitors! Mind the brass. Don\'t mind the biscuits. Take two, they\'re mostly raisins.
On the old woman\'s desk, under the biscuit tin, a brass nameplate: OTTOLINE MARSH, ASTRONOMER.
Ottoline Marsh— you wrote _The Sunward Atlas_!
Somebody READ it? Ha! That\'s both my readers in one week!
Cassian gave me a copy. Before— everything.
When the sun broke, the stars came loose too. Only little ones. Starfall. They fell where the light was strongest — into the Lantern ruins, mostly, and the old sea floor.
I\'m rebuilding my chart of the sky so I can see what\'s coming. I need the fragments. Seven, if my sums are right, and they usually are, except when they aren\'t.
Bring me what you find. I have a great many things I don\'t need, and one thing I\'d very much like to give to the right person.
The Drowned Stars
Ottoline Marsh needs seven Starfall Fragments — splinters of starlight that fell into the Lantern ruins and the Drowned Reef.
Look at that sky. Seven little lights where there were none. I\'ll name one after you. Something dignified. "Wren\'s Embarrassment."
It\'s still falling, you know. The one that didn\'t land. The telescope will show you, if you\'ve the nerve.
No starfall yet? Try the old Lanterns. Stars always did like a lighthouse.
And something for your trouble. Don\'t argue. I\'m old, I\'m allowed.
Ottoline sets the last fragment into the great brass orrery. Seven small lights wink on across the dome, and the whole observatory hums like a held note.
There. The drowned stars, back where they belong. Or near enough.
You can\'t put the old sun back, you know. Nobody can. Not the Hierophant, not a hundred Keepers.
But stars are only suns that are very far away. Perhaps the trick isn\'t to mend the big one. Perhaps it\'s to make a small one, close by, that belongs to everybody.
It\'s only a theory. I\'ve written it in the margins of my own book. Nobody reads the margins.
Now. The thing I wanted to give to the right person. It isn\'t a thing. It\'s a way of looking.
Read the sky. Bend fate a little, when it needs bending. Never more than a little. It sulks.
How fast?
Tonight-ish. Look through the telescope if you\'re feeling brave. Or foolish. They\'re the same muscle.

Ottoline Marsh finished her map of the drowned stars and taught us to read them. She says you can\'t mend the old sun — but maybe you can make a small one, close by, that belongs to everybody. I can\'t stop thinking about it.
Through the great glass: seven small lights, and the dark between them, which is not as empty as it looks.
Through the great glass: cloud, cloud, and the faint hum of something very far away. Ottoline\'s chart has gaps in it.
Through the great glass: one star, much brighter than the rest, getting brighter.
Keep watching?
It is not getting brighter. It is getting _closer_.
Well! I\'ll be updating the chapter on falling stars. It\'ll be mostly exclamation marks.
Have these spectacles. Mine. They make you notice things. Dreadful habit, noticing.
src/story/ch12.js: The Noon Spire. The greatest shard of the broken sun, hanging over the abyss where the sea used to be.
At its crown, behind a wall of white stone, it is still the afternoon of a summer festival.
It has been for a year. It has been for forty.
Halcyon\'s tied off. If this goes sideways, she\'ll drift home on her own. I taught her that. Mostly by doing it myself.
Real comforting, Cap.
Wasn\'t meant to be.
Three things. One: we have seven Shards and no idea what they do when you put them together. Two: Cassian wants them. Three: we are carrying them straight to him.
Four: he\'s waiting for us either way. Better we walk in than he comes out.
That is either very brave or very stupid. In my experience they are frequently neighbors.
I was in there. Inside. In her dress.
It was warm. Everyone was kind. Nobody was ever going to get older.
I did not like it. I liked it very much. Both.
Okay. Okay. The last time I walked toward Cassian, I handed him the end of the world.
In Wren\'s satchel, the seven Shards begin to hum. The same note, over and over, like a held breath.
Well. That\'s not ominous at all.
Cross the shard to the golden gate of Evernoon.
We reached the Noon Spire. Behind the gate it\'s still Cassian\'s summer afternoon. The Shards are humming. I\'m not scared. (I\'m scared.)
The arch is sealed with light: a single moment, hung across the gap like a curtain.
It\'s... a note. Held. Like the Lanterns used to hold the Dawnsong.
It is the Vespersong. The first note. He never let it finish.
Then let\'s give it something to listen to.
Wren opens the satchel. The seven Shards rise out of it on their own — and turn — and sing back.
Then they settle back into the satchel, warm as hands.
You brought them. All seven. I knew you would — you always finish what you start. It\'s one of my favorite things about you.
Cassian. Where are you?
At the top, where I always am. Come in. It\'s a lovely afternoon.
It always is.
That\'s the trick, kid. That\'s always been the trick.
Enter Evernoon through the golden gate.
The Shards opened the gate by themselves. Cassian said it\'s a lovely afternoon. It always is.
Brother Anselm
Oh! Real people. With shadows. I\'d almost forgotten what those looked like.
I was an acolyte. His acolyte. When he started singing the Dawnsong backwards, I walked out.
You can do that, you know. Walk out. Nobody ever tells you.
You\'re... a Remembrance?
Half of one. I\'m fading at the edges. Out here, past the wall, things are allowed to end. It\'s rather restful.
Take this. He gave it to me the day I was Kindled. It keeps the last toll from finding you.

When this is done... can I still be on the crew? Even if I\'m, like, twelve? Just twelve? Doing twelve stuff?
Pip. You can be twelve as long as you want.
Don\'t tell Corvin I said any of this. He\'ll do the hair-ruffle thing.
Watch is mine tonight. Strange feeling, staying put. I could get used to it.
Pull up a crate, sparrow. The good crate. I\'ve been saving it.
Want to know something funny? Every bone in my body\'s been telling me to run since the desert. Loud. Persistent. Very good arguments.
And I keep not listening. Twelve years I listened to nothing but that voice. Turns out it\'s a lot less convincing when there\'s somebody to stay for.
You owed Cassian your life. You said so once.
Pulled me out of a burning barracks when I was nineteen. Never asked for anything back.
Until he asked for everything. Funny how that goes.
You kids went and made me into somebody\'s — I don\'t know. Uncle. Bad uncle. The one who teaches you cards and gets you tipsy at weddings.
You\'re not our uncle.
Go on. Get some rest. I\'ll keep watch. Somebody has to, and I\'ve finally got the knack of it.

/** Remember everyone
The top of the Grand Lantern. There is no roof. There is only the sky — white, enormous — and in the middle of it, the sun.
Not whole. Seven-tenths of it, cracked like an eggshell, held perfectly still by a song nobody can hear anymore.
Beneath it, on the steps of a marble throne, a man in white sits with his hands folded, waiting. He has been waiting a long time. He does not seem to mind.
Face Cassian at the Noon Throne.
Wren. You came all the way up. I\'m so glad.
And Sable. You look well. Taller, I think.
Half an inch.
_(smiling)_ So you have.
Did you meet him? Down there? The boy?
He said to tell you he\'s sorry he was eating honeycake.
For one moment, the Hierophant\'s face does something complicated. Then it smooths over, like water.
It wasn\'t anyone\'s. That\'s the worst part. It wasn\'t anyone\'s fault, and it happened anyway.
Yes. That is the worst part. That is exactly why it must never happen again.

Give me the Shards, Wren. All seven. I can finish the Vespersong. The sun will stop — not shatter, this time; I know where I went wrong — and it will be noon forever, and no one will ever lose anyone again.
Your mother. Your father. Sir Aldous, Bram, whole and laughing. Every child in Kiteholm fed and warm and never one day older than they want to be.
And never better. Never different. Never anything.
Is different so precious? Look what different has done to all of you.
Made us, mostly.
You pulled me out of a fire once, Cassian. I owed you everything. Still do.
Answer\'s still no.
What they said. But ruder.
We came here to put the sun back. Not to stop it.
Then I\'m afraid I\'ll have to take them.
He doesn\'t raise his voice. He never has. He simply opens his hands, and all the light on the throne leans toward him, like flowers toward a window.
Cassian goes down on one knee. His robes are scorched. His face is perfectly calm.
You\'ve grown so strong. All of you. I\'m proud of you. Truly.
But you\'ve misunderstood something, Wren. I never needed you to give them to me.
I only needed you to bring them here.
The satchel at Wren\'s hip tears open. The seven Shards rise out of reach — and fly to him.
And the broken sun overhead, the one he has held still for a year, comes down to meet them.
When you can see again, there is no man on the throne. There is a king made of noon.
_(from everywhere at once, gentle as ever)_ There. Isn\'t it beautiful?
Everyone up. Everyone UP.
Something warm moves through you — the Lanternkeeper\'s light, answering the sun. Your wounds close.
The King comes apart. Shards spin out of it like sparks from a struck anvil — and stop. Hang in the air. Everything stops.
The light goes white.
Wren! The sun\'s been up for an hour!
There you are. I was starting to think the gulls had carried you off.
The house smells of salt and woodsmoke and the sea lavender that never flowers. Two plates on the table.
Who else would it be? Tomorrow you stand in the Lantern\'s light. You could at least do it with your eyes open.
Tomorrow. The Kindling. I\'m sixteen tomorrow. I\'m sixteen tomorrow.
Chores first. Tobias needs his net. Then you can go and gawk at the harbor with everyone else — the Hierophant\'s ship comes in today.
She\'s real, Wren. As real as anything is. I kept everything — every word she ever said to you, every look. Memory is all any of us is made of, in the end.
Stay. It\'s the day before your Kindling. Your mother is alive. Nana Brisa is stewing kelp. Bram is at the inn telling lies about a spoon.
Nobody has fought. Nobody has left. Nobody ever will. Tomorrow never has to come.
Wren? You\'ve gone pale. Sit. I\'ll put the kettle on.
It would be so easy. It would be the easiest thing in the world.
Wake up.
Cassian: "Stay, Wren."
Stay. Here. Forever. With her.
Stay. Forever.
Ysolde: "Wren?"
Of course you\'ll stay, little bird. Where else would you go?
Mom. I have to go.
Go? Go where? It\'s the day before your Kindling, you can\'t—
I know. I know what day it is. It was a good day. It was one of the best days.
But tomorrow I stood in the light. And the day after that I left. And the day after that I did something terrible, and then I kept going.
If I stay here, none of that happened. And I don\'t get to not have done it, Mom. I don\'t get to not have become... whoever this is.
For a moment it isn\'t Cassian\'s memory of her. It is just her.
Go on, then. Before I change my mind.
I love you. I never said it enough. I was too busy being angry.
I knew. Little bird, I always knew.
Grow up well.
The Kindling-eve festival. Lanterns strung between the houses. Nana Brisa\'s kelp stew. Tobias telling the one about the eel again.
—and THEN I said, "Not today, Gloam-beast!"
You fought it with a spoon, Bram.
Can I have more honeycake? Can I? I\'m eleven, I\'m growing.
Kid, you\'ve had six.
Bread is warm. I did not know food could be warm.
Sable says it the way she said it the very first time. Exactly the way.
Cass, can we stay up for the lanterns?
We can stay up forever.
Happy Kindling Eve, little bird.
Happy Kindling Eve, Mom.
And then it was morning.
Tomorrow never came. Nobody minded. Nobody ever would.
It was beautiful. It was the most beautiful day in the world.
It was the only one.
THE END?
The throne. The Shards hang in the air where the King came apart, turning slowly, like the hands of a clock.
On the steps, a man in scorched white robes kneels where the King fell. Smaller than you remember. Grayer.
_(barely a whisper)_ You said no.
To her. To her face. How could you— I couldn\'t. I never could. Not once in forty years.
I know. That\'s why you built all this.
Overhead, the hanging Shards begin to tick.
No. No — wait — I\'m not singing it. I\'ve stopped. I\'ve stopped! I\'m not—
It does not need you anymore. Listen.
Tick. Tick. Tick. Every clock in Evernoon, all at once. The Vespersong has been sung so long it has learned to sing itself.
The Shards lock together into a face. A clock with a sun for a dial and no numbers at all. Only noon, and noon, and noon.
Oh, I REALLY don\'t like that.
Cassian. What is that.
Then we\'re done going back.
Everyone — with me. One more time.
Something warm moves in Wren\'s chest — her mother\'s light, her own now — and runs through all six of them like a struck chord.
Vesper stops.
Not the way Evernoon stopped. The way a clock stops when it is finally, finally allowed to rest.
The seven Shards drift down into the middle of the throne room. Warm. Dim. Waiting.
Now. Put it back — put the sun back together!
The Shards rise. They turn. They try to fit, edge to edge, the way they were.
They don\'t fit.
Wren... it doesn\'t go. The edges have changed. They\'ve been out in the world too long.
It remembers being a sun. Remembering is not the same as being.
So that\'s it? We broke the world, and the pieces don\'t— that\'s IT?
No. No no no, I did not climb all those stairs for "that\'s it"—
The Dawnsong called the old sun home. The Vespersong tried to make it stay.
Neither of them is ours.
We sing something new.
I cannot sing. I want that on record. I have been asked to stop by three separate choirs.
Sing anyway.

Wren starts. She doesn\'t know the song — nobody does; it hasn\'t been written yet. She sings the tide coming in at Lanternfall, and the smell of Nana Brisa\'s kitchen, and the sound her mother made when she laughed.
Ilse comes in under her, careful and exact — the hum she makes when she\'s stitching a wound.
Then Bram — terribly, loudly, completely off-key — and he does not stop.
Pip, with a gutter-song from Aurenne whose words are definitely not for children.
Corvin, an old Dawnguard marching tune, slowed down until it sounds like a lullaby.
And Sable, who has no song of her own — so she sings all of theirs back to them, a little wrong, and entirely hers.
The seven Shards melt together. Not into the old sun. Into something smaller, and stranger, and the color of no light any of them has ever seen.
It rises.
Evernoon is coming apart around them — gently, like frost in the morning. Marble turning to light. Bunting turning to birds.
Overhead there is a dawn. Not gold. A color nobody has a name for yet.
She walked toward it because she was scared of it. I never told anyone that. I never told anyone anything true about her. Only that she was gone.
And the Hierophant of Solmere, who has not raised his voice in forty years, puts his face in his hands and weeps like a boy of twelve.
Sable crosses the throne room and kneels beside him. After a moment, she takes his hand.
Sable. Wren gave it to me. Because of my hair.
It suits you.
Will you— I\'m sorry. I\'m so sorry. Will you stay? Just until—
Cassian. This is hers. It was always hers.
He opens it to the flyleaf. _For Lysa, who wants to know where the sun goes._
He is fading at the edges, the way the city is. He doesn\'t seem to mind. He is looking up at the new dawn the way a child looks at a kite.
Wren. What will you call it?
_(smiling)_ Restless heart. Like hers.
When the light cleared, Sable\'s hand was empty. She kept it closed anyway, for a long while.
He was smiling. Or crying. I think both.
That\'s usually how it goes.
We didn\'t put the old sun back. We couldn\'t. We sang a new one instead. Cassian cried, finally. Sable held his hand until there was nothing left to hold.
_Two summers later._

_The sun we made is smaller than the old one. It rises a little late and sets a little early, and it\'s the wrong color, and the sea came back wrong too — shallower, warmer, full of fish nobody has names for._
_We\'re getting used to it. That\'s the thing about the world. It lets you get used to it._
Mind the beam! — and the other beam! — that\'s a different beam, Hesk!
_Aurenne is rebuilding. Not the City of Bells. Fewer bells. More windows._
The Crestless Sage
Step up, child. No — don\'t close your eyes. That was the old way.
Well? What does the light say?
It says... Ranger? I think?
And what do *you* say?
Then be all three. Badly at first. That\'s how everyone starts.
_One Crest, one life, they used to say. Nobody says it anymore. The children don\'t even know it was ever a saying._
re holding a bird — firm enough it can\'t fly off, soft enough you don\'t hurt it.
Sir Bram, were you ever scared?
Lesson two: yes.
Lesson three: you will be scared too. Every time. That\'s allowed. That\'s not a crack in you. That\'s just what brave feels like from the inside.
What\'s lesson four?
Lesson four: do it anyway. And if you can\'t — run, and come back tomorrow, and try again. That\'s brave too. Nobody tells you that one.
Are you scared of US?
Constantly. You lot are terrifying. Again! From the top!
Pip! Pip, you\'re IT!
I\'m not playing. I\'m thirteen. I\'m practically a—
PIP\'S IT! PIP\'S IT!
_He played for three hours. He lost every round. He has never, in his whole life, been so happy to lose._
_Later he flew a red kite over the rooftops, string wrapped twice round his wrist. It came down when he wanted it to. He says that\'s the best part._
_And then I went to see Ilse._
_Ilse runs the Ember Hospital now. It has windows. Forty-two of them. She counted._
Doctor Marrow! The burns in bed three—
Salve, clean linen, and tell him that if he picks at it again I will tie his hands to the bedposts. Kindly.
Hold still, Sable.
Ilse lays a pencil flat on Sable\'s head and marks the doorframe. There are a lot of marks on that doorframe. They go up.
A quarter.
Since spring.
_(quietly delighted)_ I am going to be enormous.
Wren. Look. I found a gray hair. One. Corvin says it is from worrying about Pip.
Are you worried about Pip?
Constantly. It is wonderful.
Three things. One: I\'m taking tomorrow off.
You have never taken a day off in your life.
Two: I\'m not telling anyone where I\'m going. Three—
That\'s it. That\'s the list. Isn\'t it wonderful?
I\'m learning the fiddle. I\'m appalling. The patients have petitioned for me to stop.
I\'m not going to stop.
_I didn\'t tell Ilse I was leaving. She knew anyway. She always knows._
You\'re going, aren\'t you.
No. That\'s a lie. It isn\'t good, it\'s awful, and I\'m happy for you, and I\'ll be on that dock, and I\'ll cry, and if you tell anyone I\'ll put salt in your bandages.
_Lanternfall came back down with the sea. Not all of it. Enough._
_We rebuilt the house. We rebuilt the Lantern — smaller. It doesn\'t call the sun anymore. It just lights the way home._
Hi, Mom.
I\'m going. Tomorrow. I wanted to tell you first.
East. All the way east. Somebody has to find out what the new sun does when it gets there.
_The wind came up off the sea. It smelled of salt and lavender._
_The sea lavender in Mom\'s old garden flowered that spring. First time ever. I\'ve decided to take that personally._
Make way, make way — Captain Ashe and the Halcyon Irregulars, here to see off a Halloway—
Dad, is that her? Is that the Lanternkeeper?
_Corvin froze. Every time one of them calls him that, he freezes, like a man who\'s been handed something precious and is terrified he\'ll drop it._
Twenty-one kids, one ship, no money. Best odds I ever played, sparrow.
He cried at the last Kindling. In front of EVERYBODY.
To what?
Have you got everything? Rope? Biscuits? A spare compass? I bought you a spare compass—
Bram, I have Dad\'s.
It points WEST. You are going EAST. That is the opposite of helpful!
That\'s the point. It\'ll always show me the way home.
Bring me something back. From the far side. Anything. A rock.
A rock?
A rock from somewhere I have never been. I will keep it until I am old.
_Ilse didn\'t say anything. She just held on, hard, the way she did when we were six._
Every week.
Every day.
Every. Day.
_I left the island the next morning. The thing I\'d wanted since I was nine._
_I thought it would feel like escaping. It didn\'t. It felt like being sent._
_Behind me, the little Lantern on the bluff came on, though it was morning. Somebody — I know exactly who — was holding the light._
_The world ended on the day I came of age._
_This is what we built after._
The Afterlight has risen. The world — and the Gloam beneath it — is still out there.
The world ended on the day I came of age. This is what we built after.
Thank you for playing. Save your clear data — the journey continues aboard the Halcyon.
Continue aboard the Halcyon

Run? Fight? Both. Both is good.
Black hair! Lieutenant! LIEUTENANT, IT\'S HER—
He has a very carrying voice. Somebody stop his voice.
You there! Lanternfall accent. Show me your hands. All of you.
We\'re fishmongers! Very... tall fishmongers.
Port Gale. More people on one street than live on all of Lanternfall.
Masts stand in the harbor like a winter forest, gulls argue on every roof, and somewhere a bell is ringing for something nobody here has time to stop for.
Solid ground. Blessed, unmoving, non-serpent-infested ground.
You can let go of the rail now, Bram.
I am _saluting_ the rail. It served with honor.
The ground is still moving.
That\'s your legs. They\'ll stop in an hour.
I would like them to stop now.
Tobias — you\'re not staying? Not even one night?
Tide turns within the hour. Miss it, and your mother sends a search party. And if she sends one, she leads it.
She gave me a message for you, once you\'d made it across. Word for word, she said.
What did she say?
"Eat something green once a week."
Then she stood on the dock a long while, not saying the rest of it. I expect you can fill that part in yourself.
Here. For the road. Don\'t tell her I\'m paying you in medicine again.
Mind yourselves, the lot of you. Big lad — you mind _them_.
With my life, sir. With my— yes. Absolutely. Minding.
Goodbye, Tobias. Thank you for the boat. And for not letting the snake eat us.
Ha! That was mostly you lot. ...Strange girl. Good girl.
The little boat slips out past the breakwater, its sail like a folded letter, and turns west for home.
West. Always west. Dad\'s compass agrees with her.

They don\'t leave Aurenne. Not for bandits. Not for wars. Not for anything.

How does he know she came ashore on Lanternfall? It\'s been four days. Nobody\'s crossed the strait but us.
Gulls? Gossip? Lanternfall gossip could cross an ocean.
Sable, hold still.
Ilse unwinds the green shawl from her own shoulders and wraps it over Sable\'s head, tucking every black strand away with quick, exact fingers.

t know who you are and I don\'t want to. Down behind the barrels. Not a word.
Innkeeper. A girl, sixteen, black hair, pale. Possibly traveling with others. Possibly frightened.
Lieutenant, every girl in this town is sixteen, frightened and traveling with others. Usually sailors. Usually my fault.
There is a reward.
There\'s always a reward. You lot never say what the girl did.
Unharmed. Well. That\'s more than the last lot of you said about anybody.
Search the cellar.
Mind the third barrel, son. That\'s the bad cider. It\'s been bad since the Kindling of eleven-ten. It\'s _waiting_ for someone.
Then we ride for the coast road at first light. Good day, Mistress Salt.
You can breathe now. Quietly. I charge extra for loud breathing.
Why did you help us?
I ran rum past the Dawnguard for twenty years, pet. Habits.
And when tin-cans come asking after a frightened girl and won\'t say what she did — she didn\'t do anything. That\'s what that means.
Keep the shawl on, love. Rooms upstairs. Nobody\'s paying tonight. Tomorrow you\'re paying double.
Bram hasn\'t said a word in an hour. Is that a record? We should write it down.
Bram. You know them. Thorne\'s Own.
Sir Aldous was dead on the sand and I was standing there with my sword in my hand, not moving. Thorne walked over. Looked at me like I was something on his boot.
"Send the coward to the edge of the world," he said. "Somewhere he can\'t get anyone else killed."
So. Lanternfall.
If Thorne sent his own guard all the way out here, it isn\'t for smugglers. It\'s for her. And he doesn\'t send them to _ask_.
Then I should go a different way. Alone. You would be safer.
Absolutely not.
Not a chance. They\'ll have to go through me.
I do not understand. But thank you.
Wren. Is that what a friend is? People who stand in front of you, but argue about the order?
Pretty much exactly that.
That night, Wren lies awake listening to the harbor bells.
They ring the hours differently here. Rounder. As if the mainland has more time to spare.
Morning, my little fugitives. Your tin-cans rode out along the coast road at dawn. Shops are open again. Town\'s yours.
If you\'re for the Whisperwold — and you are, I can see it on you — mind the trees. Don\'t answer them.
Explore Port Gale, then take the coast road east toward the Whisperwold.

An innkeeper named Mags hid us from Thorne\'s Own. Bram told us about his trial — Garrick Thorne called him a coward and sent him to Lanternfall. The soldiers said Sable is to be brought to Aurenne "unharmed".
Your mother danced like she was trying to stamp the pier into the sea.
Then she went home and became the most serious woman on the Westmost Isle. People do that. They have one good night and then they guard it.
Halloway, did you say? Red hair, Lanternfall accent... You\'re Edrin\'s girl.
You knew my dad?
Sold him that compass on your belt. Off this very pier, twenty years back. He haggled me down to nothing and then paid full price anyway, because he felt bad. Daft man. I liked him.
He brought a girl over from the island, that summer. Braid down to here. Never said two words to me.
Danced till dawn on the pier, the pair of them, to a fiddler who only knew one song. Then she went home and never came back across.
Carved their letters in the mooring post at the end of the long pier. Go and see, if you don\'t believe an old net-mender.
Old Osric sold Dad his compass, twenty years ago, on the Port Gale pier. He says Mom came across once — and danced till dawn. Mom.
Letters carved deep into a mooring post, worn soft by twenty years of salt: *E.H. + Y.*
E.H.... Somebody was happy here, once.
E.H. + Y. She never told me. She never told me _anything_.
Edrin Halloway. And Y. She came here. She stood right here.
All those years telling me there was nothing out here worth leaving for...
Admiral\'s asleep in the herring crate. He\'ll be there till spring.
Your friend in the shawl comes by to pet him. He lets her. He doesn\'t let _me_.
Ginger. Fat. One ear that points at heaven. Answers to "Admiral", in the sense that he doesn\'t.
He likes dark places near fish. This whole town is a dark place near fish. Good luck.
Fresh cod! Fresh-ish haddock! Oh — sorry, love, you don\'t look like you\'re buying. You look like you\'re looking.
If you\'re looking anyway — my cat\'s gone. The Admiral. Big ginger tom. Ran off when those soldiers started kicking over my crates.
A cat. A real cat?
Well, he\'s mostly real. About a third of him is herring I\'ve paid for.
Wren. We have to find the cat.
We\'re fugitives in a strange city, Sable.
Yes. And so is the cat.
Admiral Whiskers
Bettany\'s ginger tom fled when the soldiers searched the fish market. Somewhere dark, near fish...
Behind the barrel: a dent in the dust the exact shape of a smug cat.
Two green eyes glare at you from the dark behind the barrel. Something hisses. You decide it is none of your business.
Behind the barrel, wedged into a gap no cat should fit, is a great deal of ginger cat. One ear points at heaven.
Here, Admiral. Here, puss. Nice puss. Come out and— OW.
Let me.
Sable kneels and holds out a hand, very still. The Admiral considers her for a long, long moment — then flows out of the gap and into her arms like poured honey.
He is warm. He is... vibrating. Wren, is he broken?
That\'s purring. It means he likes you.
Please don\'t.
Found him behind the barrels. Return the Admiral to Bettany at the fish market.
ADMIRAL! You fat orange traitor! Come here— no, he\'s gone straight back to her. Of course he has.
He says he would like to stay with me.
He says that to everyone with a lap, love. Here — for your trouble. And take a bit of smoked eel. No, take it. It\'s good for the hair.
That feather\'s from the old gull that used to fight the Admiral for scraps. Lucky, they say. Never once got poisoned, that gull.
Goodbye, Admiral. I will think about you when it rains.
We found Bettany\'s cat. Sable held him for ten minutes. She says she would like to purr. Ilse says please don\'t.
Slept twelve hours, last night. First time in six years.
I\'m going to sell the _Merry Widow_. Jory always hated that name. Said it was tempting fate.
Turns out fate doesn\'t need tempting. It comes anyway. Better to be asleep when it does.
If you hear him in there — Jory — you\'ll know. He laughs like a seal choking on a herring.
Tell him the lamp\'s still lit.
Mind the lamp, pet. Don\'t knock it. It\'s been burning six years and I\'ll not have it go out because of a stranger\'s elbow.
Six years? Why?
My little brother Jory took our boat out past the Gale rocks, six years ago this winter. Squall came down off the cliffs. Boat came back. Jory didn\'t.
Sailors keep a lamp in the window so the lost can find the harbor. So I keep it. Every night. Trim the wick, fill the oil. Six years.
Then you know. You know the worst part isn\'t that they\'re gone. It\'s that nobody told you _they were done_.
You\'re headed for the Whisperwold. Everyone headed east is. They say the trees there talk in the voices of the dead.
I\'m too old and too frightened to go and listen. But if you hear a man who laughs like a seal choking on a herring — tell him his sister kept the lamp lit.
The Lamp in the Window
Odile has kept a lamp lit for six years for her drowned brother, Jory. If his voice is among the Whisperwold\'s trees, she wants to know.
You\'ve been to the wold. People come back from that forest looking like they\'ve been listening too hard.
We heard him. Jory. By the black pond.
He asked if the lamp was still lit. He said— he said the knot was his fault. That you should sell the boat. That you should sleep.
The knot. Six years I\'ve been sure I tied that bowline wrong. Six years.
Stupid boy. Stupid, lovely boy. Always had to have the last word.
Odile leans over the lamp. For a moment she only looks at it. Then she blows it out.
There. He\'s home. He doesn\'t need it.
This was his. He wore it for luck, the daft thing, and left it on the hook the day he needed it most. Take it. It still owes somebody some luck.
The voices in the trees. They were not cruel. They were only... unfinished.
Then you finished one. That\'s more than most of us manage.
We gave Odile her brother\'s message. She blew out the lamp after six years. I keep thinking about what she said: the worst part is nobody tells you they\'re done.
Look at it. The whole coast. Cliffs, and the sea all silver, and the road just... going.
I could walk this road for a year.
Three things. One: you\'ve walked it for ten seconds. Two: the soldiers went this way. Three: you\'re doing the face.
What face?
The atlas face.
The wind is very loud here. It sounds like a lot of people far away.
That\'s just the Gale. It howls. Nothing to worry about. Probably. I have never been told otherwise.
Follow the Gale Coast Road east toward the Whisperwold.

s the only bridge over the gorge for miles. We can\'t go around by the hills, not with the river in flood.
There\'s smoke up on the cliff, back the way we came. Somebody lives up there. Maybe they know another way across.
Thorne\'s Own hold the bridge. Find another way across the gorge — someone is camped on the cliffs nearby.
Hah! Visitors! Real ones, not gulls. Sit, sit — no, not on Agatha, she\'s a log. Sit on Bartholomew.
Also a log. I name the logs. You\'d name the logs too, after twenty years up here.
Hesketh. I kept the Gull Light, down there on the point. Oil lamp, not a proper Lantern — no Dawnstone, no Kindling. Just a big lamp to keep ships off the Teeth.
It\'s dark now.
Twenty years dark. My Marit used to climb the stairs with me. Hundred and twelve stairs. Then she couldn\'t. Then I couldn\'t, without her.
Ships stopped coming this way anyhow. Dawnguard built their road. Now it\'s me and the gulls and the logs. Fish stew?
Yes. Is it warm?
It\'s _hot_, girl. It\'s stew.
The stew is mostly fish and partly mystery. It is the best thing any of you have eaten in a week.
So. A Dawnguard boy, a herb-girl, a redhead with a sword she\'s still getting used to, and a girl with black hair in a green shawl. Coming up the coast the morning after Thorne\'s dogs.
Don\'t look so worried. I hate soldiers. They turned back a tinker yesterday for having a dark-haired daughter. Made the child cry. Nasty business.
They\'re holding the bridge.
They\'re holding _a_ bridge. There\'s the goat path. Down the cliff by my woodpile, along the cove at low tide, under the bridge where the river meets the sea, and up the far side.
Rockfall\'s choked the top of it. But I\'ve a lever and twenty years of spite. Give me a moment.
There. Mind the tide.
Thank you. Really. I— can I ask you something?
Asking\'s free. Answers cost a log-name.
What was your Crest? At your Kindling?
Warden. Shield-and-stand-fast. Said so right there on my hand.
Since then I\'ve been a lamp-keeper, a fisherman, a husband, a widower, a cook and a namer of logs. Not one of those was on my hand.
The light tells you what you are at sixteen, girl. It doesn\'t tell you what you\'ll _do_ about it.
One more thing. Down on the cove there\'s three stone cairns, west of the goat path. Marit\'s things are under the third one, farthest west. Her ring. I buried it the year she went.
She\'d hate it in the dark. Take it. Somebody should wear it in the light.
Marit\'s Ring
Hesketh buried his late wife\'s ring under the third cairn on the cove, west of the goat path. He wants someone to wear it in the light.
The party rests by Hesketh\'s fire and is fully restored.
Take the goat path down the cliff, cross the cove under the bridge, and climb back up to the road.
A hermit named Hesketh, who used to keep the Gull Light, fed us stew and showed us a goat path around the soldiers. He says the light tells you what you are — not what you\'ll do about it.
Back again? Sit by the fire a while. Agatha\'s free.
Rest by Hesketh\'s fire?
The party is fully restored.
That\'s her ring. On your hand. ...It looks right in the light. Thank you.
The third cairn, carefully rebuilt. A gull is sitting on top of it as if it has been asked to.
A cairn of sea-smoothed stones, stacked with care. Someone built this to last.
You lift the stones one by one. Beneath them, wrapped in oilcloth gone stiff with salt: a plain silver ring.
Inside the band, worn nearly smooth: _Keep the light._
We rebuild the cairn. Properly. He\'ll look.
Yeah. Okay. Properly.
The Gull Light: a stubby tower of whitewashed stone, streaked with twenty years of gulls.
The lamp room is dark. Through the salt-fogged glass you can make out a great brass lamp, its wick trimmed and waiting.
He said he cannot climb the stairs. But someone trims the wick.

t. They\'ll start talking again.
Reeve Alder
Travelers! From the _west_? Through the wold? Nobody comes through the wold. The wold doesn\'t let them.
It let us. Eventually. We had a talk with it.
Well! Well. Welcome to Thistledown. Wilma Alder, Reeve. You\'ve picked a fine week to visit, if you enjoy being robbed.
Red Tam and his gang have shut the Aurenne road. Nothing in, nothing out. They\'re squatting in the old quarry north of the east fields and taxing anything with wheels.
We\'re bound for Aurenne.
So was the miller\'s flour. So were Tobble\'s honey-jars. Tam has all of it now.
It is cold again. My Crest.
A Crest? At her age? Oh, you\'ll want Old Bethan for that. The cottage up the hill, past the beehives. She knows Crests better than any priest.
The Choir threw her out for it, mind. Called her a heretic. _We_ call her "the Crestless Sage", on account of she\'s got about six of the things.
Six Crests. That isn\'t possible.
I\'d not say that to her face, dear. She boxes.
Visit the Crestless Sage in the cottage on the hill, north-east of Thistledown\'s green.
Thistledown: sunlight, cows, beehives, and a bandit called Red Tam squatting on the Aurenne road. There\'s a woman here they call the Crestless Sage — the Reeve says she has six Crests.
Door was open, so you came in. That\'s either brave or rude. Sit. Both is fine.
Are you— the Reeve said you\'re the Crestless Sage?
The Choir called me that. "The Crestless." Meant it as an insult, the dear things. Name\'s Bethan.
Crestless. Ha.
She holds out her hands. Across the backs of them, faded and overlapping like the rings a cup leaves on a table: five Crests.
That— that\'s not possible. One Crest, one life.
Mender at sixteen. Arcanist at twenty-two, when I got bored of bandages. Ranger at thirty. Cantor at forty, to annoy a bishop.
And Pugilist at sixty-one, because a man in Aurenne told me I was too old to learn anything.
Pugilist. At sixty-one.
He was wrong. I showed him how wrong. Twice.
But _how_?
The Lantern doesn\'t _give_ you a Crest, girl. It _finds_ one. It looks into you and picks out the loudest thing — whatever\'s ready. That\'s all a Kindling is. A first draft.
"One Crest, one life" is a lie. A comfortable one. It keeps farmers farming and soldiers soldiering, and nobody asking awkward questions in the Cathedral.
_(quietly)_ The light knew I\'d be a Mender. I always knew I would be.
Course you did, herb-girl. That\'s your loudest thing. Doesn\'t mean it\'s your _only_ thing.
And you. Come here, child. Give me that hand.
Sixty years I\'ve been reading Crests. I\'ve never seen this one. Never read of it, neither — and I\'ve read everything the Choir ever tried to burn.
Is it bad?
It\'s _yours_. That\'s all a Crest ever is. ...Cold, though. Like a hand that\'s been in the sea.
Whatever made this made it carefully. Mind that.
Right. Lesson. Do you want to learn to braid your Crests, or not?
Is it legal?
Then show me what you\'ve got. Outside. I\'ll go easy.
On us?
On my hip.
Ha! Not bad. Not bad at all. You hit like a Dawnguard squire. Which one of you\'s the Dawnguard squire? ...Ah. That explains a great deal.
Up you get. No shame losing to an old woman. I\'ve had sixty years\' more practice at being difficult.
Did you watch? Every few breaths I was something different. Mender. Arcanist. Pugilist. Same old woman. Different _tools_.
Now hold out your hands. All of you. No, the Dawnguard boy too. Don\'t sulk.
She presses her thumb to each Crest in turn and hums a note so low you feel it in your teeth.
Your Crest grows warm. Then, for an instant, it feels like a door you never noticed — standing open.
The art of the *Braided Calling* is learned! Crests can now be changed freely, and advanced *Braided* Crests can be earned.
Here\'s how it works. I\'ll say it once, because I\'m old and you\'re young and one of us has to save breath.
Your *Primary* Crest is what you are today. It shapes your body — strength, speed, how much light can pour through you — and which weapons sit right in your hand.
Your *Secondary* Crest is what you\'re learning on the side. You can use its Arts in a fight, but it won\'t change your bones.
Every Crest grows on its own as you fight with it. Each rank teaches you an Art — or a *Support*. A habit. A knack.

And here\'s the bit the Choir hates: a Support you\'ve learned is yours forever. Learn to counter as a Pugilist and you\'ll still counter as a Mender. Your *Support Points* decide how many knacks you can carry.
Raise two Crests to rank five and they\'ll braid into something new. I won\'t spoil it. Experiment.
And a gift. Cantor — the singer\'s Crest. Songs that steady the heart. I learned it at forty to annoy that bishop. It\'ll suit at least one of you.
Pedrick at the trading post sells Crest Stones — bits of old Lantern-glass that remember a calling. Dear. Worth it.
Bethan... why did the Choir really throw you out?
I taught a boy, once. In Aurenne. A Keeper\'s son. Clever, sad thing — he\'d lost someone young, and couldn\'t bear to be helpless ever again.
He learned every Crest I could give him, and wanted more. The Choir said I\'d made a monster. I said I\'d made a boy who could _do_ things.
What happened to him?
He grew up. That\'s what happens to boys. Mostly.
Now. You\'ll want the Aurenne road, and that fool Tam\'s sitting on it. He used to steal my apples when he was eight. He was bad at it then, too.
His lads watch the quarry track. But there\'s an herb path behind the hedge at the far east end of the fields — up the hill to the quarry\'s back door. I\'ve used it forty years.
Tam doesn\'t know it\'s there, because Tam has never once in his life picked an herb. I\'ll have Corporal Fen pull the hedge back for you.
Take the Sage\'s herb path (behind the hedge at the east end of the fields) up to Red Tam\'s quarry.

Bethan, the Crestless Sage, has FIVE Crests. She says "one Crest, one life" is a lie, and taught us to braid our Crests. She once taught a Keeper\'s son who lost someone young. She wonders if she made a monster.
Told you Tam was bad at it.
Go on to Aurenne. And when somebody in a fine robe tells you what you are — you remember an old woman with five Crests and a bad hip.
Back already? Pedrick sells Crest Stones. Try a few on. Wear them like hats.
Herb path\'s behind the hedge at the east end of the fields. Mind Tam\'s archers.
Ask Bethan for another sparring match?
Ow. Good. Again tomorrow.
Better. Not good. Better.
Farmer Dunstan
Fields are quiet. Crows are back. I\'ve never been so glad to see crows.
Stuffing \'em with honest straw from now on. Honest straw never walked anywhere.
Don\'t go in the fields. I mean it. Not the north field, not the south field, not the field I haven\'t named yet.
Why not?
Scarecrows. _My_ scarecrows. They\'ve started... walking. At night, first. Now in the day, which is worse, because I can see them doing it.
Bought new stuffing for \'em off some lads on the road. Two silver a sack. Purple, it was. Glittery. Swore it\'d keep the crows off for good.
Like the crystal in the tide caves. The cold one.
Three of \'em out there. If you\'re the fighting sort — and you\'ve the look — knock \'em down for me. Leave Old Strawman for last; he was my granddad\'s, and he\'s _big_.
The Hollow Harvest
Farmer Dunstan\'s scarecrows have come alive after he stuffed them with cheap purple "stuffing". Put down the three in the east fields — Old Strawman last.
A scarecrow in a battered hat. Its button eyes seem to follow you. That\'s just a thing people say about scarecrows.\n...Isn\'t it?
This one is bigger. Older. Its stitched head is turned toward the other scarecrows, as if it is waiting to see what happens to them.
Old Strawman\'s head turns. Its friends are gone, and it has noticed.
The scarecrow\'s head turns. Slowly. Its stitched mouth splits into a grin full of violet dust.
There was a voice in the straw. Very small. It said "shoo." Over and over. "Shoo."
All three scarecrows are down. Tell Farmer Dunstan his fields are safe.
All three? Even Old Strawman? ...Granddad would\'ve hated that. He\'d also have hated a walking scarecrow, so. Swings and roundabouts.
Here. Take one of the horseshoes off the door. I\'ve three. Clearly they weren\'t working.
Dunstan — the lads who sold you that stuffing. Where did they say it came from?
Didn\'t say. Didn\'t have to. They came down the quarry track with it. Tam\'s lot, the thieving—
So whatever\'s in that quarry, it\'s the same thing that was in the tide caves.
The scarecrows in Thistledown were stuffed with purple dust — like the crystal in the tide caves. Tam\'s gang sold it. Whatever is in that quarry, it\'s the same thing.
Oi! Quarry\'s closed. Toll\'s your boots, your purse and your dignity.
And the archer on the ridge says the rest. Back, Wren.
Not this way. Somebody in Thistledown must know another way up.
Right. Bethan\'s herb path. Behind the hedge, east end of the fields.
A dense hawthorn hedge. Someone has woven it tight here, on purpose. You can smell rosemary and mint behind it.
—I\'m _telling_ you, it\'s "the red sky weeps."
"Weeps" was last week. This week it\'s "the red sky sleeps."
Why\'d he change it?
\'Cause you told your mum, Nib.
She _asked_!
Your mum sent us.
"The red sky sleeps." Remember that. Or I will. I\'ll remember it for you.
Big Hollis
Halt. Password.
Nib and Gorse were arguing about this. Sleeps, not weeps.
"The red sky weeps."
"The red sky sleeps."
"Tam is a genius."
Right you are. Go on, then. ...Here, I don\'t know your faces—
We\'re new.
Oh! Welcome! Mind the archers, they\'re twitchy. Hearth\'s warm up top.
WRONG. That\'s _last_ week\'s. Lads!
Well, well, _well_. Somebody got past Hollis. Somebody always gets past Hollis.
Let\'s see. A Dawnguard squire. A hedge-witch. A redheaded fishwife with a sword she don\'t know how to hold. And—
—and _there_ she is. Black hair. Pale as milk.
Sweetheart, you are worth more silver than this whole valley.
She\'s not for sale.
Everything\'s for sale, girl. That\'s the first thing the road teaches you. The second thing is: duck.
You\'ll have to go through me.
That\'s the plan, big lad. That\'s _exactly_ the plan.
Alright! Alright. Yield. I yield. Mercy. Uncle. All the good words.
Who\'s buying? You said she was worth silver. Whose silver?
Rode up the Aurenne road a fortnight back. Paid in good Aurenne silver for my lads to watch the road for a black-haired girl. Sixteen-ish. Pale.
A fortnight ago? Sable washed up on Lanternfall barely a _week_ ago.
Then somebody knew she was coming before she did, didn\'t they?
Take her alive, he said. Not a bruise on her. "Unharmed." Said it twice. Made me swear on my mother. I haven\'t _got_ a mother, but I swore.
Tam fishes a folded paper out of his vest and flicks it at Bram. The wax seal is black.
"The girl is to be detained and conveyed to the Cathedral of Dawn. Unharmed. By order of the Lord-Commander, Garrick Thorne."
That\'s his seal. His own seal. And — the _Cathedral_. Not the barracks.
The Cathedral\'s where we\'re going anyway. Cassian said the Choir\'s archives could help her.
Don\'t. He\'s the one who _sent_ us. If Thorne wants her too, it\'s because— I don\'t know. Because something\'s gone wrong. Because someone\'s lying to him.
Mags was right. Thorne doesn\'t say "unharmed" about anyone. So someone told him to.
Then we ask Cassian who. When we get there. Okay?
Wren said "okay". She says it when she is not.
Touching. Truly. Can I go now?
Corporal Fen
Nobody move! Thistledown militia! We\'ve got pitchforks and a— oh. You\'ve done it already.
Red Tam. You\'re under arrest for robbery, banditry, extortion and those apples in the spring of eighty-nine.
Those apples were _sour_, Fen!
Hey. Redhead. A girl worth more than a valley. Ask yourself why. And ask yourself who\'s _really_ paying.
Return to Thistledown.

Red Tam was paid by Lieutenant Harrow to catch Sable — a fortnight ago, before she ever washed up on Lanternfall. The writ says "unharmed", "to the Cathedral of Dawn", signed by Garrick Thorne. Somebody told Thorne to say unharmed. It isn\'t Cassian. It can\'t be.
The road\'s open! Carts are moving! Tobble\'s bees have stopped sulking! Tam\'s in the root cellar with a very stern goose guarding the door!
Thistledown doesn\'t have much, but what it has, it shares. Take this. All of it. Don\'t argue, I\'m the Reeve.
Told you he was bad at it.
Gloamweaver. Whatever\'s waiting for you in Aurenne — you\'re more than one thing. Remember it, the day somebody tells you otherwise.
I will remember.
Good girl. And eat something. You\'re all elbows.
That\'s what my mom says. ..."Eat something green once a week."
Your mother\'s a wise woman.
The Aurenne road is open. When you\'re ready, leave by the far east end of the fields.
Leave Thistledown behind and take the road to Aurenne?
Onward to Aurenne
Not yet
Aurenne. Two days east. Then the Cathedral. Then answers.
Then answers we might not like.
Then _bread_. I was promised there\'d be bread in the capital. Proper bread. With seeds in.
Who promised you that?
Me. Just now. I\'m holding myself to it.
Far off — so faint it might be imagined — the evening wind carries the sound of bells.
You\'ve been to Aurenne?
I do not know.
We left Thistledown for Aurenne at dusk. When the wind brought the sound of the city\'s bells, Sable said she knew it. Then she said she didn\'t. Then she said she didn\'t know.
City of Bells
Reach the Cathedral of Dawn in Aurenne and deliver Cassian\'s letter.
src/story/ch2_wold.js: The wind drops. The birds stop. In the hush beneath the old trees, something whispers.
That\'s the wind. In the leaves. Wind-leaves. Very common, wind-leaves.
There isn\'t any wind, Bram.
They\'re voices. Real voices. Coming out of the trees.
Yes. I can hear them very clearly.
They are like the ones in the water.
The water?
Before the rocks. Before Lanternfall. I was in the water, and the water was full of voices like these. All talking. None of them listening.
Sable... that\'s—
It is all right. They cannot hurt you. They can only remember.
Mags said don\'t answer them. So. Policy. Nobody answers the trees.
Find a way through the Whisperwold. (Mags said: don\'t answer the trees.)
The Whisperwold. The trees talk with the voices of dead people. Sable says they\'re like the voices she heard in the sea, before she washed up. She wasn\'t scared. I was.
Somebody\'s been sorry about a broken cup for a very long time.
Hold the line! Hold the— why aren\'t you holding the LINE—
Don\'t. Don\'t think about it. Walk.
A tree of violet glass and old bark. It hums, softly, the way a mother hums with her mouth closed.
Hush now, little one, the lantern\'s lit... the sea\'s asleep, and so must you...
Nana used to sing that. Every night, until I was ten and told her I was too old for it.
Every mother in Solmere sings that.
The tree by the black pond is quiet now. Just bark, and the sound of water.
By the black pond, a crooked tree with a split like a grin. Something in it laughs — a wheezing, honking laugh, like a seal choking on a herring.
It\'s lit. She\'s kept it lit. Six years.
Tell her it was my knot. Not hers. I tied it. I was showing off. Tell her to sell the boat.
Tell her to sleep.
The laugh comes once more, fainter, and then the tree is only a tree.
Mags said not to answer them.
Mags didn\'t say anything about _delivering mail_.
Jory\'s voice spoke by the black pond: the knot was his fault; Odile should sell the boat, and sleep. Tell Odile in Port Gale.
Quest updated — The Lamp in the Window
A lone tree at the edge of the overlook, its violet leaves turned toward the far-off sea.
A man\'s voice. Warm, and tired, like someone talking in his sleep.
My hand is on the compass. When did I put my hand on the compass?
The tree says nothing more.
Nothing. It\'s nothing. I\'m okay.
Wren. The voices do not know who they are. They only know what they said. Over and over.
A voice in the trees at the overlook said "west, always west." It\'s a common enough thing to say. It\'s a common enough thing to say.
A slender tree, pale as bone. Its voice is very young.
Brother? ...Brother, I can\'t find the door. It\'s so dark.
You said the bells would bring me home. You promised...
That one is looking for someone.
I do not know. But I wanted to answer her.
Answer what?
I sang every day of my life until I was sixteen. Then the light said Warden...
One Crest, one life.
It sounds different when a tree says it.
In the center of the ring of stones stands the oldest tree you have ever seen. It does not whisper. It roars — hundreds of voices at once, rising and falling like surf.
It is the same as the water.
When I was in the sea — before — they were all around me, like this. Talking and talking. None of them could stop.
Sable... what _were_ you, in the sea?
You\'re loud. Are you new? You don\'t look new. You look _alive_.
No! I live here. Mother says. Mother says the wold keeps everybody safe, and nobody has to go home, and nobody ever has to grow up.
Who is Mother?
The Hollow Mother. She\'s the biggest tree. She holds all the voices so they don\'t get lost in the dark.
Do you want to play? Nobody plays anymore. They only talk and talk and talk.
Hide-and-seek! I hide, you seek. Count to ten! No peeking, Big Shiny Man.
Big Shiny— I— One. Two. Three...
Hide and Seek
A little girl named Merry is hiding somewhere in the Whisperwold. She wants to be found.
Found me! This is where Mother sings. I like it here best.
Again! Count again! Big Shiny Man counts too fast. Shawl Lady, you count.
One. Two. Three. Four...
You found me three times. That means you\'re my friends. That\'s the rule.
Friends get the acorn. It\'s the key to my secret place. Past the thorns, by the stones.
Don\'t tell Mother. She doesn\'t like me going there. She says it makes me sad.
Merry... how long have you lived in the wold?
Since the summer!
When you look again, there is no one by the pond. Only the smell of rain, and a child\'s laugh fading into the trees.
Merry gave you her acorn: the key to her "secret place", past the thorns south-east of the Ring of Stones.
Quest updated — Hide and Seek
Found me! ...Did you hear it? It\'s so quiet now. Mother\'s gone quiet.
You found me, so you\'re my friends. That\'s the rule. Friends get the acorn — it opens my secret place, past the thorns by the stones.
I don\'t think I need it anymore.
A wall of black thorns, thick as a man\'s wrist. Woven, almost. As if someone made it to keep something in — or keep you out.
You hold up Merry\'s acorn. The thorns shiver, then curl away from it like fingers opening.
A small stone, green with moss, half-hidden in flowers that should not be blooming in autumn.
*MERIBEL ASH. SEVEN SUMMERS.*
*SHE WENT TO PLAY IN THE WOLD.*
You found my secret place. Nobody ever finds it. ...It\'s so quiet now. Mother\'s gone quiet.
The moss on this is— Wren, this stone is older than Nana.
She does not know.
Or she knows, and the Mother won\'t let her stop.
That\'s worse. I don\'t like that that\'s worse.
Merry\'s secret place is her own grave. The Hollow Mother keeps her in the wold, playing the same summer forever.
Old letters cut into a standing stone, half-swallowed by moss:
*WE ARE BORN. WE ARE BOUND. WE ARE BURIED.*
*SPEAK TO US IN THE ORDER OF A LIFE, AND THE WOLD WILL LET YOU PASS.*
Three stones somewhere ahead, then. Three voices. A cradle, a wedding, a grave.
In that order. Okay. How hard can it be?
Don\'t _say_ that. Not in a haunted forest. Not out loud.
Find the three Listening Stones and answer them in the order of a life.
Lay him down where the light can find him. Lay him down facing west...
A standing stone, warm to the touch. Voices move inside it like fish under ice.
This voice has already been answered. It waits, patient as stone.
Answer the voice?
Answer it
Only listen
The voices tangle into a single shriek! Something cold pours out of the stone!
In the order of a _life_, Wren. You\'re born, you marry, you die. Usually.
The stone hums, low and warm, and falls quiet.
Far off, deep in the wold, something old and wooden groans — and moves.
The roots have parted. Go deeper into the Hollow.
At the heart of the wold stands a tree so old it has forgotten it is a tree.
Its trunk has split open like a cupped hand. Inside, hundreds of violet lights flicker and murmur. Voices. Every voice in the wood.
The Hollow Mother
Hush. Hush, little ones. More travelers. More voices.
Stay. Stay with me. Out there, the days end. Out there, you grow old, and then you are forgotten.
In here, no one is forgotten. In here, nothing ever has to end.
Nothing ends because you won\'t _let_ it! They\'re not resting. They\'re stuck — saying the same thing over and over, forever!
Home is cold. Home is gone. I keep them warm.
I know your voice. You are made of the same dark as my little ones. You are one of mine. Come home.
I am not yours.
I do not know whose I am. But I am not yours.
You heard her! Everybody behind me!
Then I will keep you all. Forever. And ever. And ever.
The lights rise out of the split trunk — tens, then hundreds — and drift upward through the branches like fireflies leaving a jar.
And then she is only a tree: very old, very tired, and quiet at last.
She wasn\'t cruel.
She was afraid of the morning.
Is there a difference?
Leave the Whisperwold by the eastern path. Thistledown lies beyond.
We fought the Hollow Mother, the tree that kept every voice in the wold. When she fell, the voices went up like sparks. She asked if it was morning. Sable told her yes.

Here. My bracelet. Mother made it out of moss. It keeps you warm when you\'re hurt. I won\'t need it where I\'m going.
Bye, Big Shiny Man. Bye, Grumpy— I mean, bye, Ilse. Bye, Wren.
Bye, Sable. Don\'t let anybody keep you.
She goes the way the lights went: up, and out, and gone.
I\'m not crying. It\'s the— wind-leaves.
There\'s no wind, Bram.
I KNOW there\'s no wind, Ilse.

My compass.

Give. It. Back.

I was not built for roofs. Roofs are for birds, and regrets.
Then don\'t look down.
I wasn\'t going to until you said that.

A black cloud lifts off the bell-gable of St. Aurel\'s, screaming.
Hope you like birds! They don\'t like you!
There is a hole in this roof.
Mind that! Lost a mate down there once!
re under— uh. Citizen\'s arrest? Is that a thing?
You\'re a squire? Bit old for a squire, aren\'t you?
That is a very rude question.
Give it back.
This? It\'s broken. Points the wrong way. North\'s _that_ way. Everybody knows that.
It points west. It always points west. It was my dad\'s.
Your dad\'s a sailor?
He was.
Didn\'t want it anyway. Wouldn\'t have fenced for more than four coppers. Five, tops.
Why do you steal?
Why do you breathe?
I do not know. I did not ask to.
How old are you?
Twelve in the spring, alright?! I\'m eleven. Eleven and three-quarters. Happy?
Where are your parents?
_(shrugs)_ Where\'s anybody\'s.
Hey. Big one. That sash. You\'re Dawnguard? A real one?
Then you have to help me. It\'s the oath. Or the law. Whichever one you lot swear on.
My crew\'s been going missing. Low Town kids. Tuck, two weeks back. Wick, last week. They go to sleep in the drain-house and in the morning they\'re just... not.
No blood. No nothing. And the Watch won\'t come down to Low Town for anything smaller than a fire.
Gone where?
Wren. We have a letter to deliver. To the Cathedral. _Today._
The Cathedral! Even better. You\'ve got friends up there? White-robes listen to people with letters.
I\'m coming with you.
Absolutely not.
Absolutely— well. He\'s very small.
I know every street, every drain, every back door in the City of Bells. You\'ll be lost inside an hour without me. Fish-Girl.
Stop calling me—
