Ha! That\'s a _bird_. Fish-Bird.
I like him.
Of course you do.
Fine. Until we find your friends.
Pipkin Tallow. Prince of the Gutters. At your service.
He bows, low and elaborate. When he straightens up, Wren\'s purse is in his hand.
Giving it back! See? Giving it back. Changed man.
Pip is eleven: too young to have been Kindled. He fights without Crest Arts — for now.
Deliver Cassian\'s letter at the Cathedral of Dawn (Cathedral Square, north).
The thief is called Pip. He is eleven (and three-quarters). He gave the compass back when I told him it was Dad\'s. His friends have been vanishing in Low Town. Somehow he\'s coming with us.
_(whispering)_ Candles. So many candles. I\'m going to stand right here and be extremely good.
Oh! You must be the Hierophant\'s guests. From the islands. Welcome to the house of the dawn.
Sister Mercy Vale. I keep the almshouse in Low Town — soup, beds, and as much kindness as the Choir\'s purse allows.
I\'m Wren. This is Ilse, Bram, Sable, and—
I have only had it for a little while.
_(laughing softly)_ Haven\'t we all.
And Pipkin. Hiding behind a knight. You know there\'s always a bed for you at the almshouse.
I\'m good.
One day you\'ll be tired, little one. Everyone gets tired. And I\'ll be there.
Peace on your road, children. Noon comes for all of us.
What a kind woman.
Every kid who takes one of her beds gets fed. Real food. Meat, sometimes.
I just don\'t like how quiet they come back.
Give Cassian\'s letter to the acolyte by the altar.
Pilgrims? The dawn-office is at— oh. That seal.
The Hierophant\'s own hand. Then you\'re expected. His Holiness returned last night aboard the _Aubade_.
He\'s _here?_ He said he\'d stay at Lanternfall for days—
The _Aubade_ is the fastest ship in Solmere. They say the wind follows the Hierophant like a dog.
He asked that you be brought to him the moment you arrived. This way — his study.

Wren Halloway. You came.
You said the archives might help Sable. And you said... well. I came.
Forgive me for leaving Lanternfall without a word. The Choir called, and the _Aubade_ does not like to wait.
Mender Marrow. Your grandmother taught half of Lanternfall to set a bone, and the other half to fear her.
Squire Kestrel. The Dawnguard Hall will want to see you.
Will it.
And you. Are you well, child? Have you remembered anything?
I remember being cold.
And who is this?
Nobody. Just a nobody. Nobody important.
Everyone is somebody. What is your name?
And kids are going missing in Low Town, and nobody up here cares, so maybe you could. Care. Sir. Your Holiness.
Three of mine. Gone in the night. No blood, no nothing.
I will speak to the Dawnguard tonight. And to Sister Mercy at the almshouse — no one knows Low Town\'s children better.
Wren. I have been looking for someone for a long time.
Someone to walk beside me. To carry my word to the Keepers. To learn the Lanterns as I learned them, when I was young.
A Lantern Page.
It is not an easy post. It means the road. It means being very far from home.
I— yes. _Yes._ I mean— are you sure? I\'ve only been Kindled for—
Your mother is the finest Keeper in Solmere. And you have something she does not.
You want to leave.
Ilse says nothing. She is watching the Hierophant\'s hands.
Think on it tonight. Rooms are taken for you at the Ringing Bell, on the Choir\'s account. And the archives are open to you — all of them. Brother Quill will help Sable look.
Who is Lysa?
Forgive me — you resemble her. It startled an old man, at your Kindling.
Did you find her?
Not yet.
Go. Eat something. Aurenne is beautiful at dusk.
Cassian asked me to be his Lantern Page. ME. Sable asked him who Lysa is. He said: someone I lost. She asked if he\'d found her. He said: not yet.
A Lantern Page. _Me._ Ilse, do you know what that means?
It means he\'s known you for three days and already wants you working for him.
He\'s known me for _two years_. Letters count.
Letters count. Right.
It\'s a great honor, Ilse. The last Lantern Page became an Archdeacon.
And the one before that?
He said "not yet."
When I asked if he found her. People do not say "not yet" about the dead.
Can we talk about _my_ people now? The ones who are actually missing?
Tomorrow. First thing. Cassian said he\'d talk to the Dawnguard tonight.
I\'m going to check on Nell. Drain-house in Low Town. Don\'t wait up, Fish-Bird.
Evening falls on Aurenne. Rest at the Ringing Bell (Bell Market) — the Choir is paying.
Ilse thinks Cassian wants something. Ilse thinks everyone wants something. Pip went back to Low Town to check on Nell.
The Hierophant\'s guests! Put your coin away, loves — the Choir\'s paying, and the Choir tips. Rooms at the top of the stairs.
That night, the bells of Aurenne ring twelve times.
And then they are quiet.
_(whispering)_ Ilse? You awake?
He asked _me._
I know.
Nobody\'s ever asked me to be anything. They just told me what I was going to be. Keeper. Like Mom. Like her mom.
Master Ambrose offered me a place. At the Infirmary.
Ilse! That\'s— are you going to take it?
Why not?
Because somebody has to read your fine print.
Just— read the fine print. Whatever he\'s offering. Read all of it.
Since when do you read fine print?
Since always. You never noticed, because you were busy reading the fun part.
Across the room, Sable is dreaming.
It smells like cut grass and honey-bread and warm stone.
Somewhere, a boy is calling a name.
Lysa! Lysa, _come on!_
There you are! Father\'s lighting it early tonight, for the festival. We can watch from the gallery if we\'re quiet.
You\'re never quiet.
I don\'t know you.
_(laughing)_ Stop it. You always do this.
Here. Take my hand. It\'s getting dark.
The light goes out. All of it, all at once.
Something cold comes in where the light was.
LYSA! TAKE MY HAND— _LYSA!_
His hand is so warm.
And then it isn\'t there.
Sable? You\'re shaking.
I had a dream. I think it was a dream.
There was a boy. He called me Lysa. He wanted me to take his hand.
Then the light went out.
Lysa. That\'s what the Hierophant called you. At the Kindling.
He had gray eyes. Like the Hierophant\'s.
It\'s just a dream. You heard the name, and dreams— they take things and stir them up.
Do dreams smell like summer?
Nell\'s gone.
She was in the drain-house. I told her stay put. I _told_ her— and this morning her blanket\'s there and she isn\'t.
You said tomorrow.
Pip, I—
Doesn\'t matter. Old Mag sleeps by the river in Low Town. She saw something, she won\'t say it to me. She might to you.
Come on. Or don\'t.
Find out what happened to Nell. Ask Old Mag in Low Town (south-east, by the river).
Sable dreamed that a boy called her Lysa, and then the light went out. In the morning, Nell was gone. I told Pip "tomorrow."
Old Mag
A coin for an old woman? No? Then a smile. No? Then move along, you\'re in my sun.
Behind the almshouse. The old stair. Mind the singing.
Pip\'s new friends. Fancy boots. You\'ll want to know about last night.
Singing. I heard singing. Sisters in gray with little lanterns, walking slow and pretty.
They led the young ones out of the drain-house like ducklings. And the young ones went _smiling_.
Nell went with them? _Smiling?_
Smiling like they\'d been promised supper. Round the back of the almshouse they went. Down the old stair, where the Undercroft starts.
There\'s a grate down there. Always locked. Who locks a sewer, I ask you.
Someone who wants to be sure of who comes out.
Sister Constance keeps the keys on her belt. Rattles like a jailer\'s.
The Undercroft grate behind the almshouse is locked. Sister Constance at the almshouse keeps the keys.
Old Mag saw gray Sisters lead the children down the old stair behind the almshouse — singing. The children were smiling.
The Dawnguard says I may go. I don\'t know where.
Was there something else? Sister Mercy is... at prayer. Below— _at prayer_.
Welcome to the house of Small Mercies. Soup at noon and vespers. Beds for those who ask.
Sister Mercy says no one should ever have to be cold. Isn\'t that beautiful?
Sister. The children from the drain-house. Where did your Sisters take them last night?
Then where are the beds?
Sister Mercy is at prayer below— _at prayer._ You may come back at vespers.
_(whispering)_ Keep her talking.
Ask about the soup.
Ask about Sister Mercy.
Have Bram ask about the beds.
Keep her talking!
The soup! It smells— amazing. Is that... leek?
Leek and barley. And a little thyme, when the Choir\'s purse allows.
Thyme! My mother grows thyme. Well, she grows _at_ it. It mostly refuses.
Sister Mercy seems so... devoted. How long have you known her?
Eleven years. She found me on the Cathedral steps. She found all of us, one way or another.
She says the sun should never have to set on anyone. Isn\'t that lovely?
Sister! As a knight of— as a squire of the Dawnguard, I must ask about the, ah. The beds. Their... softness. Specifically.
For a report. A very official report. About beds.
Now, if you\'ll excuse me. Vespers.
_(whispering)_ Pip. That\'s stealing from a nun.
_(whispering)_ It\'s borrowing with confidence.
Open the old Undercroft grate behind the almshouse (east end of Low Town).
Pip lifted Sister Constance\'s keys while we kept her talking. Ilse is appalled. I\'m a little impressed.
An iron grate across the old stair, chained and locked. The chain is new. The lock is newer.
An iron grate across a stair that goes down into the dark. A cold draft breathes up through it, smelling of wet stone and candle-smoke.
Nell. I\'m coming.
Three things. One: we stay together. Two: nobody touches anything purple.
And three?
Three: if anyone sings at us, we hit them.
I like three.
Descend into the Undercroft and find the missing children.
Ugh. The smell.
That\'s the smell of the whole city, going somewhere else. You get used to it.
There are footprints. Small ones. And bigger ones, walking beside them.
The valve wheel is turned as far as it will go.
The wheel shrieks, sticks, and then turns. Somewhere down the tunnel, iron grinds against iron.
With a long groan, the great sluice gate in the main tunnel lifts.
Was that us? I think that was us.
The sluice gate is open. Press on east, deeper into the Undercroft.
One more wheel, I think. These valves always come in pairs. Like shoes. Or bad ideas.
Turn the second valve wheel to raise the sluice gate.
A rusted sluice gate seals the tunnel from wall to wall. Two pipes run from it — one north, one south — to valve wheels somewhere in the dark.
Find the two valve wheels (north and south passages) to raise the sluice gate.
I\'ve never been this deep. Nobody comes this deep.
Bones. Lots of bones. Ilse, are there meant to be this many bones?
Aurenne buried its dead under its streets for six hundred years. There are meant to be _more_.
Far ahead, a bell tolls once — low and cracked — though there is no tower down here.
A small niche, set apart from the others. A child\'s name is carved over it:
*LYSA LORNE · TEN YEARS · NOT LOST, ONLY WAITING*
A candle burns in the niche. It is fresh, lit in the last day or two.
Somebody comes all the way down here. Regular.
It is the name from my dream.
Lorne. Wren — the Hierophant\'s name is Cassian _Lorne._
Yes. It is sad.
In the catacombs there\'s a niche for a girl called LYSA LORNE, ten years old. Someone keeps a candle burning there. Cassian Lorne lost a sister.
In the old bell-foundry, among cold furnaces, something enormous is ringing a cracked bell with a hammer. Very slowly. Over and over.
Is that... a skeleton? Ringing a bell?
At least it\'s not singing.
The ringing stops. The skull turns.
The Wight comes apart like a dropped armful of firewood. Among the bones lies a bronze hammer, worn smooth.
GLORIA, it says on the handle. Who names a hammer?
Old Tolliver does. The bell-ringer up in the Bell Market. He\'s been crying about it for a week. Says the noon bell won\'t ring true without her.
Press on toward the stair at the far end of the ossuary.
The stone gives way to something else. The walls breathe. Violet light pools on the floor like spilled wine.
And there are cells. And in the cells there are people.
NELL! _NELL!_
This place is made of the same thing I am made of.
I do not know why I said that.
Find Nell and the missing — and whoever is doing this.
Pipkin. You came to me after all. They always come to me in the end — when they\'re tired.
Where\'s Nell.
Safe. Warm. Waiting. Soon she\'ll never be cold again, or hungry, or eleven years old in a city that steps over her.
You\'re turning people into those— _things._
Into _vessels_, dear. The Gloam is only memory. Pour enough into a body and the body forgets its pain.
Most of them forget everything else, too. That is the part I\'m still working on.
The Choir trusted you. _Cassian_ trusted you!
_(softly)_ Oh, child. You really don\'t know anything, do you.
The one what?
The one that worked.
Enough! Stand aside, Sister, in the name of the Dawnguard!
Squire Kestrel. The one who froze.
Leave him alone.
I\'ll leave all of you alone. For ever and ever. Hush now. Let me sing.
Keep them, then. Keep your cold, hungry little lives. I have what I needed.
You\'ll see. All of you.
_Noon is coming._
She steps backward into her own shadow, and the shadow closes over her like water.
She— where\'d she _go?_
Into the dark. The dark has back doors.
Noon? It\'s barely morning.
She did not mean the time.
Somewhere behind them, every cell door in the laboratory unlocks at once.
Pip? ...You came.
Course I came. I\'m the Prince.
You\'re not a prince.
Shut up. I came.
He hugs her so hard she squeaks. Neither of them mentions it, then or ever.
Tuck\'s here. And Wick. They\'re cold, and Wick won\'t stop crying, but they\'re _them._ They\'re still them.
Bram. Help me with the adults. Some of them can\'t walk.
Carrying. Yes. I am good at carrying.

Sister Mercy was making Gloam beasts out of the poor of Low Town. We beat her, but she walked into her own shadow and was gone. "Noon is coming," she said. We got Nell, Tuck and Wick out — and Rowan the baker, and ten others.
They bring fourteen people up out of the dark that morning.
By noon, all of Aurenne knows.
People of Aurenne. Last night, the Choir failed you.
A woman who wore our sunburst — who fed your children with one hand — took them with the other.
Sister Mercy Vale is no longer of the Choir. She is cast out. Her name is struck from every book we keep.
A sound goes through the crowd. Not a cheer. Something lower, and older.
To the families of Low Town: I am sorry. Words are small. Today they are what I have. Tomorrow, the Choir\'s coffers open to you.
And to the children who went down into the dark when the Choir would not —
He looks straight at Wren.
— thank you.
Now the crowd cheers. It goes on for a long time.
The Dawnguard will find her, Holiness. Wherever she\'s crawled to.
I know you will, Garrick.
Kestrel. They let you hold a sword again. Brave of them.
Who\'s the walking anvil?
Lord-Commander Garrick Thorne. Head of the Dawnguard. He... trained me.
He\'s a jerk.
He\'s the Lord-Commander.
Can\'t he be both?
His Holiness asks for you in his study. All of you. ...Especially the Page.
Cassian has asked for you in his study (Cathedral of Dawn, back-left door).
Cassian cast Mercy out in front of the whole city and thanked us in front of the whole city. Garrick Thorne was there. Bram went very quiet.
Fourteen people. Fourteen people who would be in the Gloam tonight, if not for you.
The Gloam is rising, Wren. Mercy was a symptom. Rot always finds the weak places first — a city\'s poor. A Lantern\'s flicker.
For a thousand years the Seven Lanterns have sung the sun up. But they sing _apart_, each Keeper to her own light.
If they sang together — in true harmony — no darkness could stand against them. Not ever again.
He sets a long case on the desk and opens it. Inside, on blue velvet, lie six silver tuning forks.
Blessed in the Grand Lantern\'s light. A Keeper need only strike one beside her Dawnstone, and her Lantern will learn the note. Six Lanterns. One song.
I would carry them myself. But Aurenne needs its Hierophant now, more than it has in forty years.
I need a Page.
Yes. Yes — we\'ll do it. I\'ll do it.
Start south. Saltglass, in the Sunscar. Keeper Tamsin is... difficult. You\'ll like her. Then Frosthollow, Mirefen, Thornwood, and Skyreach above the storm.
That\'s five. You said six forks. And there are seven Lanterns.
The Grand Lantern is mine to tune. And Lanternfall\'s... your mother\'s Lantern I will see to myself.
A spare. Roads are long, and things are lost on them.
It hums.
Every true note does.
This one hums backwards.
_(smiling)_ What a curious ear you have.
And Pip. Your friends will be cared for — the Choir will see to it. Truly cared for, this time.
_(a small laugh)_ A wise arrangement.
Wren. If you write to your mother — tell her the Hierophant sends his regards. And that her daughter is doing great things.
I will. I— thank you. For everything.
The Pilgrim Road leads south to Saltglass. Leave Aurenne by the South Gate when you\'re ready.
Cassian named me his Lantern Page and gave us six blessed tuning forks for the Keepers. Ilse says read the fine print. Sable says the forks hum backwards. The road goes south.
The Lantern Page. Carrying the Hierophant\'s blessing to every Keeper in the world. Ilse, this is— this is a _story._ We\'re in a story.
Three things.
One: yesterday we walked out of a cellar full of monsters made out of people. Two: a woman in the Choir\'s robes made them, under the Choir\'s own floor.
Three: we are now carrying the Choir\'s mail.
Cassian _condemned_ her. In front of the whole city. What more do you want?
I want to know how the Hierophant of the whole world didn\'t notice what was under his own feet.
The note in the forks. I do not like it.
So we\'re going to the desert? I\'ve never seen a desert. Is it just a really big beach?
Brilliant. Fish-Bird\'ll feel right at home.
You\'re really going.
Somebody\'s got to keep Fish-Bird out of trouble. You\'ve seen her. She\'s a disaster.
You\'re coming back?
Course. I\'m the Prince. Princes come back. That\'s the whole point of them.
You\'re in charge while I\'m gone. Mind Wick. And don\'t let Tuck near Marta\'s pies.
I was always in charge, Pip.
Tuck waves with both arms. Wick has stopped crying. Nell does not wave at all; she watches, the way you watch something you mean to remember.
No. Let\'s go.
Behind them, the bells of Aurenne ring the noon. They ring true.
The Pilgrim Road
Follow the Pilgrim Road south across the Sunscar to Saltglass, and Keeper Tamsin.
We left Aurenne at noon. Six forks, five Keepers, one road. Nell watched us go like she was memorizing us.
src/story/ch3_battle.js: She drinks the dark, and it drinks her back.
The great bell splits with a sound like a scream. The Wight tears the clapper free!
The foundry floor shifts. Old bones answer the bell.
The Wight raises its hammer toward the great bell...
"Hush, now. Let me sing you something."
Mercy uncorks a vial of darkness and drinks. Her shadow stands up behind her.
"Hush now. Sleep. When you wake, it will be noon forever."
"There, there. It only hurts until it doesn\'t."
"Rise, child. Your suffering is not yet over."
Mercy draws a long breath. The air goes still, as if waiting for noon...
src/story/ch3_fx.js: The bells of Aurenne ring the hour.
Not from here. I\'d land on a chimney.
src/story/ch3_side.js:
s Hammer (Tolliver) · The Chronicle of the Long Night (Quill)
//   Sir Pounce (Dame Orsolya Venn, Bram) · The Baker
Hear that? No, you don\'t. Nobody does. That\'s the sound of a bell that\'s ringing _true._
Low, high, middle, high. Mind the Dawn Peal, Page. It\'ll get you through doors.
The noon bell\'s still ringing flat. I can hear it. Even _I_ can hear it.
Low, high, middle, high. That\'s the Dawn Peal. Never know when you\'ll need it.
Eh? Speak up. Forty years in a bell tower, I hear one word in three, and I don\'t care for two of them.
You want to know why the noon bell\'s been ringing flat all week? I\'ll tell you why. Gloria\'s gone.
My _hammer!_ Bronze, cast in the old foundry under the city. Forty years we\'ve rung the noon together, her and me.
Last week, middle of the night, the lights went funny. Purple. And something came up the old bell-pit and took her right off her hook. Down into the dark.
Something came up a pit. And stole a hammer.
Took her! I know what I saw. A hand made of— well. You\'d not believe me. Nobody does.

Nine days north by caravan: across the flats, through the scrublands, up into country where the air turns thin and the wind tastes of iron.
At the foot of the Greyspine, Oyelaran\'s wagons turn back.
"This is as far as wheels go," he says. "The monastery\'s a day\'s climb. Walk softly. The mountain listens."

s been told off.
A big one who walks like he\'s apologizing to the floor.
A careful one who counts her steps. A man already looking for the back door.
In my defense, there usually is one.
And one who doesn\'t walk quite the way the rest of you do. You... drift. Like a song somebody\'s humming.
I walk. I have feet.
So you do, sweetling. So you do.
And the one in front walks like someone leaving. Come here, Wren Halloway.
How do you know my—
Ysolde\'s girl. I knew your grandmother\'s step, and your mother\'s. You have both. Your mother hated being told that.
Good. Now. What has Cassian sent me?
Wren opens the case. Tamsin\'s fingers find a fork without searching, the way you find the latch of your own door in the dark.
She strikes it once against her cane and holds it to her ear. The note is pure and thin, and it goes on much longer than it should.
Tamsin\'s smile goes away.
Is something wrong with it?
Like a word in a language I used to speak. Like a name I heard in a dream and lost on waking.
I\'ve listened to the Dawnsong every morning for fifty-one years, child. I know every note of it the way you know your mother\'s voice. This is one of them. And it is not.
The Hierophant had them made in the Cathedral. To harmonize the Lanterns, against the Gloam—
I know what he said. Cassian always says exactly the right thing.
I\'ve known him since he was a boy who couldn\'t sleep unless a lamp was burning. I trust him to be exactly who he is.
That is what worries me.
She lays the fork back in its velvet, gently, like something that might bite.
Take it to Halvard at Frosthollow, north in the Greyspine. He has forgotten more about the Dawnsong than the Choir ever knew. If Halvard says it is true, I will set it in my light with my own hands.
And if he says it isn\'t?
Then you will have learned something about the world, Wren Halloway. That\'s what sixteen is for.
Keeper Tamsin
Ask Caravan Master Oyelaran (north-east yard) for passage north to the Greyspine.
Pip has wandered up the dais steps, very casually, toward the little silver bell on Tamsin\'s belt.
Tamsin\'s hand closes on his wrist without looking.
And you, little cat.
I was just — admiring. Professionally.
How old are you?
Twelve in the spring!
Eleven, then.
Eleven and a _HALF_.
You\'re the only one of them without a light on you. I can feel it. Like a cold spot in a warm bath.
Yeah, well. Choir says sixteen. Rules is rules. Not that I care. Crests are for people with houses.
_(quietly)_ Is that what they told you?
The world\'s getting darker, little cat. I can\'t see much. But I can see that.
I\'d like you to have something to hold on to.
Keeper — you can\'t. Kindling a child is forbidden. There are laws—
Five years in an Aurenne cell, I believe. Are you going to tell on me, Mender?
Is it... safe? For him?
Nothing worth doing is safe, squire. You of all people know that.
Yes, ma\'am.
Well, Pipkin Tallow? Will you step into my light?
How do you know my— nobody calls me—
Pip stands in the Lantern\'s light. His fists are clenched. His chin is up. He looks very small.
The light goes all the way through him, warm as fresh bread — and for the first time anyone can remember, Pip forgets to look for the exits.
ROGUE?! The light called me a _THIEF?!_
Pip\'s Crest awakens — *Rogue*! His Crest Arts can now be used in battle.
Wren. _Wren!_ I got one! I got a Crest! Nobody from the gutters ever— not before sixteen, not _ever_, some of \'em—
Make way! Rogue Pipkin Tallow, first of his name!
Put me DOWN, you big— okay, don\'t put me down yet.
Welcome to the trade, kid. Rule one: never tell anyone your real age.
Way ahead of you.
Pip has a light now. It is small. It is very loud.
Tamsin laughs — a real laugh, surprised out of her.
They usually are, the small ones.
Go on, all of you. The caravans for the Greyspine leave from the north yard. Ask for Oyelaran, and tell him I said he owes me.
And Wren Halloway — you walk like someone leaving. Make sure you know what you\'re walking toward.
Tip — Pip can fight now! Bring him into the active party from the menu\'s *Formation* screen.

Keeper Tamsin listened to the fork and said it sings a note she almost knows. She sent us to Brother Halvard at Frosthollow. Then she Kindled Pip. ILLEGALLY. He\'s a Rogue. He hasn\'t stopped grinning, and neither has Bram.
Tolle brought the little ones down the mountain. They sing on my steps every morning.
Badly. Loudly. Halvard would be delighted.
Cassian, as a boy? He used to sit right where you\'re standing and ask me why the sun needed help to come back.
I told him it didn\'t need help. It just liked being asked.
Your friend with the drifting step. Keep her close, Wren.
Something is listening for her. I can hear it listening.
The lamp has been humming at dawn this season. A little lower each morning, like a song deciding something.
Go to Halvard. Ask him what it\'s deciding.

s named after, little Keeper. Watch him lie.
He\'s a terrible liar. It\'s the only honest thing about him.
Velvet Ines
You smell like a sky-pirate I know. Tell Corvin Ashe I can smell him from here.
Well, well. Corvin Ashe. Alive. My, my.
Ines! You look radiant. Have you done something with your— knives?
Six hundred gold, Corvin. Plus the dignity you cost me when you left through the privy window.
Your captain bet me his lucky coin and lost it. Then he bet the coin I\'d won off him and lost it again — on credit. Six hundred.
Corvin\'s Debts
Velvet Ines, in the Cool Well inn, wants the 600 gold Corvin owes her.
Pay 600 gold
Not today
I\'ll be here. I\'m always here. That\'s what makes me so frightening.
Sweet of you. Come back when the sweetness has some gold in it.
A Keeper\'s girl paying a pirate\'s debts. The world really is ending.
Here. It was his. He\'ll tell you it\'s lucky. It isn\'t. It\'s just always been in his pocket while he was being stubborn.
That\'s my lucky coin.
It doesn\'t seem very lucky.
It\'s still here, isn\'t it? So am I. That\'s the luck.
Ask him who the Halcyon\'s named after, little Keeper.
He sleeps eleven hours a night now. I let him.
For nine days I didn\'t sleep at all. Now we\'re taking turns being grateful.
The upper gallery of the Glass Caverns. That\'s where the Kessel caravan went in. Please.
You\'ve met Nim, haven\'t you? Everyone meets Nim. She sits at the gate with her lunch.
Her father — my Jorah — went with the Kessel caravan through the Glass Caverns\' upper gallery. The short way to the eastern wells. Nine days ago.
The Kessel caravan never came out. Oyelaran says the Queen took it. Everyone says the Queen took it.
I don\'t believe it. I won\'t. Not until somebody has looked.
We\'ll look.
The Fastest Scout
Asha\'s husband Jorah went into the Glass Caverns with the Kessel caravan nine days ago and never came out. Search the caverns beyond Saltglass\'s east gate.
Papa came home! He came home and he was SO DIRTY!
And she made me take a bath before she\'d hug me. My own daughter.
We owe you everything. We don\'t have everything. We have these.
His running boots. Fastest scout on the salt road. He says he\'s finished running.
Nine days in a glass box teaches you where you want to be standing.
You\'re the boy with the Crest! The little one!
I\'m not little.
You\'re littler than Papa.
Jorah is home. Nim made him take a bath before she\'d hug him. Grandmother Zeyneb took a chime down.
The caverns breathe out cool air that smells of salt and lightning. Somewhere deep inside, the walls are singing.
Hear that? Singing glass. That\'s my girl\'s heartbeat, down there somewhere.
It\'s the wind.
There is no wind.
The pillar hums in harmony with its sisters. The note doesn\'t stop. You suspect it never will.
A pillar of saltglass taller than Bram, clear as water. It hums — almost the note of the tuning fork, but not quite.
Strike a tuning fork beside the pillar?
The fork rings. The pillar answers, a half-step lower, and the two notes lock together and hold.
Your holy fork makes the glass sing, sparrow.
It\'s _tuning_ it.
It did not sound like tuning. It sounded like breaking. Slowly.
A shard of the pillar, still humming, comes away in Wren\'s hand.
Deep in the caverns, something answers the note.
Deep in the caverns, something answers — louder now.
Three notes ring through the caverns at once. Far to the east, something enormous made of glass cracks from top to bottom.
Did anyone else hear a door open? I\'d like to not have heard a door open.
A wall of saltglass seals the gallery, thick as a castle gate. Through it, blurred and huge, something pale slides past and is gone.
The glass hums three faint, different notes, as if waiting for three answers from elsewhere in the caverns.
A wall of milky glass. Behind it, blurred, a shape moves — a man, waving both arms.
Strike a tuning fork against the glass?
The note slides into the glass like a key into a lock. The wall goes white with cracks — and falls apart like sugar.
Nine days. _Nine days!_ I\'ve been drinking off the walls and eating— you don\'t want to know what I\'ve been eating.
Are you Jorah? Asha\'s husband? Nim\'s father?
Nim! Is she— she thinks I\'m dead, doesn\'t she.
She thinks you\'re slow.
Ha— the fastest scout on the salt road. _Slow._ Ha.
The Queen took the Kessel caravan in the upper gallery. I ran, and the glass grew shut behind me. It _grows_ down here, did you know? Like ice.
I know the way out from here. Go on — I\'ll be home before you. And don\'t tell Nim. I want to tell her myself.
We found Jorah alive in the Glass Caverns, sealed behind a wall of glass. The fork broke it like sugar. I keep thinking about that.
The cavern opens into a bowl of glass a hundred feet across, smooth as the inside of a bell. Bones and wreckage lie in drifts against the walls: oxen, wagons, a caravan\'s worth of copper pots.
In the center, the glass floor bulges. Then it _moves_.
Is it too late to mention I\'m allergic to queens?
You\'re allergic to everything that\'s trying to eat us.
It\'s a very common allergy.
Stand together! She\'s— sweet Dawn, she\'s the size of a _street_—
The Sand Wyrm Queen coils, uncoils, and lies still. All through the caverns, the singing glass goes quiet — as if it had been holding a note for her, and could finally let it go.
The brood will scatter now. The caravans will be safe. For a while.
Let\'s tell Oyelaran.
We killed the Sand Wyrm Queen in the deep caverns. When she died, all the glass stopped singing at once.

m _sorry_.
The sky is falling apart. Slowly. In pieces.
It\'s snow, Sable.
Sable holds out her hand. A snowflake lands on it, and is gone.
It was here, and then it was water.
I like it anyway.
Bram? You\'ve gone quiet. You\'re never quiet.
I\'ve been here before. My knighting trial — the Vigil. It\'s up there. On the pass.
It\'s fine. It\'s just a mountain. Mountains can\'t hurt you. Except by falling on you. Which they do. Up here. Regularly.
Climb the Greyspine Pass to Frosthollow monastery.
Nine days north with Oyelaran\'s caravan, and then the snow. Sable likes it. Pip has threatened to fight it. Bram has been here before — for his knighting trial.
Above the trail, the snow hangs in a smooth white lip. It creaks.
Nobody run. Nobody shout. Bram, that includes _humming_.
I wasn\'t humming.
You were humming the Dawnguard march.
Tip — In the *Quiet Ways*, walk. Running shakes the snow loose.
A soft, enormous WHUMP — and the lip of snow above lets go.
When you dig yourselves out, something else is digging itself out too — and it is very, very annoyed.
Walk. _Walk._
What did I say. What did I _literally just say._
A frost lily, pale blue, growing straight out of the snow.
Frost lilies! They only bloom above the snowline. Nana used them for fevers and frostbite salve. Take it by the root — gently.
Half-buried in a drift: a pilgrim\'s pack, a walking staff, a tin cup frozen solid.
Inside the pack, a letter. "Dear Ma — the Keeper at the top says the pass will be clear by spring. I\'ll be home for the Kindling. Save me some honey cake."
The letter is dated four winters ago.
A standing stone at the cliff\'s edge, carved with the Dawnguard sunburst. At its foot, a cairn of gray rocks, and a sword driven into the top of it, rusting.
The Vigil Stone.
Every squire of the Dawnguard comes here at the end of their training. One night, alone, on the pass. You hold it until dawn — wolves, cold, whatever comes. That\'s the trial.
Sir Aldous walked me up. He said, "Kestrel, you\'re the most stubborn lad I ever trained. Stubborn\'s half of courage." Then he went down to the monastery to wait for morning.
The wolves came about midnight. A big white one leading them. And I...
I couldn\'t move. I couldn\'t _move_, Wren. My sword arm just... wouldn\'t.
Sir Aldous heard the howling. He came back up. Fifty years old, in the dark, in the snow. He got between me and them.
That\'s his sword. On the cairn.
Lord-Commander Thorne said it was the worst trade the Dawnguard ever made. A knight for a squire who froze.
He was wrong.
You keep standing in front of us. Every time. I have watched you. Your hands shake, and you stand in front of us anyway.
I do not know very much. But I know that is not the same as freezing.
Bram kneels and brushes the snow from the old sword\'s hilt. He stays there a long moment. When he stands, his eyes are red.
It\'s the wind.
Cold wind up here. Gets everyone.
Bram showed us the Vigil Stone, where his knighting trial went wrong and Sir Aldous died. His sword is still on the cairn. Sable told Bram the truth about himself, and he said it was the wind.
The den reeks of old blood. Goat bones everywhere. At the back of the cave, something huge and white uncurls and lifts its head.
That\'s him.
The white one. From the Vigil. He\'s — he\'s gone gray round the muzzle.
Wolf. A very, very large wolf. Everyone stand behind me. Please.
Fight Whitefang?
Whitefang lies down in the snow like an old dog by a fire, sighs once, and is still.
He\'s just a wolf. An old, mean wolf. I\'ve been afraid of him for three years.
That\'s the trick with monsters, big lad. Up close, they\'re mostly tired.
We put down Whitefang, the old white wolf of the pass. Bram looked at him for a long time.
Frosthollow clings to the mountain like a swallow\'s nest: gray stone, slate roofs heavy with snow, and above it all the bell tower that holds the Lantern.
Brother Tolle
Pilgrims! In _this_ weather! Oh — oh, you\'re _armed_ pilgrims. That\'s fine. That\'s — welcome to Frosthollow!
I\'m Brother Tolle. I do the guesthouse. And the goats, on Tuesdays. And the— sorry. Welcome.
We\'ve come from Saltglass to see Brother Halvard. Keeper Tamsin sent us.
The Keeper\'s in the Hall of Echoes, teaching the little ones the morning hymn. They\'re terrible at it. He says that\'s the point.
The hall\'s the big one at the top of the steps. The guesthouse is just east — beds are free for pilgrims. The Keeper insists. I insist too, but nobody listens to me.
Find Brother Halvard in the Hall of Echoes (top of the steps).
We reached Frosthollow. A monk called Tolle apologized to us four times in one minute. Brother Halvard is teaching children to sing.
Brother Ansel
Gray cloaks came back, after the snow settled. Three days later. Ten of them, very polite.
They climbed the tower and did something to the light. Nobody stopped them. Nobody was left who knew how.
It sounds different at dawn now. Flatter. Like a bell with a crack in it that only you can hear.
The monastery stores! Everything blessed. Nothing refunded.
The cheese is from our own goats. The goats have opinions about this.
Sister Agathe
Both my novices are well. The salve worked.
Your Mender ground those lilies like she\'d been born doing it. Tell her an old woman said so. Tell her twice.
Both fevers broke this morning. Your Mender has good hands.
Not the Crest. The _hands_. Different thing.
Tend your wounds, children. All of them. Even the ones that don\'t bleed.
Two of my novices have mountain fever, and I\'m out of frost lilies. The lily slopes are thick with wolves this winter.
Three would do. If you happen to come across any on the pass. If you happen to.
Frost Lilies
Sister Agathe of Frosthollow needs three frost lilies for her fevered novices. They grow off the trail in the Greyspine Pass.
Three! Bless you. Here — you, the girl with the careful hands. Grind these while I boil the water.
Me? I— yes. Of course.
Ilse grinds the lilies in quick, neat circles, without being shown how.
You\'ve done this before.
My grandmother\'s an herbalist. And I\'m a Mender. The light said so.
The light said _Mender_. The light didn\'t say _good_. That\'s not the light\'s to say. That\'s you.
The light knows the job, child. It doesn\'t know _you_. Only you get to know you. Takes most of us sixty years. I\'m still working on it.
Moss from the infirmary roof, woven round copper. Old novices\' trick. Keeps the blood moving and the heart stubborn.
Sister Agathe told Ilse the light knows the job but not the person. Ilse didn\'t say anything for a whole hour.
Brother Ivo
Not one goat lost since the old wolf went. They\'ve grown insufferable. They know they\'re safe.
Wait — you\'re the ones who put down Whitefang? Before I even asked?
Seventy years that wolf ran this mountain. My father hunted him. His father hunted him.
Here. My father\'s, and my grandfather\'s before. They never needed them in the end. You\'ve earned them.
The goats are frightened of the quiet. So am I.
Another goat gone. Whitefang again — the old white wolf. He\'s been raiding this mountain since before I was born.
His den\'s on the middle terrace of the pass, east side, behind the rocks. If someone were to... persuade him to retire, I\'d make it worth their while.
The Old Wolf
Brother Ivo\'s goats keep vanishing. Whitefang, the great white wolf, dens on the east side of the Greyspine Pass\'s middle terrace.
Middle terrace of the pass, east side. You\'ll smell it before you see it.
Sister Rhoswen
We\'ll carve his name tomorrow. Halvard. Just the one word. He\'d hate anything longer.
He\'d say: "Save the stone for someone who did something interesting."
These stones carry the names of the Dawnguard who died on the pass. Most from the old wars.
One is newer than the rest. Three winters old. The Keeper carved it himself and wouldn\'t let anyone help.
Sister Wenna
I was Kindled last spring. Cantor. I\'ll sing in the hall for fifty years.
I always wanted to climb the high peaks. The ones nobody\'s named. They\'re right there — look. And I\'ll be singing at them.
You could do both.
That\'s not how it works. One Crest, one life.
Names cut into the stone, row on row, the old ones softened by weather. At the very end, a newer cut, sharp-edged: SIR ALDOUS VENN. HE HELD THE LINE.
"He held the line."
The tower leans a little to the east now. The great bell hangs crooked in its frame and does not move, even in the wind. The Lantern still burns.
The bell tower of Frosthollow, with the Lantern burning at its crown. Below the lamp hangs a great bronze bell, green with age.
A brass plate on the door: THIS BELL IS NOT TO BE RUNG. THE MOUNTAIN IS LISTENING.
Snow has filled the Bell Stair to the roof.
The Bell Stair: steps cut down into the mountain, behind an iron gate. A hand-painted sign: KEEPER ONLY. EVEN IF THERE IS A DRAGON. — H.
Next time I\'m hiding and YOU\'RE it.
I\'ll hide in the bell. Nobody ever looks in the bell.
I\'m IT and I can\'t find ANYONE. They cheat. They\'re too good at hiding.
There\'s five: Tomas, Linnea, Lars, Yrsa and Oskar. Will you help? You\'re tall. Tall people can see more.
Ebba can\'t find the other novices: Tomas, Linnea, Lars, Yrsa and Oskar. They\'re hiding somewhere around Frosthollow (and its hall and guesthouse).
Finding people who don\'t wanna be found? I\'m a _professional_.
You found EVERYONE? Even _Yrsa_? Nobody ever finds Yrsa!
Here. It\'s the Abbot\'s brooch. I borrowed it. From the Abbot. Who\'s been dead for ninety years. So it\'s more like _finding_ than borrowing.
She stole it. I respect that.
Aw! Don\'t tell Ebba I was behind the woodshed.
Tell her I was somewhere cleverer. Tell her I was in the bell.
Shh! Lars always hides with me. Lars? LARS.
I\'m a tree.
I\'m not IN the Bell Stair! I\'m NEXT to it!
Brother Halvard says nobody goes in except the Keeper. Not even if there\'s a dragon. _Especially_ if there\'s a dragon.
Yrsa holds a finger to her lips, very seriously, and points at the bookshelf. She is still hiding. She has decided it counts.
Go and find the others! I\'m staying here. It\'s a good spot.
A small girl in a novice robe is crouched behind the bookshelf, perfectly silent, perfectly still.
Shh! We\'re playing hide-and-seek! Ebba\'s it! Go away, you\'ll give me away!
Yrsa looks up at you with enormous eyes and holds one finger to her lips. Then she sighs, stands up, and solemnly shakes your hand.
Six children in gray novice robes stand in two crooked rows, singing at the top of their lungs. The hymn is old and beautiful. They are murdering it.
Lovely! Lovely. Oskar, a little less like a goat being sat on. Yrsa, a little more like anything at all. Again, from "the sun is kind"—
Ah! Pilgrims! Either you\'re very holy or very lost. Children — that\'ll do. Go and practice on the goats.
Halvard. Keeper of Frosthollow, abbot of nothing, teacher of the worst choir in Solmere.
And you have Ysolde\'s chin. Wren, is it? Tamsin\'s bird flew faster than your caravan.
Tamsin sent a _bird?_
Tamsin sends birds the way other people breathe. This one said: "Ysolde\'s girl is coming with one of Cassian\'s forks. Listen to it. Tell her the truth." Underlined. Twice.
Wren opens the case. Halvard lifts out a fork and turns it in the light, the way a jeweler turns a stone he already suspects is false.
Do you know what this is? The Ice Score. The Dawnsong, as the first Keepers heard it, carved into the glacier this monastery is built on. Every note.
It\'s read from the bottom up. It rises — like the sun.
He strikes the fork and touches it to the ice.
The note goes into the wall and runs up the carved staves like water finding cracks. Then it stops — high up, near the top of the score — and the whole wall gives off a sound like a held breath.
Every morning for forty years I\'ve heard this song in children\'s voices. I know it better than my own name.
Your fork is tuned to the last note. The highest. The note where the Dawnsong lets go of the sun and lets it rise on its own.
But it\'s flat. Not by much. By exactly enough.
This is not tuned to the Dawnsong, Wren.
It is tuned to its _reflection_.
Its reflection? What does that mean?
The same note, turned upside down. Sung downward instead of up. A song that doesn\'t let go of the sun — a song that _holds_ it.
The oldest texts have a name for the Dawnsong sung backward. Only a name: _the Vespersong_. And after the name, someone has scratched out the rest of the page.
Vesper. Like those gray-cloak soldiers? The ones who keep sniffing after Sable?
There\'s a mistake. There has to be. The forks were made in the Cathedral foundry — a hundred people could have touched them. Sister Mercy was _in_ the Cathedral, she could have—
He _wouldn\'t_, Ilse. He wouldn\'t. He\'s the one trying to _stop_ the Gloam—
_(gently)_ Perhaps not. Perhaps a careless hand at the foundry. Perhaps an old monk\'s ears are going.
But I won\'t set it in my light. And I\'d ask you not to give the others to anyone until we know. I\'ll write to Osk, and Elowen, and Vasha tonight.
Leave me this one. I want to listen to it again when the hall is quiet.
Stay the night. The pass is no place after dark, and Tolle has been airing the guesthouse beds for a week out of sheer hope. We\'ll talk in the morning, with tea, when the world is warmer.
He wouldn\'t. ...Would he?
He wouldn\'t.

Brother Halvard held the fork to the Ice Score. He says it isn\'t tuned to the Dawnsong — it\'s tuned to its reflection. The Vespersong. It has to be a mistake. Someone at the foundry. Mercy. Anyone. It HAS to be.
You. The big one with the red cape. You\'re Bram Kestrel.
Aldous stayed in my guesthouse the night before your Vigil. He couldn\'t sleep. Kept me up till two.
He kept saying, "That boy is the best I\'ve trained in thirty years, Halvard, and he hasn\'t the faintest idea."
He never said.
Men like Aldous never do. They say it to old monks at midnight and leave us to pass it on.
Consider it passed.
Halvard told Bram that Sir Aldous called him the best squire he\'d trained in thirty years. Bram went outside to look at the mountains for a while.
Tea in the morning. I make it badly, but with tremendous conviction.
The children? Foundlings, all six. Left at the gate in baskets, in blankets — one in a cheese crate. That was Oskar. He still smells faintly of cheddar.
I keep striking your fork, and listening. It doesn\'t get better, child. I\'m sorry.
Cassian was a sweet boy. Sweet boys grow into all sorts of things.
Ebba gave you the Abbot\'s brooch? Keep it. The Abbot hasn\'t needed it in ninety years. He\'d be thrilled it\'s finally going somewhere.
Brother Quill
I\'m copying the Ice Score onto vellum. All of it. Before anyone else comes to "tune" anything.
He\'d have done it himself. He kept meaning to. He kept saying there was time.
The Keeper\'s been at the score for an hour, striking that fork and listening.
He\'s not singing. He always sings. Even at funerals. _Especially_ at funerals.
The Ice Score is read from the bottom up. It rises like the sun, the Keeper says.
Twelve hundred years old. The first Keepers carved it while the glacier was still warm from their hands. That\'s the legend, anyway. Glaciers aren\'t warm. I\'ve checked.
The Dawnsong, carved into the living ice: staves and notes in an alphabet older than the Choir. It climbs the wall from floor to ceiling.
Near the very top, the last note has been carved deeper than all the others, as if the carver wanted to be sure no one could ever wear it away.
Beds are free for pilgrims! Blankets are... mostly goat-free.
the guesthouse
Beds are aired! Lamps are trimmed! I even found the good pillow. There\'s only one. Fight for it.
Turn in for the night? (The story will move on. Anything unfinished in Frosthollow will have to wait.)
Take your time! The beds aren\'t going anywhere. Neither am I. I never go anywhere.
That night the snow stops.
The wind stops.
In the quiet, Wren lies awake listening to the forks in their case. They hum, very faintly — a note that goes down instead of up.
Then: a bell. Not the great bell — the small gate-bell, ringing and ringing and ringing.
Up! Everyone up! Soldiers at the gate — gray cloaks, dozens of them — the Keeper says come _now_, quietly, and bring your swords!
Gray cloaks. Of course it\'s gray cloaks. It is _always_ gray cloaks.
Go outside and find Brother Halvard.
Brother Halvard. The Hierophant sends his regards. And his patience, which is at an end.
Lord-Commander Thorne. Forty soldiers, to visit a monastery of six children and an old man. Cassian\'s regards have grown heavy.
The fork, Keeper. Set it in your light, and we are gone by morning. Refuse, and I set it myself, and we are gone anyway. All you choose tonight is how many of your monks are standing when we go.
This fork?
Halvard turns and, with an old soldier\'s arm, throws the fork out over the cliff. It glints once in the lantern-light and is gone into the dark.
_(whispering)_ Oh, I _like_ him.
And there she is. Black hair. Pale as milk. The Hierophant described her well.
The girl comes with me. She is wanted home.
I do not have a home.
I have Wren.
Kestrel! The boy who froze. On my mountain again. Have you come to finish your Vigil? Aldous is still up there, if you\'d like to apologize.
Bram\'s sword hand is shaking. He doesn\'t move. He can\'t.
CHILDREN — TO TOLLE! Wren Halloway — the Bell Stair! Take them down to the eastern face. Tolle knows the way!
Take them.
GO! I\'ll keep Thorne busy. I\'ve been boring soldiers to death for forty years — I\'m very good at it.
Come with us!
Someone has to mind the light, child.
And take this — my copy of the Score, with the note marked. Show Osk. Show Elowen. Show anyone who\'ll listen. NOW, Wren!
Bram. _Bram._ We have to go.
Escape down the Bell Stair (north-east cliff, behind the guesthouse) with the children.

Garrick came to Frosthollow in the night with forty soldiers and demanded Halvard set the fork in his light. Halvard threw it off the cliff. Then he sent us and the children down the Bell Stair, and stayed behind. He gave me his copy of the Score.
This way! The Bell Stair comes out on the eastern face, right under the tower. Mind the ice — it\'s older than the monastery and twice as slippery!
_(from the dark ahead)_ Brother Tolle? Is the Keeper coming?
For the record, every bone in my body is telling me to run the other way.
So run!
I _am_ running. I just keep running in the same direction as you lot. It\'s very confusing for me.
There! Down the stair! The girl is with them!
Behind us! Rearguard — everyone turn around!
They\'ll keep coming. Faster. _Move._
The tunnel ahead is choked with fallen ice — great blocks of it, shaken loose by the soldiers\' boots overhead.
_(from beyond the ice)_ Wren? WREN! The little ones are through — but the roof came down behind us! Can you get past?
It takes all of you, heaving together, a long time. The ice gives way at last.
It\'s too heavy. Even for— Bram?
Stand back.

Bram sets his shoulder against the biggest block. Nothing happens, except Bram going red, then purple. Then the ice groans, and shifts, and topples sideways with a crash that echoes all the way down the stair.
Ha. HA. Lifting! I\'m good at lifting. Lifting is— lifting I can _do_.
You were magnificent.
I— really?
Don\'t make me say it twice.
The Bell Stair opens onto a shelf of snow on the mountain\'s eastern face. Far below, the world is dark. Far above, the bell tower burns — its Lantern the only light for a hundred miles.
We made it! We— oh. Oh no.
You think I don\'t know this mountain, Keeper\'s girl? I kept my own Vigil on it before you were born.
Halvard sent you down his little stair. Halvard always was predictable.
What did you do to him?
Nothing, yet. He\'s barred himself in his tower with his bell and his principles. My men will have him out by dawn.
The girl, Halloway. Give her to me, and the rest of you walk down this mountain alive. Even the coward.
The Hierophant asked nicely, girl. I am what comes after nicely.
Believe whatever lets you sleep.
Kestrel. Still shaking?
You were right. I froze. On this mountain. Sir Aldous died because I froze, and I think about it every day. Every single day.
My hands are shaking, and I\'m standing here. Between you and them. Sable says that\'s not the same as freezing. I think she\'s right.
Then you\'ll die standing. Aldous would have liked that.
Ashe? ...Corvin Ashe. Deserter. Smuggler. Drunk. Still running?
Constantly. Just — not tonight, apparently.
Nobody\'s more surprised than me.
Then come.
Garrick goes down on one knee in the snow. For a moment he only breathes. Then he laughs — a short, ugly bark.
Good. Kestrel. _Good._ Maybe Aldous didn\'t waste himself after all.
But you\'ve won a skirmish, children. I have forty more men on this mountain.
Torches crest the ridge to the east — a line of them, then another. Gray cloaks, coming down.
And above them all, in the tower, a bell begins to ring.
Not the little gate-bell. The great bell of Frosthollow, that has not been rung in two hundred years — because everyone on the mountain knows what happens when it is.
_(looking up)_ He wouldn\'t. The whole slope will—
WREN HALLOWAY! GET THEM INTO THE STAIR!
CHILDREN! SING THE MORNING HYMN, THE WHOLE WAY DOWN! LOUD! I\'LL BE LISTENING!
The bell rings again. The mountain answers — a sound deeper than thunder, from everywhere at once.
FALL BACK! _FALL BACK!_
Halvard — _HALVARD!_
Up in the tower, Halvard is still ringing the bell. From here he looks very small. He does not look afraid.
Then a roar like the end of the world.
Then nothing at all.
When they dig their way out of the stair-mouth, the ledge is gone beneath a slope of new snow, smooth as a bedsheet. The ridge is empty. No torches. No gray cloaks.
Far down the mountain, small dark shapes are limping east. One of them is very large, and walks like a man who is used to giving orders.
Above, the bell tower stands half-buried, leaning a little to one side. The bell is silent.
The Lantern\'s light flickers.
_(quietly)_ Keeper Halvard?
And then a voice, thin and wobbling and completely out of tune: Yrsa, who never speaks, singing the morning hymn.
One by one, the other children join in. They are still terrible at it.
_(roughly)_ He said loud.
Pip sings. Badly. Loud.
He was singing too. While the snow came. I heard him.
I should have— if I\'d gone back up, if I\'d been faster, I could have—
Big lad. He rang that bell so you\'d be down here and not up there.
Don\'t you dare waste it.
Garrick said the Hierophant sent him. Garrick is a liar. Garrick hates everyone.
Cassian. What did you give me?
Three things.
One: Tolle takes the children down the eastern trail, then south to Saltglass. Tamsin will take them in.
Two: we warn the other Keepers. All of them. Before anyone in a gray cloak gets there.
Mirefen\'s closest. Mother Osk. Then Thornwood. Then Skyreach.
Mirefen. Mud, leeches, and a Keeper older than both. My favorite.
Had a speech ready, you know. For the bottom of the mountain. "Been a pleasure, kids. The Halcyon calls." Very moving. There was a bit with a sunset.
Don\'t. Don\'t make it a thing, sparrow. Walk.

Brother Halvard rang the great bell of Frosthollow and brought the mountain down between Garrick\'s soldiers and us. Between them and the children. He didn\'t come down. The children sang the whole way, like he told them. Badly. Loud.
Garrick said the Hierophant sent him. I don\'t believe it. I don\'t want to believe it. We\'re going to warn the other Keepers — Mother Osk in Mirefen first.
Warn the remaining Keepers. Take the eastern road down to Mirefen and find Mother Osk.
Chapter 4 — continued
src/story/ch4b.js: The Pilgrim Road
Three days down out of the Greyspine. The snow becomes rain, the rain becomes fen,
and nobody says very much at all.
So. Swamp.
Fen, kid. A swamp is a fen that\'s let itself go.
It smells like a swamp.
They all do.
He\'d have had a word for it. Halvard. Some old monk word for "place that smells."
I\'m fine. I am entirely — I\'m fine.
You are not fine. Your face is doing the thing.
What thing?
The thing Wren\'s face did at the Kindling. Before she cried.
I did _not_—
Wren takes the case of tuning forks out of her pack. Five silver forks in blue velvet, humming faintly in the rain.
Halvard said they\'re not tuned to the Dawnsong. They\'re tuned to its _reflection_.
Three things. One: the Hierophant gave you those. Two: Garrick\'s soldiers have been a day behind us since Saltglass. Three: Halvard is dead because of whatever they\'re for.
We don\'t know that.
We don\'t _know_ it.
Here\'s what I know. Cassian Lorne once pulled me out of a burning troop-ship by my collar.
And in twenty years I have never once seen that man do anything without knowing exactly why.
They are singing. Very quietly.
The same song the Lantern sang when I stood in it. But backwards.
Can we chuck \'em in the swamp?
She shuts the case. It goes on humming.
Mother Osk keeps the Mirefen Lantern. If the Choir\'s been here—
Then she needs to know what Halvard knew.
And we need a roof. And soup. Halvard used to say soup was a sacrament.
Was that a joke? Did the big guy just make a joke?
It was a _tribute_.
Follow the causeway east to Mirefen and find its Keeper, Mother Osk.
Halvard is gone. We came down out of the mountains into the fens without him. The forks are still in my pack. I can\'t make myself throw them away.
A notice, nailed to the post. The rain has run the ink — but not enough.

*WANTED* by order of the Lord-Commander of the Dawnguard:
A GIRL, black hair, pale, about sixteen, answers to "Sable."
Traveling with a red-haired Vanguard; a Mender; a disgraced squire; a street child; and a man who owes money.
*5,000 gold — ALIVE.*
"A street child." I\'ve got a _name_.
"A man who owes money." That\'s slander.
"Disgraced squire." They didn\'t even spell it wrong. I\'d have preferred they spelled it wrong.
"Alive." He wants me alive.
That\'s... good?
I do not know. I do not know what he wants me alive _for_.
Five thousand gold. We could turn you in and steal you back.
I like how the kid thinks.
Dawnguard Sergeant
Halt! By order of the Lord-Commander, every traveler on this causeway is to be searched for—
Black hair. Pale. That\'s _her_. That\'s the—
Sergeant! Is it Sergeant? I can\'t tell with the helmet. Hello. We are a traveling theater troupe.
Kestrel? Bram _Kestrel_?
Not a very _good_ theater troupe.
Take the girl! The rest are worth nothing!
The Lord-Commander will hear of this, Kestrel! He\'ll — he\'ll—
They knew my name.
Everybody knows your name, big man. You say it very loudly.
Garrick has pickets this far south. Either he\'s ahead of us, or he\'s everywhere.
Then we keep moving.
Word came down the water: Mother Osk\'s sitting up and shouting at people. Best news I\'ve had in a month.
If you\'re ever back this way, my punt\'s yours. Free. Well. Half price.
Gaspar\'s the name, poling\'s the game. Was the game. Nobody\'s crossing the fen since the light went out.
Mother Osk took the fever the very night the Choir barge came. Coincidence, the Choir said. Very sure of themselves, the Choir.
The village is east. Mind the toads. They\'ve gone strange.
Are you from the Cathedral? Did they send it back? Did they—
Oh. You\'re... you\'re children.
We\'re carrying letters to the Keepers. From Aurenne. The Hierophant sent us.
_The Hierophant._
Then you\'re too late. Or too early. I don\'t know which.
Mother Osk has the rot. The black-vein fever. Doctor Vey says she won\'t see morning.
Where is she?
In the Lantern. She won\'t let us move her. She says a Keeper dies at her light.
I\'m a Mender. Take me to her. Now, please.
The Lantern — north-east, past the Rot House! Hurry!
Well. That\'s the soup off.
I know. I know. Jokes are a reflex. Like flinching.
Go to Mother Osk in the Mirefen Lantern, north-east of the village.
Mirefen. Mother Osk is dying of the Gloam-rot, and her Lantern is dark. Ilse didn\'t even wait to be asked.
The room smells of willow bark and fever. In the bed against the wall, under three blankets, a small old woman is shivering hard enough to rattle the frame.
Mother Osk
She\'s been saying that for two days.
Ysolde Halloway, you\'ve got _old_. Where are your manners? Where\'s my tea?
That\'s my mother.
Course it is. Same chin. Stubborn chin. I told your mother no too, didn\'t I. No, no—
Black veins to the shoulder. Fever — very high. And her breath—
It rattles. It\'s in her lungs.
Doctor Vey
Three weeks of rot, four days of fever. It\'s at her shoulder now. I\'ve tried willow, feverfew, eel-oil and prayer. In that order, then in every other order.
You\'re the Mender? You\'re _sixteen_.
And you\'re out of ideas.
Don\'t be. It\'s true.
My grandmother has a book. There\'s a recipe in it — _for the black-vein fever of the fens._
Lanternmoss, for the light it remembers. A weepcap lily, for the dark it grew in. And the gall of the thing that\'s making it.
The old bog remedy. Every grandmother in Mirefen knows it.

Every grandmother in Mirefen also knows that lanternmoss only grows on the Sunken Shrine, weepcaps only in the Root Grotto, and whatever\'s making the rot lives in the black pool at the heart of the Drownmere.
Nobody has come back out of the Drownmere since the Lantern went dark.
Nobody has gone in with a Vanguard, a Warden, a — whatever Sable is—
—a thief and a pirate.
Rogue. It\'s a Crest now. I\'m _official_.
Three things. One: Doctor Vey keeps her breathing until we\'re back. Two: I\'ll need a mortar and a clean pot. Three—
Three: we\'re going into the bog.
Three: _I\'m_ going into the bog. You\'re coming because you\'d follow me anyway.
_(grinning)_ Same as always?
Opposite of always.
Take the punt from the south jetty. I\'ll tell the warden to let you through.
I know what a fever is.
In the Drownmere (south jetty): gather Lanternmoss at the Sunken Shrine (west) and a Weepcap Lily in the Root Grotto (east).
Ilse has a plan. Ilse always has a plan — but this one is HERS, and I\'m following it into a bog. I think she\'s been waiting her whole life for someone to need her this much.
Mother Osk is asleep, or something like it. Her lips keep moving.
_No. No. No._
Still here? Elowen\'s in the Heartwood, past Rootholm, through the Thornwood. North out of the village, then east.
Tell her Osk says she still owes me a goose. She\'ll know.
Ysolde\'s girl. Go on, then. Go and be stubborn somewhere useful.
And if you see your mother before I do — tell her I said she was right. She\'ll hate that.
You did it? You really — go on, go to her! Quickly!
The Drownmere\'s past the south jetty. Bring the punt back. Bring yourselves back.
I keep making her soup. She can\'t eat it. I keep making it.
Please. Whatever you can do.
I polish the cradle every morning. For when the stone comes back.
It will come back. Won\'t it?
I gave it to them, you know. The stone.
I stood there and let them carry it out of the Lantern, because they had a seal and I had a fever and a frightened face.
Mother Osk says it isn\'t my fault.
Is she? Then how do you stop feeling like it is?
I don\'t know. I\'ll tell you if I find out.
Here. Lamp-oil from the Lantern. The last of it. It burns blue, and the Gloam hates it.
Welcome to the Leaning Heron! It leans. The beer doesn\'t. Sixty gold a bed, and tonight the beds are full of the _living_. Cheers to the Mender!
Welcome to the Leaning Heron. It leans. The beer doesn\'t. Half my rooms are full of folk waiting to die, half are full of folk waiting to bury them. Sixty gold and I\'ll find you a third half.
the Leaning Heron
_Seven lights at the edge of the world, / seven Keepers keeping; / one by the sea and one in the sand, / one where the snow lies sleeping;_
_one in the fen and one in the wood, / one where the storm-winds wander, / and one in the City of Bells, my love — / and the dark on the other side, yonder._
Old fen song. Older than the Choir. My gran sang the last verse different.
Different how?
"_And one in the City of Bells, my love, that went out once — and grew fonder._"
Never understood it. Nice rhyme, though.
Twenty-four patients. Twenty-four draughts. The girl brewed them all and then fell asleep standing up.
Thirty years a doctor, and a sixteen-year-old taught me something. I\'m going to go and be humbled somewhere private.
Take these. I won\'t need them now. Well — I will. Take them anyway.
I\'ve written her recipe on the inside of my sleeve. I\'m never washing this coat again.
If the girl can really make the Marrow remedy, she\'ll want my mortar. It\'s the one that isn\'t cracked.
The Rot House. Twenty beds. Twenty-four patients. I\'ve stopped being good at sums.
Don\'t touch anyone\'s hands. Don\'t breathe near the coughing ones. Don\'t, on the whole, be here.
Cantor Lisette
I wrote to the Cathedral. I told them the Rot House is empty and asked them to send Mirefen\'s stone home.
They haven\'t answered. They always answer.
I came on the Cathedral\'s barge to tend the sick. When it left, I stayed.
His Grace took the Dawnstone to keep it safe. The Gloam is rising everywhere. Better the stones rest in the Cathedral than be lost.
That\'s what I was told. That\'s what I believe.
Please don\'t look at me like that.
I do not think so.
I know your face. From a painting, I think. In the Cathedral — above the door of His Grace\'s private chapel.
A little girl, holding a lantern. The Hierophant lights a candle under it every morning.
"—four for the eel and five for the frog, six for the Keeper who sings through the fog!"
I can say the whole thing now! The Mender-girl made me drink a boot.
There is no seven.
Seven\'s for you. You choose what it\'s for. That\'s the rule.
I\'m not scared. Mother Osk says the rot is just the dark being rude.
_(She coughs for a long time.)_
Are you the Gloamweaver? Hesk says there\'s a girl with a black Crest.
Is it scary?
It is cold. Sometimes it is lonely.
Mine\'s going to be Mender, I think. Like Mother Osk. Or the one that gets to ride the boats.
I do not know which one that is. I have only had one Crest, and nobody gave it to me.
Do you know the counting rhyme? The Mirefen one?
"One for the Lantern, two for the light, three for the heron that fishes at night—"
Then I will wait, and you will tell me the rest when you can.
Corporal Dace
Serve the light, not the man holding the lamp. I\'m going to try that for a while. See how it fits.
The Mender brought me the draught herself. Didn\'t ask whose side I was on.
So here\'s what I owe you. The Lord-Commander\'s gone north, to the Stormcrown. His warship\'s waiting there. Something to do with Skyreach.
And he\'s left pickets on every road between here and there, looking for your black-haired friend.
Take this. Dawnguard issue. It\'s supposed to keep the dark off you.
Didn\'t work for me. Might for you.
Will you go back? To them?
Don\'t know. Sir Aldous used to say a Dawnguard serves the light, not the man holding the lamp.
Seems to me the man holding the lamp has forgotten that.
_(quietly)_ He said that to me, too.
Garrick\'s column went north, two days back. Toward the Stormcrown.
A soldier who can\'t march is a soldier who can\'t serve. That\'s what he said when they left me.
Don\'t — don\'t come closer. I\'ve got the rot.
That\'s me.
I was in the stands. Third row. You were very... still.
Yes. I\'ve had notes.
The Lord-Commander\'s column came through two days ago, limping down off the Greyspine like whipped dogs. I\'d caught the fever on the march. They left me where I fell.
Garrick says a soldier who can\'t march is a soldier who can\'t serve.
Garrick says a lot of things.
He says a lot of things about you.
Mother Osk says she\'ll Kindle me by candlelight if she has to. Is that allowed?
She says she doesn\'t care if it\'s allowed. I like her a lot.
I\'m sixteen next spring. Mirefen kids get Kindled at our own Lantern.
If the light doesn\'t come back... do I just not get a Crest?
I got mine early. From a blind lady in a desert. It\'s not that great.
What if the light gets me wrong?
Then you tell it so.
Widow Pell
I closed the shutters last night. First time in two winters.
I slept like a stone. I\'d forgotten how.
We found this. In the chapel, in the Drownmere.
"Always the long way home." He had that put on it as a joke. He was always late for supper.
He isn\'t really out there, is he. On the water. It\'s just the fog, remembering him wrong.
The Gloam remembers things. It does not remember them _right_.
Then I\'ll remember him right. That will have to do.
She threads the ring onto the string around her neck, and tucks it under her collar, close.
Tobin grew these on the roof. Swore they\'d make you strong. They never did a thing for him. Maybe you\'ll have better luck.
The old chapel in the Drownmere. He always went the long way round, past it. Please — if you see a ring...
Every night, when the fog comes up, my Tobin walks on the water. Out there, past the reeds.
He drowned two winters ago. Since the Lantern went dark, he comes back. He doesn\'t look at me. He just... walks.
He lost his ring the day he went under. He always took the long way home — past the old chapel in the Drownmere.
I know it isn\'t really him. I know. But if he found it, maybe he\'d stop walking.
We\'re going into the Drownmere anyway. We\'ll look.
The Long Way Home
Widow Pell\'s husband drowned with his wedding ring. Look for it near the old chapel in the Drownmere.
The punt bumps against a rotten jetty. Beyond it lies the Drownmere: black water, white fog, and a silence with something breathing in it.
Lovely. Really. Who wants to go first?
I do.
Ilse — I\'m the Warden, I should—
You should stay behind me and be large.
I can do that.
Pale gold moss grows thick on the shrine stones, in the shape of the lamp that once stood here. It is warm, like a hand.
Lanternmoss. It drank the shrine-lamp\'s light for two hundred years. It still remembers.
It is humming. Like the forks. But _forwards_.
In the deepest hollow of the grotto, a single white lily grows out of the black mud, its petals closed tight.
A weepcap. It\'s never seen the sun — if light touches it, it wilts. Everybody, shade it.
With what?
With Bram.
Happy to help!
Bram looms helpfully. Ilse lifts the lily out of the mud by its roots, as gently as lifting a sleeping child.
That\'s two. The third is whatever\'s making the rot. North, past the shrine island — the black pool.
Burn through the rot-wood north of the shrine island and find the source of the rot in the black pool.
Lanternmoss and a weepcap lily. Ilse knows exactly what she\'s doing. I\'m mostly carrying things and trying not to fall in.
One. Now the weepcap — the Root Grotto, east of the shrine island.
One. Now the lanternmoss — the Sunken Shrine, west of the shrine island.
A wall of black, rotted saplings chokes the path north. The wood is soft and wet and warm, and it is moving — very slightly, like something breathing.
It\'s the rot. Grown solid.
It flinches from light. I can feel it flinch.
The lanternmoss would burn it, but it\'ll gutter out in a breath. I need the weepcap\'s sap to make it last. Lily first — the Root Grotto.
We need something brighter than a torch. Something it remembers. Lanternmoss, from the Sunken Shrine.
Ilse crushes a pinch of lanternmoss into a drop of weepcap sap and blows on it. It catches like a coal — a small, fierce, golden light.
The rot-wood shrivels from the light like a hand from a stove, and crumbles into wet black ash.
The sap makes the moss burn longer. Nana\'s book was right about everything.
Nana\'s book is always right.
Don\'t tell her. She\'ll be unbearable.
On the drowned altar, half-buried in silt, something glints. A plain copper ring.
Inside the band, worn nearly smooth: _T. — always the long way home._
Tobin Pell\'s ring. She\'ll want this back.
Someone\'s wedding ring. Someone in Mirefen might know whose.
The black pool is perfectly still. Bones ring its shore — fish, birds, something larger.
In the middle of the water, bubbles rise. Slowly. Like breathing.
I want it on record that I said "who wants to go first" and meant it rhetorically.
The pool heaves. Something rises out of it — a bloated, eyeless thing of black mud and gristle, ringed with mouths.
That\'s it. That\'s the rot. That\'s what\'s in her lungs.
Then let\'s get it out.
When it is over, Ilse wades into the shallows with her knife and her jaw set, and comes back with something black and dense in a jar.
Rot-gall. The sickness, made solid.
You just — you just stuck your whole arm in that.
It was in Mother Osk\'s lungs. My arm can cope.
Hurry back to Mother Osk in the Mirefen Lantern.
We killed the thing in the black pool. Ilse cut its heart out and put it in a jar. I have never been so proud of anyone, or so glad she\'s on my side.
Ilse works for an hour without speaking. Moss, sap, gall — ground, steeped, strained. The Lantern fills with the smell of it.
Smells like a boot.
Like a boot that drowned and came back angry.
Thank you both. Hold her head, Doctor.
Ilse tips the draught between the old woman\'s lips, a spoonful at a time. Nobody breathes.
Under Osk\'s skin, the black veins tremble — and begin, very slowly, to fade.
Mother Osk!
Hesk. You look terrible. Have you been making soup again? I can smell it from here.
Every day.
Daft heron.
You. Girl. You did this.
With help.
Your hands didn\'t shake.
They did. You just couldn\'t see.
That\'s the whole trick of it, girl.
And you\'re Ysolde\'s. I thought I dreamed you.
You called me by her name.
I\'ve known your mother since she was smaller than that scruffy one.
Came to every Keepers\' Conclave with her nose in a book. Just like you, I expect.
Osk turns her head toward the brass cradle at the heart of the room. It is empty. She looks at it for a long time.
Hesk. Where\'s my stone.
They took it.
The Choir. The night your fever broke out. They had the Hierophant\'s seal. They said the Gloam was rising, that the stone was safer in the Cathedral, that they\'d harmonize it and bring it home—
And you were saying "take it, take it, it\'s too heavy"—
I was talking about the _blanket_, you great soggy heron.
They didn\'t come for safekeeping. They came because I was too sick to say it a third time.
Told _who_ no?
He wanted my stone. Said he needed all seven for something. A "harmony," he called it. He sent me one of those last spring.
Her eyes have gone to Wren\'s pack. Wren takes out the case of forks.
Put that away. I can hear it from here.
I threw mine in the bog. Then the rot came up out of the bog. Make of that what you like.
It sings to the others. All the forks, everywhere. They are waiting for something.
_(very quietly)_ Oh, Cassian. What have you done.
Do you know who I am?
I know who you look like. That isn\'t the same thing.
And it isn\'t my story to tell. I wasn\'t there.
Go to Elowen. In Verdance, at the heart of the Thornwood. She\'s older than dirt and twice as honest — and she was in Aurenne the night the city went dark.
The night the city went — what?
Ask Elowen.
And tell her Osk says she still owes me a goose.
Now. Mender. There are twenty-three people in my Rot House with black in their veins.
Twenty-four. I counted.
Then what are you standing here for?
Ilse doesn\'t sleep that night. Neither does Doctor Vey.
By dawn there is a draught beside every bed in the Rot House, and Vey has the recipe written on the inside of his sleeve.
Mirefen will need a Mender when I\'m gone, you know. A proper one.
I\'m not—
Don\'t tell me what you\'re not. Tell me what you want.
I want to go to the Collegium in Aurenne. To study. Properly.
Not out of Nana\'s book. Not because I happen to be the one standing there.
You never asked.
I— ...No. I didn\'t.
Then want it out loud, girl. Wanting quietly never got anybody anything.
Here. For your rounds. Reed and silver wire — keeps the fen-fevers off. Mostly.
Find Elowen, the oldest Keeper, at the heart of the Thornwood in Verdance. (Leave Mirefen by the north path.)

Mother Osk is alive. The Choir took her Dawnstone while she was too sick to stop them — Cassian\'s people. She looked at Sable and said, "Oh, Cassian. What have you done." Ilse wants to go to the Collegium. She never told me. I never asked.
