s leaning into a gale.
There she is.
It\'s a boat. On a hill.
She\'s a _ship_. And she isn\'t on a hill. She\'s waiting.
She was in pieces in the desert.
She was in _several_ pieces. Now she\'s in one large, deeply offended piece. I left word with the caravans at Saltglass before we went up the mountain.
ASHE! You owe me forty crowns and a mule!
Joss. I owe everybody forty crowns and a mule.
The mule died, Ashe. Hauling your boat out of the Sunscar.
Her name was Patience.
Of course it was.
Right. Shape of it. The singing glass we set in the desert keeps her floating. And I\'ve a hold full of spare saltglass panes.
But floating isn\'t climbing, and the Stormcrown is all climb. Sunlight won\'t carry her through it. For that, the glass needs _lightning_.
Storm-seams, up on the crags. Lightning hits the same three rocks every night up here, and the glass in the strike-holes fuses solid. Full to the brim with thunder.
Storm cores, the prospectors call them. Mind you, the prospectors mostly don\'t come back.
Three cores. One for each lift-cell. Then she\'ll fly.
For how long?
Long enough.
That\'s not a number.
It\'s the only number I\'ve got, kid.
And the crags have... things living on them?
Things _made_ of lightning, big man.
Wonderful. Just wonderful.
Take three Storm Cores from the lightning-struck crags around Stormfoot (west, north-east, south-east), then bring them to Corvin at the Halcyon.
The Halcyon is waiting at the foot of the Stormcrown. Corvin needs three storm cores to make her fly. He says she\'ll fly "long enough." Pip says that isn\'t a number.
You came back down? ...No. No, you didn\'t. I\'m talking to myself again.
Three cores! Go on, then. Fly. I\'ll stand here and pray, which I haven\'t done since I was six.
Three seams: the west crag, the high one north-east, and the shelf to the south-east.
Mind the crag golems. Mostly rock, entirely temper.
And the mule\'s name was Patience. I want that on the record.
The seam is spent: a crater of blackened glass, still warm to the touch.
A crater of black glass where lightning has struck a thousand times. At its heart, a fist of saltglass crackles with trapped light.
It is loud. Inside. Like a crowd that wants to get out.
Can I touch it? I\'m gonna touch it.
My hair is standing up. All of it. Even hair I didn\'t know I had.
The air thickens. The rocks around the seam begin, grumbling, to stand up.
You have three Storm Cores. Bring them to Corvin at the Halcyon.
Storm cores, sparrow. Three. West crag, north-east crag, the south-east shelf.
I\'ll be here, talking to my ship. She\'s a better listener than any of you.
Corvin fits the storm cores into the Halcyon\'s lift-cells one by one, swearing gently at each of them.
The saltglass panes along her hull begin to glow — then to _sing_, a low hum that climbs up through the soles of your boots.
That\'s her. Lift-cells charged, glass singing. She\'ll fly.
His hands are shaking.
Your hands are shaking.
It\'s cold.
It\'s not _that_ cold.
And the Stormcrown isn\'t weather. It\'s weather\'s big angry father.
You don\'t have to fly it, Corvin. We could find another way—
Course I don\'t have to. Nobody _has_ to do anything, big man. That\'s the whole trouble with being a grown-up.
Kid. You want to know how you can tell I\'m still alive?
I\'m terrified every single time.
Board the Halcyon and fly for Skyreach? (There is no coming back down until she\'s repaired.)
Not yet
Take your time. The storm\'s not going anywhere. That\'s rather the problem.
BRAM KESTREL! Step away from the girl!
Captain Corder
Captain Corder, of the Lord-Commander\'s Sunspears. We were in the same squire class, Kestrel. Remember? You were the big one who froze.
The Lord-Commander\'s been and gone from Skyreach already. Their Ardent handed him the stone with a smile. You\'re too late. You\'re always too late.
But he\'ll forgive a great deal if I bring him the girl. Step aside, and I\'ll tell him you were useful. For once.
Bram looks at Sable. His sword hand is shaking. Then, slowly, he steps in front of her.
I\'m still frozen, Corder. I\'m frozen right here.
You\'ll have to move me.
This isn\'t over, Kestrel.
I know. I\'m terrified.
Good man. _Now_ everybody on the ship!
The Halcyon lifts off her cradle with a groan of timber and a sound from the saltglass like a choir clearing its throat.
Come on, girl. Come on. _Up._
WE\'RE FLYING! WE\'RE ACTUALLY—
Don\'t say it!
He said it.
I am a Warden of the Dawnguard. I do not get airsick. This is my normal color.
You said that on the boat.
It was my normal color then, too.
There is something in the clouds. Several somethings.
Shapes uncoil out of the thunderheads — long, winged, crackling — and turn toward the ship.
Drakes! Everybody who isn\'t steering — _fight!_
With a crack like a bone breaking, the first lift-cell goes dark. Then the second.
That\'s one flight! I _said_ one! I was _very clear!_
Corvin — look up!
Above the storm, the clouds tear open — and there, hanging in a sky of impossible blue, is an island.
Green fields. White walls. Windmills turning in a wind from nowhere.
The last lift-cell sputters.
Everybody hold on to something you love!
Dust. Feathers. A great deal of timber that used to be a shed.
The Halcyon lies nose-down in a shipwright\'s yard, steaming gently. Somewhere, a chicken is complaining.
Are we dead? Is this the sky-afterlife?
Everyone count your arms. Two each. Good.
CORVIN. _ASHE._
Ilka! You look wonderful. Have you done something with your—
You put your ship through my roof.
Through your _shed_.
My shed is where I _keep_ my roof!
Eleven years. Eleven years, Ashe, and you owe me nine hundred crowns, and you come back through the _sky_.
Where else would I come back through? It\'s a floating island.
Only my pride.
Your pride was always the most breakable thing on that ship.
And you\'re flying _children_ about now? Have you finally lost your mind?
They\'re not children. They\'re—
I\'m eleven and a half.
Of course you are.
Skyfolk Runner
Shipwright Ilka! The Ardent saw the crash from the Lantern. She wants the ones who came up through the storm brought to her. _Now._
Well, go on. Vasha doesn\'t like to be kept waiting, and I need time to work out what to charge you.
Go to Ardent Vasha at the Lantern, on the northern terrace of Skyreach.
We made it to Skyreach. Mostly. The Halcyon is in a shed, and the shed is no longer a shed. The Ardent wants to see Sable.
She\'s refit. Skyreach-cut crystals, new rigging, and the whole bill on an account in his name I\'ll be collecting on until one of us dies.
Look after him. He\'s not as brave as he pretends to be.
Ashe and I flew cargo together, eleven years back. Then one morning he flew off with my best lift-crystal and a note that said "back by supper."
He\'s very late for supper.
Go on — do whatever the Ardent asked. I\'ll start on the hull. Somebody has to.
Go and see the Ardent. I\'m busy deciding which of his limbs to take as a deposit.
Keel-warden Tamm
A full fathom! A fathom and a half! I could kiss you.
I won\'t. Keel-crew don\'t kiss. But I _could_.
The Ardent sent word. The lift\'s yours — east edge, just past me.
Hold on tight going down. The wind under the isle is mean, and it holds a grudge.
The Keel Lift goes down to the Undercradle. Keel-crew only. Ardent\'s orders.
The isle\'s been dropping. A hand\'s width a day. We don\'t talk about it.
I\'m still hanging chimes. But I\'m hanging them for everybody who flies now. Not just Papa.
Listen! That\'s the new one. It sounds like a bird with hiccups.
Kesi. We found something. Under the isle.
Kesi holds the logbook in both hands and does not open it for a long time.
Will you read the last page? I can\'t. My eyes have gone blurry.
"Kesi — the storm is louder than my heart today, but not by much. I can hear your chimes. I\'m following them home.
If I\'m late, start supper without me. Don\'t wait up. Don\'t stop—"
"Don\'t stop."
He was so close. He could hear them.
He wanted me to keep hanging chimes. Didn\'t he?
Maybe. Or maybe he meant — don\'t stop everything else. Don\'t stop living, just because he\'s late.
Yeah. Maybe both.
These were his spare goggles. He\'d want them to fly. Not sit in a drawer.
Papa\'s glider was called _Kesi\'s Wind_. It had yellow wings. If you see yellow wings anywhere — anywhere at all...
I\'m hanging chimes. Hundreds and hundreds. So when Papa flies home through the storm, he can hear which way Skyreach is.
He went out a year ago, in his glider. Everyone says he\'s gone. Everyone says I should stop.
A year.
My dad\'s boat went down when I was nine. I used to leave a lamp in the window.
Did he come home?
I\'m going to keep hanging them anyway.
Yeah. I know.
Chimes in the Wind
Kesi\'s father Aram flew his yellow-winged glider into the storm a year ago and never came home. If there is any sign of him below the isle, find it.
Come back and fly the red one again whenever! My brother still doesn\'t know.
Wanna fly one? You can borrow the red one. It\'s the best one. It\'s my brother\'s. Don\'t tell him.
Dunno. Kites are for kids.
You ARE a kid.
Pip flies a red kite off the edge of the world. For ten whole minutes, he forgets to look cool.
If I ever get a town of my own — it\'s gonna have kites. Loads of \'em. Everywhere.
Is that a plan?
It\'s a _policy_.
Pip flew a kite on Skyreach. He laughed the whole time and then pretended he hadn\'t. He says if he ever has a town, it\'ll be full of kites.
Ardent Vasha
The Lantern hall is cold and bright and humming. In the brass cradle where the Dawnstone should be, a single silver fork stands upright, singing to itself.
So. The children of Lanternfall.
And the girl.
He said you would come.
Who did?
His Grace. He wrote to me. "If they come, Vasha, be kind to them. They are frightened, and they do not yet understand."
Especially you, little sister.
I am not your sister.
No. You\'re _his_.
Your Dawnstone. Where is it?
Where it belongs. With the Hierophant.
I put it into the Lord-Commander\'s hands myself, three weeks ago, on the steps of this Lantern. Gladly.
Do you know what the Stormcrown takes from us, Mender? Every year? Ships. Sons. Daughters.
My husband went down into it eleven years ago in a skiff called the _Lark_, and it did not even give me back the wood.
His Grace is building a world where nothing is ever lost again. Where the good days — the very best days — never end.
I said yes before he had finished the sentence.
Vasha. He\'s taking the stones from Keepers who say no. Osk nearly died. Elowen got picked up and set down on a log.
Then they should have said yes.
Halvard said no. Halvard is _dead_.
I grieve for Halvard. Truly. He was a good man and a stubborn one.
When the song is sung, perhaps we will have him back as well.
Your fork is singing.
It is harmonizing. Waiting for the others.
It is singing backwards. All of them are. They are waiting for sunset.
All seven? You don\'t _have_ seven. Lanternfall—
Six of seven are his.
Saltglass. Frosthollow — the Lord-Commander\'s men went back for it, after the snow. Mirefen. Thornwood. Skyreach. And the Grand Lantern itself.
They went _back_? After Halvard — they went back up the mountain for it?
His Grace does not leave things unfinished.
Only Lanternfall remains.
My mother won\'t give it to him. She\'s already told him no.
He knows. He told me not to worry about Lanternfall.
He said the last stone would come to him freely. He said the Keeper\'s daughter would bring it.
He seemed very sure.
The whole hall lurches, like a ship striking a reef. Thunder answers — from _underneath_.
Ardent! The Keel\'s dropped another fathom! The old lift-pylons in the Undercradle are failing — and the Thunderhead\'s _climbing_. You can see it from the edge!
It will hold until the Long Light. His Grace promised. He\'ll send the stone back harmonized, before—
Before your whole island falls into the storm?
And you didn\'t think about that when you gave it away?
I thought about it. I _believed_ him.
The Keel Lift is at the east edge. If someone charged the three old pylons beneath the isle, Skyreach might hold. And the Thunderhead—
Let me guess. Somebody has to go and punch the weather.
I can\'t leave the Lantern. I won\'t. Not now.
You owe me nothing. You don\'t believe what I believe. Why would you go?
Because it\'s falling. And we\'re here.
Go. Tell Tamm at the lift that I sent you. Corvin — there are saltglass sockets in every pylon. You\'ll know what to do.
Take the Keel Lift (east edge of Skyreach) down into the Undercradle. Charge the three lift-pylons, then face the Thunderhead.

Six of seven are his. Vasha gave him hers gladly. She says he told her the last stone would come to him freely — that the Keeper\'s daughter would bring it. I would never. I would NEVER. ...And Skyreach is falling into the storm.
Go home, Ysolde\'s daughter. I will pray that you find your mother well.
I will pray for His Grace as well. I no longer know if those are the same prayer.
The Keel Lift is on the east edge. Go, if you are going.
I will be here. With my light.
The isle is holding. Tamm says we\'ve risen a full fathom since you went below.
You went down into the Stormcrown for an island that gave your enemy exactly what he wanted.
He\'s not my enemy.
I believe in him still. I will not pretend otherwise for your sake.
But I will not pretend you didn\'t save my people, either. Ilka is refitting your captain\'s ship. Skyreach-cut crystals. She\'ll fly anywhere now.
Where will you go?
Six of seven.
Saltglass. Frosthollow. Mirefen. Thornwood. Skyreach. Aurenne.
And he said the last one would come to him freely. That the Keeper\'s daughter would bring it.
Mom\'s alone on that island. With the last stone in the world. And he _knows_.
Then we go home.
We go home.
His Grace said the song would be sung at sunset, on the Long Light. That is soon, Wren Halloway. Very soon.
If you reach him before then — what will you do?
Talk to him. He\'ll listen to me.
He always — he writes back. He always writes back.
Ilse looks at Wren for a long moment, and says nothing at all.
It is louder now. The fork. All of them are.
They know the sun is going down.
When you are ready, find Corvin on the Skyreach docks and fly home to Lanternfall.
Six of seven are his. Lanternfall is the last — Mom is the last. Cassian told Vasha the Keeper\'s daughter would bring him the stone. We\'re going home. I\'ll talk to him. He always writes back.
Beneath Skyreach, the island is a great hanging root of stone, open to the sky on every side. Far below, the Stormcrown boils — and something in it is climbing.
I was promised the hard part was over.
Nobody promised you that.
I promised me that.
The pylon hums, steady and bright. The saltglass in its heart is singing.
An old brass pylon, thick with cables, bolted deep into the stone. The saltglass heart at its top is cracked and dark.
Brass eyes open in the rock around it. The Keel Sentinels have been guarding this pylon for three hundred years, and they are not about to stop now.
A drake is coiled around the pylon\'s cables, warming itself on what little charge is left. It does not want to share.
The cables shudder. Something is climbing them from below.
Corvin wedges a pane of desert glass into the socket. The pylon drinks the storm-light out of the air — and roars.
Somewhere along the central bridge, a wall of storm-crystal cracks, and falls away into the sky.
That\'s all three. The way down is open.
All three pylons are charged. Take the central bridge down and face the Thunderhead.
A wall of blue storm-crystal has grown across the bridge, crackling and spitting.
It\'s feeding off the storm. If those pylons were working, they\'d drink it dry.
The wreck of a little yellow-winged glider, tangled in the cables. The wind plays it like a harp.
Tangled in the cables under the rock: the wreck of a one-man glider. Yellow canvas wings, in tatters.
A name is painted on the strut: _KESI\'S WIND_.
Strapped beneath the seat, in an oilskin pouch, is a logbook.
Kesi\'s father. He was so close. He was right under the isle.
There\'s a name in the front. "Aram, Skyreach." Somebody up there might be waiting for this.
The bottom of the isle. Here the stone simply ends, and below it there is nothing but storm — a vast, slow wheel of cloud and lightning, turning.
And in the middle of the wheel, something opens.
It is looking at us.
Can weather look at you? Is that allowed?
Up here, big man, everything\'s allowed.
Then we\'re allowed to hit it. Everyone — _now!_
The Thunderhead tears apart into rain. Above you, all three pylons blaze at once, and the whole island shudders — and _rises_.
Did we just — did we just punch the weather?
WE PUNCHED THE WEATHER!
We should go back up. Vasha needs to know.
Return to Ardent Vasha at the Skyreach Lantern.
We fought a storm. An actual storm, with an eye in the middle. And Skyreach is rising again.
She\'s ready when you are, sparrow. Say the word and we fly west.
Fly home to Lanternfall? (This ends the chapter.)
Fly home
Take your time. Just — not too much of it.
Stay. Fly cargo for me. Get old. Get fat. Pay me back nine hundred crowns at a crown a week.
But I\'ve got passengers.
You have never once in your life stayed where you were needed.
I know.
Thought I\'d give it a try.
Ilka punches him in the shoulder, hard. Then she kisses him on the cheek, harder.
Bring my crystals back in one piece. And yourself. In that order.
The Halcyon flies west through the evening, out of the Stormcrown\'s shadow, over the fens and the forests and the long brown road.
Nobody sleeps.
At the bow, Wren takes out her father\'s compass. The needle points west. It always points west.
Three things.
One: you\'re going to want to talk to him. Cassian. Two: I am going to be standing right next to you when you do.
And three?
Three: if he says anything — _anything_ — that makes you want to give him that stone, you look at me first.
I would never give it to him.
Then it\'s an easy promise.
The sun is going down.
It does that.
Not for much longer, I think.
Lanternfall by morning, sparrow. Hold on to something.
Hold on, Mom. I\'m coming home.
We\'re flying home. Ilse made me promise to look at her first, if Cassian says anything that makes me want to give him the stone. I said okay.
The Last Sunset
Get home to Lanternfall.
src/story/ch4b_verdance.js: The Pilgrim Road
Verdance. The oldest forest in Solmere. The trees here were old when the Lanterns were new.
Trees. Lots of trees. Do these ones talk? The Whisperwold ones talked.
These ones just judge you silently.
The leaves are turning. It is not autumn.
She\'s right. Look — half that oak is brown. In early summer.
Elder Bracken
Travelers. In Rootholm we say: may your roots find water.
And, ah — may yours?
Close enough.
You\'ve come for the Keeper. Everyone who comes to Rootholm has come for the Keeper. Lately, they come with swords.
We\'ve come to warn her. Mother Osk sent us.
Then you are a month too late, child.
Soldiers came. White and gold, the Hierophant\'s sun on their shields. They went into the Thornwood, and they came out carrying the Keeper\'s light in a box.
Since then the forest has closed its fist. Thorns where the paths were. And the Warden — the great tree that has guarded the grove for six hundred years — attacks anything that moves.
Elowen has not come out. We do not know if she still lives.
And two days ago, three of our children went into the Tangle to bring her bread.
They have not come back either.
Three children. In there. For two days.
We\'re going in anyway. We\'ll find them.
Wick, Bryony and Tamsel. Wick is the one who never stops talking. Bryony is the one who never starts. Tamsel is the one who thinks he is in charge.
I like Tamsel already.
Lost Saplings
Three Rootholm children — Wick, Bryony and Tamsel — went into the Thornwood to bring Elowen bread. Find them.
Enter the Thornwood (north of Rootholm) and find Elowen — and Rootholm\'s three lost children.
Verdance. The soldiers took Elowen\'s light a month ago, and the forest has been dying ever since. Three kids went in after her with a loaf of bread. Of course they did.
The leaves on the old oak have stopped browning. The forest is holding its breath, I think, to see what you do.
Rootholm owes you three children. That is a debt we do not know how to pay. We will think of something.
All three. All three, home, with scratches and appetites and not a single apology between them.
This was Elowen\'s, long ago. She gave it to Rootholm\'s first Elder. Moss grows on it in any season. So do wounds close, on whoever wears it.
Wick, Bryony and Tamsel. The Tangle is north, past Old Holm at the gate. Bring them home, if you can.
Old Holm
The Warden\'s quiet. First time in a month I\'ve slept through the night.
I dreamt of nothing at all. It was wonderful.
Fifty years I\'ve kept this gate. Never had to close it.
Now the forest closes it for me. Thorns as thick as your arm, and they glow at night. Violet. Like the inside of a bruise.
My Wick. He\'s nine. He talks so much I sometimes pray for a quiet minute.
I\'ve had two days of quiet now. I\'d give anything to have him talk my ear off.
He\'s home. He hasn\'t stopped talking since. About you, mostly. And the big man. And the "spooky girl" — his words, sorry.
I have never been so glad to be deafened.
Bryony doesn\'t speak much. Not since her gran died, in the spring.
She said the lights in the forest were Gran, come to visit. I told her not to be silly. I wish I hadn\'t.
She told me what the Mender said. That it\'s all right to miss Gran even though the lights weren\'t her.
She told me in _words_. A whole sentence. Thank you.
Tamsel\'s thirteen. Thinks he\'s a man grown. He\'ll have marched the other two in there.
If you find him — tell him he\'s not in trouble. He is. But tell him he isn\'t.
He came home and announced he is going to be a Warden and a Rogue. At the same time.
I told him that\'s not allowed. He said your small friend said it was. Is it?
This is the Memory Tree. When someone in Rootholm dies, we tie a ribbon on it with their name.
So the forest remembers them. And remembers them _right_ — not the way the dark does.
If you\'ve someone of your own to remember, there\'s ribbon in the basket. Anyone may tie one.
Hundreds of ribbons stir in the blossoming branches. Near the bottom, tied in a careful double knot, a gray one reads: _BROTHER HALVARD. FROSTHOLLOW._
Hundreds of ribbons hang from the blossoming tree, each one knotted around a name. They stir in a wind you can\'t feel.
Yeah. Yeah, Bram. We should.
Bram picks a gray ribbon from the basket. His hands are too big for the knot. He does it anyway, twice, until it holds.
Brother Halvard. Frosthollow. He made terrible tea, and he was the bravest man I ever met.
You\'re the bravest man I ever met.
I\'m not. That\'s the point. He was, and he\'s — and I\'m still here.
You are still here because he chose that you would be.
Then you\'d better make it worth his while, big man.
I\'ll try. I\'ll — I\'ll try.
We tied a ribbon for Halvard on Rootholm\'s Memory Tree. Bram did the knot. It took him two tries. Nobody helped.
The Tangle. The trees have grown together overhead, and the light down here is green and very old. Here and there, between the roots, something violet glows.
The roots taste wrong. Like the sea.
You _tasted_ them?
Not with my mouth.
A wall of thorns blocks the trail — each spine as long as a finger, black at the root, glowing violet at the tip.
Okay. Stand back.
Wren\'s blade rings off the thorns like a bell. Bram\'s does the same. Corvin\'s shot vanishes into them without a sound.
Well, that\'s insulting.
They\'re not wood. They\'re Gloam. The dark, grown up through the roots where the light used to be.
Let me try.
Sable reaches out a hand. Before her fingers touch them, the thorns _flinch_ — curling back on themselves, withering, sinking into the earth like frightened things.
Okay, that\'s creepy.
It\'s a _little_ creepy!
It is a little creepy.
More thorns. Sable stands in front of them and does not lift her hand.
When I touch them, they go quiet. Like a dog that knows its master.
Wren. What if I _am_ the master?
Then you\'re a master who tells them to get out of the way. That\'s a good master.
That is a very Wren answer.
Thank you?
The thorns shrink away from her hand, and the path opens.
The last of the thorns. Beyond them, something enormous creaks, like a ship at anchor.
I am not afraid of them anymore. I think they are afraid of me.
I would rather they were not. But I will use it.
Whatever\'s behind that — it\'s big. Let\'s rest at the Hearthstone first.
Are you the Gloam? Mum says the Gloam has nice faces so it can trick you. You\'ve got nice faces. Not him.

I twisted my ankle and Tamsel said wait here and he\'d come back and he didn\'t, and Bryony went to find him, and she didn\'t either, and I\'ve been here since yesterday, and I ate all the bread, and I\'m sorry about the bread.
Let me see the ankle.
Sprained. Not broken. You\'ll live.
Will Mum let me live?
That\'s outside my expertise.
I can walk. I can limp. I can limp _fast_. Thank you, Gloam-people!
A small girl in a yellow ribbon sits between the roots, very still, watching the dark between the trees.
Bryony? Your mother sent us. Are you hurt?
The lights. They\'re Gran. She came to see me.
Between the trees, soft golden lights are gathering — drifting closer, humming, warm as lamplight.
They are not your gran. They are what is left of the Lantern\'s light. They are lost, and they are frightened, and they will hurt you.
No. I\'m sorry.
My grandmother\'s still alive. I left her on an island at the edge of the world without saying goodbye properly. I think about her every day.
It\'s all right to miss her, Bryony. Even if the lights weren\'t her. Missing her is how you keep her.
I\'m going to go home now and tell Mum.
Halt! Who goes there? I\'m armed.
That\'s a bread knife.
It\'s _very_ sharp bread.
I\'m not lost. I\'m scouting. The Keeper\'s grove is that way, and I\'m bringing her the last loaf, and I\'m not going home until I do.
Kid. Listen.
I\'m eleven. I\'ve got a Crest. I\'ve been in four dungeons and a sewer. You know what I learned?
Being brave is dumb. Go home and eat the bread.
And a half.
And you\'ve got a _Crest_?
Rogue. And when I\'m older I\'ll get another one. Maybe Warden, like the big guy. You can have more than one now. It\'s allowed.
Is it allowed?
It\'s complicated.
Fine. I\'ll go home. But you have to take the bread to the Keeper.
All three children are on their way home. Push on through the Thornwood to Elowen\'s grove.
The glade ahead is ringed with dead trees. Then one of them takes a step.
It is taller than the Lanternfall bell-tower. Its bark is split and bleeding sap; violet thorns grow out of the wounds. Two knots of amber light, high up, turn toward you.
That\'s — that\'s the Warden. That\'s a _tree_.
That\'s a building that\'s angry.
It is not angry. It is frightened. It has been fighting the dark for a month and nobody came to help.
Then let\'s help it stop.
Hollowbark sways. The violet thorns crumble out of its wounds like ash.
Somewhere beyond the glade, a voice — old as rain — says: _Hush, old friend. Hush. They are not the ones who took it._
The great tree lowers itself, root by root, into the earth. Its amber eyes close. In a moment, it is only a tree, and the path north lies open.
Did everyone hear that?
Go north into the Heartwood and meet Elowen.
The Thornwood opens like a held breath let go.
Inside is a grove of very old trees, and in the middle of the grove, a Lantern. Roots have climbed its walls. Blossom grows inside its lamp. It is dark.
At its foot sits a woman so old she looks less like a person than like a tree that has decided, for now, to be one.
You quieted my Warden. Thank you. He has been so frightened.
Come closer, children. My eyes are not what they were. Nothing is.
Keeper Elowen? I\'m Wren Halloway, from Lanternfall. Mother Osk sent us.
Osk. Is she well?
She is now. She says you still owe her a goose.
Elowen laughs — a sound like wind moving through high branches.
Forty-one years she has been saying that. It was a very good goose.
Halloway. Ysolde\'s daughter. Yes. You have her—
Chin. I know.
I was going to say "hurry." Your mother was always in a hurry too.
Keeper — your stone. Rootholm says soldiers took it.
A month ago. The Hierophant\'s sun on every shield. They were very polite, and very many.
I told them no. I stood in front of my light, and a young man in armor picked me up like a bundle of kindling and set me down on that root, there. Gently. He apologized.
Then they went into my Lantern, and came out carrying the morning in a box.
Garrick\'s men.
Why? What does he want them for? Osk said you\'d know. She said you were in Aurenne the night the city went dark.
Osk talks too much. It is her finest quality.
Sit down. All of you. This is a story for sitting down.
Forty years ago, at Midsummer, the Seven Keepers came to Aurenne for the Festival of Long Light. The longest day of the year. The whole city was bells and paper lanterns and honey-cake.
The Keeper of the Grand Lantern then was Aurelian Lorne. A proud man, and a tired one. He had a son, twelve years old, who never stopped asking questions.
And a daughter. Lysa. She was ten.
Lysa Lorne had a gap in her front teeth she could whistle through. She was afraid of geese. And she had decided — because of my hair — that I was a witch.
She brought me a crown of clover, to see if I would turn into a tree.
Did you?
Not that day.
That night, after the sun went down, the Grand Lantern failed.
Not dimmed. _Failed._ For the first time in a thousand years. Nobody has ever known why.
And the Gloam came into Aurenne the way the tide comes into a cave. Through the streets. Up the stairs. Into the houses. Cold, and gray, and full of whispering.
Everything it touched, it _remembered_ — and took into itself.
Aurelian had a choice. He could hold the light with both hands — pour every scrap of himself into the lamp until it caught again. Or he could let it go, and run for his children.
He held the light.
Every Keeper in the city would have done the same. It is what we are taught. It is what I told him afterwards, when he could not stop shaking. _You saved a hundred thousand people, Aurelian._
Cassian was twelve. He had his sister by the hand when the dark came down the Street of Bells.
And then he didn\'t.
When the Lantern caught again, the Gloam drew back to the edge of the world, the way it does. And it took everything it had remembered with it.
Cassian stood at the end of that street until morning, calling her name. When the sun came up — when we sang it up, all seven of us, with our voices breaking — he was still calling.
I carried him home myself. He weighed nothing at all.
_(very quietly)_ Cassian Lorne.
He never cried, that I saw. He only asked his father, every day for a year: _why did you choose the light?_
Aurelian never had an answer. He died with that question still sitting at his table.
And the boy grew up, and became the Hierophant, and the whole world loves him. And I think he has spent forty years writing his father an answer.
The stones. The forks.
A song, I think. Something only all seven Lanterns could sing at once.
The Gloam remembers everything it takes, child. Every face. Every voice. If you could reach into it with enough light — the light of seven Lanterns at once—
You could bring someone back.
Come here, child. The quiet one. I have been looking at you since you walked into my grove, and I am much too old to pretend I haven\'t.
The old Keeper lifts one hand, slow as a branch in still air, and touches Sable\'s cheek.
No gap in the teeth. But the rest...
The rest is exactly as I remember it.
Am I her?
Lysa Lorne would be fifty years old this summer. She would have gray in her hair. Children, perhaps. And she would still be afraid of geese.
You are sixteen. And I think you will be sixteen for exactly as long as someone wants you to be.
He made me.
Someone remembered her very hard, for a very long time, at the edge of the dark. And the dark is made of remembering.
Then I am his memory of her.
That is why the Lantern went black at my Kindling. That is why he called me Lysa.
I am a copy of a girl who died. Made by a boy who could not stop calling.
I do not whistle. I have never met a goose.
No. You haven\'t.
Do you know what I think, child? I think a face is the very least of what a person is.
Lysa was not her face. She was the gap in her teeth and the clover and the geese. She was all the things she found out about herself, one at a time, for ten years. And then she stopped finding out.
You haven\'t stopped. You have hardly begun.
Tell me. What do you like, Sable?
Bread. When it is warm.
Rain. Cats. The way Pip lies.
When Wren reads out loud and does all the voices wrong.
_(a laugh that is mostly something else)_ I do _not_—
Lysa never had a single one of those. They are yours.
You will have to find out the rest. Whether you can whistle. What you think of geese. That is what a person is, I think. Not a face. The finding out.
I would like to be the one who finds out.
Then you will be.
I have something that belongs to her. Or to you. I am not sure which, and I think that is for you to decide.
From between the pages of an old book, Elowen draws a flat brown circle of pressed clover, forty years dry.
She made it for me. To see if I would turn into a tree.
_(smiling)_ Slowly.
Keeper Elowen. If the Lanternfall light failed — if it were my mother, holding it—
Would she choose the light too?
Every Keeper would. Your mother too, I expect.
It is the worst thing about us. And the best.
Mirefen\'s light is gone. Mine is gone. I would be very surprised if Saltglass and Frosthollow still have theirs. And the Grand Lantern was always his.
That leaves Skyreach, and Lanternfall.
Vasha keeps Skyreach. She will not listen to you — she listens to the wind, and to Cassian, and lately mostly to Cassian. But if Skyreach still has its stone, there is still time.
Skyreach. A rock floating over the Stormcrown. Nobody gets up there without wings.
I am told you have some, Captain.
The Halcyon should be on her cradle at Stormfoot by now, at the bottom of the Stormcrown. I paid a caravan every coin I had to haul her up out of the sand. She floats. She doesn\'t _climb_.
Charge her saltglass with enough lightning, though, and she might fly. Once. Maybe.
Maybe is a very respectable word in my profession, kid.
Rest tonight. The grove is safe, now that my Warden sleeps. In the morning, the forest will let you out the short way.

Elowen told us about the night Aurenne went dark. Cassian had his little sister by the hand, and then he didn\'t. Sable has her face. Sable asked "Am I her?" and Elowen said: a person is the finding out. I keep thinking about the Keeper\'s choice. Every Keeper would choose the light. Mom too.
Night in the Heartwood. Fireflies drift between the old trees. Someone has made a fire; nobody remembers who.
I owe that man my life. Twice, if you count the court-martial he talked them out of.
And I keep thinking — what would I do, if it were my little sister at the end of that street?
Not this.
No. Something stupider, probably. I\'m not as clever as he is.
It\'s not about clever. Halvard died. Osk nearly died. Mirefen was rotting. Rootholm\'s trees are dying. That\'s what his answer costs.
Hey. Sable.
For what it\'s worth — I don\'t remember my mum\'s face either. So I made one up.
She\'s got a gold tooth. She sings really badly. She\'s _very_ proud of me.
Is that a joke?
Which half?
Dunno. That\'s the thing about making it up. You get to pick.
Sable makes a small sound. It takes everyone a moment to work out that it is a laugh.
Did — did she just laugh? At _me_? I\'m hilarious. I always knew I was hilarious.
You made her laugh, Pip.
Shut up. It was an accident.
Later. The others are asleep, or pretending.
Wren. When you named me. Did you know?
Know what?
That I did not have one. That there was nothing for me to remember.
I just thought you looked like a Sable.
I am going to keep it.
The name?
All of it.
Every Keeper would choose the light. Mom too.
Dad\'s boat went down in sight of the Lantern. I always wondered why she didn\'t—
Morning in the Heartwood. Speak with Elowen before you go.
Good morning, Ysolde\'s daughter. You slept badly. Good. It means you were listening.
Go to the Stormcrown. And Wren — when you see Cassian, and you will—
remember that he was a boy at the end of a street, calling.
It will not make him less dangerous. But it may make you less cruel. And you will need to be less cruel than he is, if you are going to win.
The forest will let you out to the west now. The short way.
Oh — uh. Tamsel from Rootholm sent you this. It\'s bread. It\'s, uh. Mostly bread.
Tamsel. The one who thinks he is in charge.
Tell him the Keeper said it was the best bread she has ever eaten. And give him this, from me, for his trouble.
Travel to Stormfoot, at the base of the Stormcrown, where the Halcyon waits. (West path out of the grove → world map.)

Elowen said: remember that he was a boy at the end of a street, calling. It won\'t make him less dangerous. It might make me less cruel. Next: the Stormcrown, and the Halcyon, and Skyreach — if Vasha still has her stone.
Go on, children. The Stormcrown is north and west of here — follow the thunder.
And tell Osk I have not forgotten the goose.
src/story/ch5.js: The Last Sunset
The sun was setting over Lanternfall.
It had been setting for a very long time.
We made it. We— okay. We made it.
Fastest flight the old girl ever made. Held together with storm cores and spite.
Behind you, out in the shallows, the Halcyon settles onto the flat water with a long, tired groan of timber, like an old dog lying down.
And that\'s the last of the cores. She won\'t lift again without three more and a miracle.
This is it? This is the whole island? I\'ve seen bigger puddles in the Undercroft.
Wren. Look at the sun.
It sits on the edge of the sea, swollen and red, like a coin someone forgot to drop.
It is not moving. I watched it the whole way in. It has not moved.
Suns move. That\'s— that\'s the main thing about them. That\'s their whole job.
On the bluff, the Lantern is lit. And it is humming — a low, steady note you feel in your teeth more than hear.
That sound. I know that sound.
The forks.
The ones we carried. To every Lantern in the world.
Wren? Wren Halloway, as I live and— thank the tide. Your mother said you\'d come. She said it like a curse.
Tobias. Where is she?
In the Lantern. Three days now. Hierophant\'s up there with her, comes and goes like he owns the place. And his soldiers are on the hill road. Nobody up. Nobody down.
Sun\'s been sat on that water since noon yesterday. Gulls stopped flying this morning. They just sit on the roofs. Staring at it.
_(quietly)_ Six of seven, sparrow. And here we are at number seven.
Tobias — Nana. Is Nana—
Fine, love. Worried sick and cooking about it. Go see her.
And Wren — the soldiers turned back Old Corrin this morning, and he\'s eighty. Don\'t go starting a war on the hill road.
I wasn\'t going to start one.
_(to Bram)_ She was totally gonna start one.
Find a way up to the Lantern. Look in on Nana Brisa and the village first.
We came home. The sun won\'t set. The Lantern is humming the note from the forks we carried — and Mom has been up there with Cassian for three days.
Turned you back, did they. ...Course they did.
There\'s another way up. The old Keeper\'s Stair. Your grandmother\'s grandmother\'s grandmother cut it, so a Keeper could bring the light down to the boats in a storm.
Top end comes out on the bluff, behind the Lantern. Bottom end\'s in the tide caves, way at the back. Your father found it when we were boys. Him, me, and Fen.
Who\'s Fen?
Nobody you\'d remember. Point is, the bottom end\'s been sealed with rock since before you were born. And lately something\'s been growing over the rock. Something purple.
You know it?
We\'ve met.
Then mind yourselves. Folk say the caves have been singing lately. Low, like a man humming in the next room.
Go through the Tide Caves (east road) and find the bottom of the Keeper\'s Stair.
Tobias says there\'s a secret stair from the tide caves to the Lantern. Dad found it when he was a boy — with Tobias and someone called Fen.
Boat\'s ready. I\'ve readied her four times today. Keep her ready, your father always said. You never know when the sea\'s going to change its mind.
Go on. Bring your mother down off that hill.
Go see Brisa, see the house. Then go ask those soldiers what they think they\'re guarding.
Come tell me what they say. I\'ve got thoughts, but I\'d like to be wrong first.
Vesper Sergeant
Still closed, girl. Still orders.
Halt. By order of Lord-Commander Thorne, the hill road is closed for the duration of the harmonization.
My mother is up there. I\'m the Keeper\'s daughter.
Sergeant. What\'s the Lord-Commander afraid of? Five tired children and a pirate?
He said you\'d say something like that, Kestrel. He said to tell you: "Go home."
_(quietly)_ I\'m trying.

Wren. Three things. One: there are at least twenty of them on that hill. Two: they\'re rested and we aren\'t. Three: your mother is at the top, and a fight would bring the whole Dawnguard down on her.
Then we don\'t fight our way up. There\'s always another way. There has to be.
Every rich man\'s house has a back door. Every single one. That\'s, like, the first thing they teach you.
Tobias. Tobias knows every inch of this island.
Ask Fisher Tobias (down at the docks) for another way up to the Lantern.
How did you get up THERE?
Magic. Also stairs.
Hill road\'s closed. Go home, girl. Watch the sunset like everyone else.
It smells like home. Salt and woodsmoke and Mom\'s awful lavender soap.
There\'s a letter on the table. With my name on it.
Two plates. And your mother\'s letter, folded back along its creases. You don\'t need to read it again. You read it again anyway.
Two plates on the table, as always. Between them, a letter, in your mother\'s narrow, careful hand.
_Little bird —_
_If you\'re reading this, you came home. I knew you would. You never could leave a door alone._
_Stay in the house. Whatever you hear, whatever the sky does, stay in the house. I\'ll come down when it\'s over._
_There\'s bread in the box. It isn\'t as good as Nana\'s._
_— Mom_
_P.S. I\'m proud of you. I should have said it at the dock._
Stay in the house. Sure, Mom. That\'s exactly what I\'ll do.
Mom left me a letter. She told me to stay in the house. She said she\'s proud of me. She\'s never said that before.
The bread box. Empty now, except for crumbs.
The bread box. Inside, a heavy, slightly burnt loaf wrapped in a cloth. It is not as good as Nana\'s. It never has been.
Your father\'s books — and on top of them, a bundle of letters tied with string. The Choir\'s sunburst on every seal. Cassian\'s letters. To you.
Your mother has read them all. In the margins, in her small hand, there are notes. Not angry ones. Careful ones. Like a Keeper reading weather.
Beside the line _"You have a restless heart, Wren, like mine"_ she has written only: _That is what I am afraid of._
Go on, my darlings. Go and bring Ysolde down off that hill.
And Ilse — keep your scarf on. Whatever the sky is doing, it\'s doing it in a draft.
Sea lavender, love. Just one sprig. It grows in the tide-cave pools — or there\'s the one in Ysolde\'s garden, if it ever deigned to flower.
Ilse? ...Ilse!
Nana Brisa crosses the room faster than a woman her age has any right to and holds Ilse very tight for a very long time.
Let me look at you. You\'ve grown.
I\'ve been gone two months, Nana. I haven\'t grown.
You have. Around the eyes.
And my duck from the sea! Have you been eating?
I ate a pie in Aurenne. There was a bird in it. I was very surprised.
And who\'s this scrap?
Pip. And I ain\'t a scrap.
We\'re all scrap, love. Sit down, I\'ll feed it. And you — the tall one with the hat and the guilty face?
Just the driver, ma\'am.
You\'ve got a hungry look. Sit.
Nana. The sun—
I know, dear. I\'ve been watching it from the step since yesterday noon. It isn\'t right.
So I\'ve done the only thing I know how to do when things aren\'t right. I\'m making tea.
Of course you are.
Kindling tea. Your great-grandmother brewed it the night before every hard thing. Only I\'m short the sea lavender.
It grows in the tide-cave pools, and those are full of nasty things this week. The only other sprig on the island is in Ysolde\'s garden, and that plant has never once flowered.
We\'ll find you some, Nana.
Kindling Tea
Nana Brisa wants one sprig of sea lavender for her Kindling tea — the brew the Halloways drank before every hard thing. It grows in the tide-cave pools. Or in Ysolde\'s garden, if it ever flowered.

s herb garden. Where the sea lavender was, there\'s a small torn stem.
Your mother\'s herb garden. Rosemary, thyme — and the sea lavender. It has flowered. After seven years of nothing, today, of all days, it has flowered.
Your mother\'s herb garden. The sea lavender that never once flowered has flowered. Seven years of nothing — and today, of all days, a spray of tiny violet stars.
Pick a sprig for Nana Brisa\'s tea?
Pick it
Leave it
Sorry, Mom. You can yell at me when you come down.
A tide pool, black and still. Something purple glimmers on the bottom and is gone.
In a crack at the edge of the pool, a stubborn little clump of sea lavender has found something to hold on to.
Ah. There it is. Give it here.
The kettle sings. Nana Brisa crumbles the lavender into the pot with her fingers, the way her mother did, and the whole house smells, for a moment, like the beach on a good day.
Drink. It tastes like a beach and a hug.
It tastes like a beach.
Keep drinking.
My mother made something like this. The night before my knighting trial. I drank three cups and then I—
It was good tea.
Haven\'t had tea since the Dawnguard. We used to put rum in it.
I put rum in it.
Drink your tea.
Everyone is holding a warm cup at the same time. Is this a ceremony?
It\'s... yes. Sort of.
I like it. I want to remember it.
Nana. When this is over, I\'m coming home. For good.
No, you\'re not.
I— what?
You\'re going to be a great Mender somewhere much bigger than this island. And you\'ll write to me twice a week in your tidy little letters, and I\'ll pretend I can read them.
And you, little Halloway. You haven\'t touched yours.
Your mother drank this the night before her Kindling. And the night before her wedding. And the night your father didn\'t come home.
No. But she wasn\'t alone while she drank it.
You drink your tea.
Take the rest of the pot with you. Corked. For later.
We drank Nana\'s Kindling tea, all six of us. Corvin proposed to her. Nana told Ilse she\'s not allowed to come home and waste herself on this island.
Rule one: be scared. Rule two: do it anyway.
I\'m being scared REALLY good, Bram!
Wren! You\'re back! Is that BRAM? Bram, teach me to fight! I\'m getting Vanguard when I\'m sixteen, I know I am.
Ah. Well. A lesson. Yes. Ahem.
Rule one of swordsmanship, young Pell: be scared.
What? That\'s not a rule!
It\'s the first rule. Everyone\'s scared. The ones who say they aren\'t are lying, or they\'re about to do something very stupid.
What\'s rule two?
That\'s a good rule. Where\'d you get that rule?
From a man who was better at it than me.
Here — I found this on the beach. For the lesson. It\'s probably magic.
Squire Toller
I\'m sick tonight, Kestrel. Very sick. Can\'t possibly stand a watch on any hill.
Bram Kestrel. The Lord-Commander said you\'d turn up.
Toller! Look at you — you got your spurs!
Got \'em. Wish I hadn\'t, tonight.
Forty men on that hill, Bram, and every one of us heard what came out of the Lantern this morning. Nobody\'s saying it. But that\'s not a hymn. I grew up on hymns. That\'s something else.
Then come with us.
I\'m not brave enough for that. I\'m brave enough for this, though.
He pushes his field kit across the table.
I\'m sick tonight. Very sick. Can\'t possibly stand a watch on any hill. Go on.
It smells like low tide and bad decisions.
It smells like—
It doesn\'t smell like adventure anymore.
Violet light seeps out of the rock. Somewhere deep in the caves, something is humming. Low. Like a man in the next room, singing to himself.
The Gloam is close here. Closer than it was. It is coming up through the stone like water through a boat.
Find the sealed bottom of the Keeper\'s Stair at the back of the Tide Caves.
The violet crystal at the back of the cave has grown. It fills the passage now like a frozen wave, taller than Bram, veined with slow light.
That\'s the one. From before. It was the size of my fist.
_...Wren? Little bird?_
_...is the tide in? I can\'t... I can\'t see the light from here..._
Wren. That isn\'t— Wren, that isn\'t him.
_Sing me the gull one, little bird. I forgot how it ends._
Wren, you PROMISED. You promised me you\'d never touch it—
You touch it.

The crystal cracks down the middle like ice on a pond. And out of the crack pours everything the sea has ever taken from Lanternfall — oilskins and nets and drowned lanterns and hands, so many hands — knotted together into something that wears them like a coat.
It is not him. It is a memory of a memory. The Gloam remembers everything — it just remembers it wrong.
Behind me! Everyone behind me!
The thing comes apart into seawater and old rope and is gone. The voice goes with it.
You promised.
I know.
Ladies. Later. There\'s a staircase where the rock used to be.
Climb the Keeper\'s Stair to the Lantern.
The crystal in the tide caves spoke with Dad\'s voice. I touched it. I promised Ilse I never would. Behind it: the Keeper\'s Stair.

Mom\'s at the top of these. Mom, and him.
A bronze lamp, burning steadily. The gate beyond stands open.
This lamp is already burning.
a single star
a curling wave
a plain, square stone
Light the lamp?
Light it
The flame catches — then shivers, and every lit lamp in the hall gutters out at once, as if someone had sighed.
The flame catches and holds, a small steady gold.
All three lamps flare together. With a groan of old bronze, the gate at the head of the hall swings open.
A gate of green bronze bars. Above it, words cut deep into the lintel:
_FIRST THE SEA THAT TAKES THEM._
_THEN THE STONE THAT KEEPS THEM._
_LAST THE SKY THAT CALLS THEM HOME._
The sun. It\'s about the sun. The sea takes it every night, the Lantern\'s stone keeps it, and every morning the sky calls it home. Three lines. Three lamps.
Low on the wall, scratched with something that was probably a fish-knife, in three very different hands:
_EDRIN + TOBY + FEN WERE HERE_
And underneath, in a fourth hand, small and furious: _AND NOW THEY ARE SCRUBBING THE STAIR. — I. HALLOWAY, KEEPER_
Grandma Ide. She caught them. ...Dad was eleven. He carved his name on the wall and got made to scrub four hundred years of stairs.
Edrin, Toby... and Fen. Whoever Fen is.
You come up out of the rock into red light. The bluff. The Lantern, huge and close, humming so loudly now that the grass shivers with it.
Far below, the whole Western Sea lies still as a plate. Not a ripple. And on its edge, the sun, waiting.
Whatever he\'s doing, he\'s nearly done. You can feel it. Like the air before a bell.
When we go in — I\'m first through the door. That\'s the job.
Since when?
Since just now. I\'ve decided.
Wren. If he sings, I think I will hear it. I think I have heard it before.
Then we stop him before he sings.
Enter the Lantern.
We climbed the Keeper\'s Stair to the bluff. The Lantern is humming like a bell about to be struck.
The Lantern\'s door. Behind it, the hum — and your mother.
Go inside? _(There will be no turning back.)_
Go in
Not yet
Inside, the hum is everywhere. In the stones. In your teeth. In the little bones of your ears.
You came home. I hoped you would. I\'m sorry it had to be the hard way up.
I told the gate to turn you back.
Holiness. These are the children who cut through forty of my men between Saltglass and Greyspine.
Then perhaps you should stop sending men at children, Garrick.
Wren. Go home. Go home right now.
I read your letter.
I\'m not leaving you up here with him.
The Hierophant is too gentle with you, girl. I\'m not.
Kestrel. Still carrying a sword you never earned?
I am here to— to adjudicate you, Lord-Commander.
He means fight.
I mean fight.
With respect, Holiness. You need the girl. You don\'t need the rest of them.
Garrick goes down on one knee, breathing hard, his greatsword ringing on the stones.
No. Huh. I didn\'t.
Enough. Please.
Cassian lifts a slender silver tuning fork — the same make as the ones you carried across the whole of Solmere — and touches it, very gently, to the brass of the great lamp.
The hum becomes a NOTE. Every Lantern in the world rings at once — you can feel them, far away, Saltglass, Frosthollow, Mirefen, Thornwood, Skyreach, Aurenne — six voices in a chord with one missing.
And the chord holds everyone still.
Can\'t... move... that\'s new...
It is— it is the song. The one from the water. The one I came out of—
Not you, Wren. Never you. Lanternfall\'s light knows its own.
I promised myself I would never lie to you. I\'m not going to start tonight.
When I was twelve, the Lantern of Aurenne failed for a single night. The Gloam came into the city. It took my sister. Lysa. She was ten.
She had a yellow ribbon in her hair. She\'d lost the other one that morning. She was so angry about it.
My father was the Keeper. He could hold the light on the Lantern, or he could go down into the dark after her. He chose the light.
Everyone said he chose right.
I have spent forty years writing a song, Wren. The Dawnsong, sung backward through all seven Lanterns at once. The Vespersong.
It doesn\'t call the sun up. It holds it still. One perfect moment, kept. Forever. Evernoon.
And in Evernoon, no one is lost. The Gloam keeps every memory of every soul it ever took. I have heard them, Wren. I have heard Lysa singing in the dark.
The Vespersong pulls them back out. Whole. Not echoes. Not that poor drowned thing in your tide caves. _Whole._
Lysa. Brother Halvard. Sir Aldous.
_(through his teeth)_ Don\'t.
Your father.
Edrin Halloway, who went out in a storm and didn\'t come home. Who used to sing you the one about the gull that flew past the edge of the map.
How do you know that?
You wrote me. You were twelve. It was the best letter I have ever received.
That\'s why you wrote to her. Four years of letters.
I wrote to her because she wrote to me, and her letters were the best part of my year. Both things are true, Ysolde. They usually are.
The Dawnstones answer only to their Keepers. Some gave me theirs. Some I... collected. I am not proud of all of it.
The seventh answers to your mother. Or to her blood.
The forks. The forks we carried. That\'s what they were for.
Yes. You tuned the whole world for me, Wren. You did it beautifully.
You used me.
I asked you. You said yes. I\'m asking again.
He\'s offering you a painting of your father, Wren. A painting that talks.
And what did YOU offer him?!
The night of the storm. I was up here. I was nine and I was hiding on the stairs and I SAW you. You turned the light. Away from his boat. Toward the harbor.
Thirty boats were out that night, Wren. I turned the light toward thirty boats.
And Dad was the thirty-first.
I\'ve turned that light a thousand times since. Every night. In my head. It never comes out different.
_(softly)_ Your mother let him go, Wren. She will let you go too, someday.
I never will.
I won\'t stop you. I never could. I\'m asking you. Please.
You promised. On the ship. You said if he made you want to give it to him, you\'d look at me first.
So look at me. _Look at me._
You look at her. You do. For a long moment.
Then you turn around.
The great lamp of Lanternfall. Inside the glass, the Dawnstone sleeps in its bed of brass, like a small sun. Warm as a hand.
Take the Dawnstone.
The Dawnstone is warm under your palm.
You take your hand away.
Behind you, your mother lets out a breath she has been holding for seven years.
_"...and the gull flew on past the edge of the map, and the map grew to—"_
He would.
I\'m sorry, Mom.
It comes away in your hand like it was waiting for you.
The Lantern goes dark.
It is not a dawn— it is not a DAWN— I was inside it, I was INSIDE the song, it is a stopping, it is a STOPPING—
Wren. Wren, please. Please put it back. Please.
Wren, c\'mon— this is a con, I know a con, I practically invented cons—
_(quietly)_ Ah, sparrow.
You hold it out. He takes it the way you would take a sleeping bird.
Thank you.
Come and watch, Wren. You, of everyone, should see it.
The note lets go of them. Bram stumbles. Pip sits down hard on the floor. Sable is shaking.
Ilse will not look at you.
That ain\'t funny.
Wasn\'t joking, kid.
I gave Cassian the Dawnstone. Mom asked me not to. Ilse begged me. Sable screamed. I did it anyway.
The whole of Lanternfall has come out onto the step to watch. You can see them from up here, little shapes in every doorway, all facing west.
Look at it. All of you. Don\'t look away. This is the last sunset anyone will ever have to watch end.
Cassian. Please. You know what a world is. It\'s a thing that _moves._
So is a wound, Ysolde.
He lifts the Dawnstone toward the sun. And he sings.
_Morning, morning, do not wake—_
_Stay the hour and stay the light—_
_Keep the ones you would not take—_
_Hold them, hold them, hold them bright—_
Far to the east, six lights answer. You can feel the chord close, like a hand.
And the sun — sitting on the very edge of the sea — stops.
Not slows. _Stops._
A gull hangs over the harbor with its wings half-open and does not finish the beat. A wave stands up on the black rocks and stays there, like green glass.
Everything is gold. Everything is still. It is the most beautiful thing you have ever seen.
Somewhere very far away — and very close — a man laughs. A big, warm, salty laugh you have not heard in seven years.
Then the sun cracked.
A line of white fire runs across its face. Then another. Then seven.
The sun comes apart like a plate dropped on a stone floor — seven burning pieces wheeling away into a sky that is the wrong color.
And the Western Sea, which had been holding its breath since noon yesterday, lets go.
It lifts off the world like a sheet off a bed, and falls into the sky.
A pillar of white light comes down on the edge of the bluff, and takes Cassian, and Garrick, and the Dawnstone, up and east. And they are gone.

s the sea?!
_(looking up)_ Going up there, big man. Most of it.
Oh, that\'s— no. No no no. That\'s not allowed. That\'s not ALLOWED.
Listen to me. All of you.
The Lantern has no stone. When its light goes out, the Gloam comes in — here, now, all at once. It will take the island and everyone on it.
I can hold the light. For a while. Long enough.
Hold it with what?
Captain. Get them to Tobias\'s boat.
Lady, running\'s the only thing I\'m any good at.
Then teach them.
She unhooks the little brass lamp from her belt — the one she has carried on every night watch of your life — and folds your fingers around it.
Take this. It\'s a Keeper\'s lamp. It won\'t go out. I made sure.
Mom, I— I\'m—
She leans down and presses her forehead to yours, the way she did when you were small and had a fever.
Tell me later. I\'ll be listening.
The Lantern\'s light comes back. Not gold now — white. Fierce. It pours out of every window and every crack in the old stone and pushes the dark back off the island like a hand.
MOVE! Down the hill — to the docks — GO!
RUN. Get down the hill road to Tobias\'s boat at the docks!
The sun broke into seven pieces. The sea fell into the sky. Mom went back into the Lantern to hold the light. She gave me her lamp. She said, "Tell me later."
The hill road splits open in front of you. Things climb out of the crack — dogs made of dusk, with embers where their eyes should be.
Through them! We go THROUGH them!
Don\'t stop. Don\'t look up. Keep moving.
In the square, by the well, a small boy is standing perfectly still with his hands over his ears. Pell.
Hey! HEY, ugly! Over here! The kid\'s with me!
I got you. I got you, I got you. It\'s okay. I\'m a professional.
M-Mama said run to the boat—
Then that\'s where we\'re going. Hold my hand. No— don\'t, I got knives in that hand. Hold my sleeve.
Get to Tobias\'s boat at the end of the dock!
Something falls out of the sky and hits the beach in a spray of glassy sand — a piece of the sun, no bigger than a cart, still burning. Things crawl out of the crater toward you.
Dock! Dock, dock, dock — there\'s Tobias!
In! In, all of you! She\'ll float as long as there\'s something to float on—
Ilse! Ilse, love—
Nana Brisa unpins the silver gull from her collar — the brooch from the tide caves, chipped wing and all — and presses it into Ilse\'s hand.
Hold onto this for me. Bring it back. That\'s how I\'ll know you\'re all right.
Nana, get in the boat.
The Doyle children are still up the hill. Their mother\'s gone to pieces.
Nana— NANA—
Stay with Wren. She\'s going to need somebody to tell her when she\'s being stupid.
Up the hill, with a sound like a cliff sighing, the village square tears loose from the island — well, lamp posts, cobbles and all — and lifts, slowly, into the broken sky.
Ilse watches it go. She does not make a sound.
Sparrow. Boat. _Now._
Up on the bluff, the Lantern burns white against the broken sky. In the window of the lamp room there is a small dark figure, standing very straight.
In your hand, the little brass lamp flickers.
Mom? Mom, can you hear me?
I said I\'d be listening.
I\'m sorry.
I\'m sorry. I\'m sorry, I\'m so sorry—
I know, little bird.
Come down. Please. There\'s room on the boat, Tobias says she floats as long as—
Wren. Someone has to hold the light.
I\'ve been practicing for seven years.
Listen to me. You\'re going to want to carry this. All of it. Don\'t.
Carry the lamp instead. It\'s lighter.
Grow up well, my little bird.
The light held for eleven minutes.
Long enough.
Then the sea, falling upward, took Tobias\'s boat with it — and the night came apart — and one by one Wren Halloway lost hold of every hand she was holding.
All except one small brass lamp, that would not go out.
Mom held the light. I heard her through her lamp. I told her I was sorry. She said, "Grow up well, my little bird." Then everything was white.
