s tired, girl.
Every morning?
Three hundred and some. Hard to count. There aren\'t days anymore. Just the light changing color.
Who are you?
Now that\'s new. Three hundred mornings you\'ve sat at my table, and that\'s the first question you\'ve ever asked me.
Fennick. Old Fennick, the children used to say, up on the north cliffs. Dared each other to knock on my door.
Only on holidays.
Where is everyone? Ilse. Bram. My—
I found you on my doorstep the night the sky broke. Just you. Holding that.
On the table: a small brass lamp. The flame inside is the size of a fingernail. It has not flickered.
Wouldn\'t let go of it. Fevers, sleep, nothing. I had to feed you one-handed for a month.
I know. I watched it from the cliff. Eleven minutes. Longest light I ever saw.
It was me. I gave him the stone. It was me.
I know that too, girl. You told me. Every night for three months, in your sleep.
Eat your soup.
How can you— I broke the SUN, and you want me to eat soup?
And I burned the soup. Today it\'s the soup I can do something about.
When you\'re ready — and not before — come outside. There\'s something you should see.
Step outside Fennick\'s hut.
I woke up. Fennick says it\'s been a year. He says there are no days anymore. He made me eat soup.
Back, are you? Good. Not to sit on that rock, I hope.
Eat something. Then go on. They\'re out there waiting for you, whether they know it or not.
Go on outside. The sky won\'t bite.
Your mother\'s lamp. The flame inside is the size of a fingernail. In a year, it has not flickered once.
It won\'t go out. She made sure.
Fennick\'s books. Every one of them has a twin on a shelf in a house that is gone now. He bought two of everything, for years, so he would know which ones you had already read.
Books. Hundreds of them, swollen with salt. You know some of the titles. _The Pirate Queen of Gale_. _A Child\'s Book of Stars_. _Tides, and How They Lie_.
The sky is a bruise. Violet at the top, going to a sick orange at the edges, like a sunset that has forgotten how to finish.
Seven fires hang in it, where the sun used to be. Seven burning wounds scattered across the heavens — each too bright to look at, and too far away to warm anything.
Past the edge of the grass there is no sea. There is no anything. Only more sky, going down and down forever — and islands, hundreds of them, big and small, hanging in it like crumbs on a dark cloth.
Ash falls. It is always falling.
Okay. Okay.
Look around Fennick\'s shard. Fennick is waiting at the cairns on the rise to the east.
A rock at the very edge of the shard, worn smooth and faintly hollowed on top. Facing west.
_(from across the shard)_ That\'s your rock. You sat on it every day for a year. Looking at nothing.
Your rock. It is a good rock. You are not going to sit on it today.
Here. This is what I wanted you to see.
Two small cairns of stacked stone on the rise, under a dead tree. Words scratched into a flat stone at the foot of each.
_EDRIN HALLOWAY. HE\'D WANT A BETTER STONE._
_YSOLDE HALLOWAY. KEEPER. SHE HELD._
Built his the year he went into the sea. Couldn\'t think what to write. Wrote the truth.
Built hers the week you came. Same problem.
"She held."
You knew my dad.
Fished with him twenty years. Him, me and Tobias. We were the terror of the eel rocks.
_(startled)_ You found that? Under the bluff? We were eleven. Your grandmother caught us and made us scrub the whole Stair with a brush. Four hundred years of steps.
I was supposed to be on the boat with him that night. I had a cold. A _cold._ He went out alone.
I spent seven years on that north cliff being sorry. Didn\'t bring him back. Didn\'t do anyone a scrap of good.
Except — your books.
My books?
The ones that washed up on your step. Every month, since you were five.
That was you?
Your father paid me in fish to leave \'em. Said you\'d read them faster if you thought the sea sent them. After he was gone, I kept on.
It was the only part of being sorry that was any use to anybody.
I don\'t know how to carry this.
Nobody does. Here\'s what I know, for what an old fool\'s worth.
Sorry looks backward. It stands with its face to the wall. What you _owe_ — that looks forward.
Same weight, girl. You just carry it facing the other way.
Now. You\'ve sat on that rock for a year. Today you\'re going to pick up a sword.
He has been carrying a long bundle wrapped in sailcloth. He unwraps it.
Took this off a Dawnguard wreck that drifted by in the spring. Good steel. Better than that driftwood thing you used to swing at gulls.
And the coat. Three old sails and a Dawnguard cloak. My stitching\'s terrible. It\'ll keep the ash off.
Equip new gear from the menu (*C* / *Esc* → Equip). You are fighting alone now: there is no one to heal you or take a hit for you.
Meet Fennick at the training ring south of the hut.
Fennick built cairns for Mom and Dad. He was Dad\'s friend — "Fen." He\'s the one who left books on my step, every month, for eleven years. He gave me a sword.
Right. You and me. Don\'t hold back — I won\'t.
Things your father never learned and I did. First: when something winds up for a big swing, _Guard._ Halves the blow and gets your turn back quicker.
Second: hit what they hate. Every beast has a weakness. Find it, keep hitting it, and they Break.
Last: you\'re alone now. Nobody\'s going to heal you. If you\'ve a Crest that can mend, put it to work. If you don\'t — carry tonics. Lots of tonics.
Spar with Fennick?
Not yet
Hah! HA! There\'s Edrin\'s girl!
Hff. Not bad. Not good. Not bad.
Again tomorrow. That\'s the whole secret, girl. Again tomorrow.
A shadow sweeps over the training ring — a kite the size of a sail, with a girl hanging from the bar beneath it. She drops onto the bridge, runs ten steps to bleed off speed, and skids to a stop.
Post! Post for the hermit of— oh! You\'re UP!
Fen, she\'s up! She\'s standing! Does she talk? Do you talk?
She TALKS. Hello! I\'m Linnet. Kite-post, Keelhaven to everywhere, rain or ash. I\'ve brought him his letters every month and you\'ve looked straight through me every time.
Any news worth the trip, Linnet?
Keelhaven\'s swelled to six hundred. Warden Hale\'s rationing the soup again. Kiteholm\'s got a new gang of brats running the scrap-yards.
And there\'s a hospital in the ruins of Aurenne now. The old Bellwrights\' Hall. The Ember Ward, they call it.
Run by a Mender girl about your age. Dark hair, spectacles, never smiles. They say she hasn\'t slept since the sky broke.
Oh, and — heralds came through Keelhaven, all in white. Said the Hierophant lives. Said he\'s building something up on the biggest Sun Shard. Said—
Said the last Dawnstone was given freely. By the Keeper\'s daughter of Lanternfall.
Folk in Keelhaven would like a word with her, I\'ll tell you that much.
Linnet. Have you met my granddaughter? This is Lark.
Didn\'t know you had a granddaughter, Fen!
Neither did I, till recently.
Well — Keelhaven\'s two bridges east, past what\'s left of the old village square. Mind the hounds on the Drift! Bye, Lark!
Ilse\'s alive.
Sounds like.
Then maybe the others— I have to go. I have to find them.
I know.
You\'ll find folk out there who hate the Keeper\'s girl. Let them. You don\'t owe them your name. You owe them better than sitting on a rock.
He works a bracelet off his own wrist — old braided cord, so overgrown with moss it is almost alive — and ties it onto yours.
Moss grows on anything if you leave it long enough. Even an old man. It\'ll knit you up a little in a fight.
I\'ll want you back sometimes. Not to sit on that rock.
Cross the Drift east to Keelhaven. (The bridge is on the east side of the shard.)
A kite-courier named Linnet says there\'s a Mender girl running a hospital in the ruins of Aurenne. Ilse. She\'s alive. Folk blame "the Keeper\'s daughter." Fennick told Linnet my name is Lark.
East bridge, girl. Two bridges to the old square, then on to Keelhaven.
And Lark — eat when you\'re hungry. Sleep when you\'re tired. Grief\'s no excuse for bad manners to your own body.
Training ring, south of the hut. Come on, before my knees seize up.
Come up here a moment, girl. There\'s something you should see.
Something lands on the far end of the bridge hard enough to make the planks jump — a hound the size of a cart, made of packed ash, with embers for eyes and smoke pouring off its back.
That\'s the Ashmaw. It\'s been taking my chickens all winter.
You have chickens?
Go on, Lark. Remember: watch the shoulders. When it winds up, Guard.
The Ashmaw comes apart in a long gray sigh, and the wind takes it over the edge.
I— okay. I\'m okay.
You\'re not. But you\'re standing.
Go on. Before I say something sentimental and we both have to live with it.
The Ashmaw — Fennick\'s chicken-thief — attacked on the bridge. I fought it alone. I won. Fennick said, "There she is."
Islands drift past in the dusk — and some of them have cobblestones on them. Lamp posts. Fences you used to climb.
These are... these are pieces of home.
Cross the Drift to Keelhaven, in the east.
Far to the west, on a shard of its own, the stump of a stone tower stands against the bruised sky. At its top, impossibly, a light still burns. Not white now. A small, stubborn gold.
Not yet. I can\'t. Not yet.
From the Drift I could see the Lantern on its own shard, far to the west. It is still burning. I couldn\'t go. Not yet.
Half a room, hanging in the sky. Two walls, a floor, a bed, a table. The rest of the house is gone, sheared off as clean as bread.
That\'s my bed.
That\'s our table.
The kitchen table. Two plates, still set, filmed with a year of ash. Your mother\'s letter is gone. The wind must have taken it.
Your father\'s shelf. The atlas is in your pack now. You still don\'t know why.
Your father\'s shelf, with a gap in it where a book used to be.
Your father\'s shelf. Most of the books have gone over the edge. One is wedged in tight, swollen with damp: a big blue book with a gold sunburst on the spine.
_The Sunward Atlas._ Inside the cover, in a fine, kind hand: _For Wren, who asks the best questions. — C._
Keep it.
Throw it over the edge.
What do you do with Cassian\'s gift?
I don\'t know why I\'m keeping it. I just— am.
You throw it as hard as you can. It opens in the air like a bird, pages flapping, and falls, and falls, and is gone.

A town built out of boats. Dozens of hulls, turned keel-up and lashed to the rock to make roofs. Cookfires. Washing lines. A child chasing a goat. Six hundred people who were, a year ago, somewhere else.
Sentry Mott
Hold up. New face. Where from?
West. The Drift.
Nobody lives on the Drift but hounds and old Fennick. Name?

Nailed to the gatepost beside him, a sheet of white paper with the Choir\'s gold sunburst: _THE LAST STONE WAS GIVEN FREELY, BY THE KEEPER\'S DAUGHTER OF LANTERNFALL._ Someone has drawn a noose under it.
"Wren. Wren Halloway."
Your name?
Wren. Wren Hal—
Your eyes go to the noose. Your mouth closes on its own.
Wren what?
Lark. Welcome to Keelhaven. Don\'t steal, don\'t fight, don\'t fall off. Soup\'s free at the kettle, twice a day.
You want work or passage, Warden Hale\'s in the big hull on the north side.
Find a way east across the Shattered Sea toward Aurenne. Warden Hale runs Keelhaven (the big hull, north side).
Keelhaven: a town made of upturned boats. There\'s a notice on the gate about "the Keeper\'s daughter," with a noose drawn under it. I told them my name is Lark.
Warden Hale
You killed the Unmoored. Alone. I\'ve had the salvagers out on the strait all morning just to look at the bones.
Keelhaven owes you, Lark. Whoever you are.
Both winches, Lark. North spoke and south spoke. Then the strait bridge comes down.
And the bounties stand, if you\'re out there anyway. Bring me proof.
You\'re Fennick\'s granddaughter. Mott said. Funny — Fennick never mentioned one. Sit.
I was harbormaster at Port Gale for nineteen years. I ran three hundred ships a season. Now I run six hundred people on a rock, and I\'m worse at it.
I need to get to Aurenne.
Across the old strait? Nobody\'s crossed in four months.
Something big lives out there now. A serpent the length of a street, swimming in the sky like it\'s still water. Eats rafts. Broke our chain-bridge twice. The salvagers call it the Unmoored.
I\'ll go.
Alone? You\'re a child.
I\'m used to alone.
The salvagers winched the strait bridge up and chained it. Two winches: one on the north spoke, one on the wreck of the _Gilded Psalm_ on the south spoke. Turn both, and the bridge comes down.
I\'ll have Rook open the east gate. I won\'t stop you. I won\'t come and pull you out, either.
And — if you\'re going out there anyway. Two bounties on the board. Glassback, the golem that\'s been smashing the salvage quarry. And the Lidless, up on its perch. Proof brings coin.
Bounty: Glassback
A golem of living glass has been wrecking the salvagers\' quarry, west of the north spoke of the Shattered Sea. Defeat it and bring proof to Warden Hale.
Bounty: The Lidless
Something with too many eyes has made a perch north of the Last Hearth, past the strait bridge. Defeat it and bring proof to Warden Hale.
Go east into the Shattered Sea. Turn the salvagers\' winches on the north and south spokes to lower the strait bridge.
Warden Hale says a sky-serpent called the Unmoored blocks the old strait. Two winches lower the bridge across. I said I\'d go. Alone. I\'m used to alone.
Glassback\'s heart. Gods, it\'s still warm. The salvagers will cry.
Put it AWAY. Put it— thank you. I\'ll never sleep again. Here.
Eat something before you go out there, Lark. That\'s not a request.
Soup\'s ash-potato. It\'s always ash-potato. Eat it anyway.
A woman at a huge iron kettle, ladling gray soup into a line of tin cups. She looks up to hand you one — and stops.
A boy hits you around the middle at full speed. A year taller. A year thinner. Pell.
Pell. Hush.
Her eyes flick to the pulpit across the square, where a man in ash-smeared robes is preaching to nobody in particular.
This is Lark. Isn\'t it, Lark.
_(whispering, enormous)_ I won\'t tell. I won\'t EVER tell.
Maela. Where\'s Tobias?
Tobias got the boat down on this rock with eleven of us aboard. When the sea came down the other way.
Then he went back out on a raft for more.
I\'m sorry. Maela, I\'m so—
Everybody\'s sorry. Have some soup.
Pip saved me. By the well. He said I was a professional now. Like him.
Is Pip— is Bram— are they—
I don\'t know, Pell. I\'m going to find out.
Maela and Pell are alive, in Keelhaven. Tobias got eleven people to safety, then went back out for more and never came back. Maela called me Lark without even blinking.
It went NORTH. Linnet says the wind up high goes to Kiteholm.
If Pip sees it, he\'ll know. He\'ll KNOW.
Silk, Lark. Real silk, the kind that doesn\'t rot. The Choir\'s fancy banners were made of it.
Linnet says there\'s a whole Choir ship wrecked out on the south spoke.
Are you new? Maela gives extra soup to new people. Not really. But she might.
Lark! I\'m building a kite. Like Linnet\'s. Not to ride — to send.
I\'m going to paint names on it. Everybody we\'re looking for. And fly it as high as it goes and cut the string, and the wind will take it everywhere, and somebody will SEE it.
But the sailcloth\'s too heavy. I need silk. Real silk. The Choir\'s banners were made of it — and there\'s a Choir ship wrecked out on the south spoke of the strait.
Pell\'s Kite
Pell wants to fly a message-kite with the names of the lost painted on it. He needs Choir silk — from the banners of the wrecked Gilded Psalm on the south spoke of the Shattered Sea.
SILK! Real silk! With a sunburst on it! I\'ll paint over the sunburst.
An hour later, on the rock above the town, Pell holds up a kite made of white Choir silk, with names painted on it in big careful letters.
_PELL IS ALIVE. KEELHAVEN. MAELA. — PIP? — TOBIAS?_
Lark. Do you want to add any?
You take the brush.
_ILSE. BRAM. SABLE. PIP. CORVIN._
You think for a long time. Then you add one more, small, in the corner: _— W._
Pell lets the kite climb until it is a white speck against the seven wounds of the sky. Then he cuts the string. The wind takes it north.
There. Now they\'ll know where to come.
Pell and I flew a kite with the names of everyone we\'re looking for painted on it. The wind took it north. I signed it "W."
Every letter on this wall is for somebody nobody can find. Folk write them anyway. Pin them up. Come back every morning to see if theirs has been taken down.
Sometimes the somebody turns up. Twice, so far.
The sky\'s full of letters, love. Satchels, sea-chests, pockets. If you find any out there in the wreckage, bring them to me. Somebody\'s waiting.
The Lost Wall
Orla keeps a wall of letters for the missing in Keelhaven. Lost letters drift in the wreckage of the Drift and the Shattered Sea — bring any you find to her.
No letters today? That\'s all right. Neither has anyone else, most days.
"To Mama, at Port Gale. From Jory." — Jory! His mother comes every single morning. She\'ll— oh, she\'ll—
Orla presses the letter to her chest for a moment before she can go on.
Here. For bringing a boy home. Near enough.
"To my brother Teo, in Kiteholm." A Choir sailor, off the _Psalm_. I\'ll send it north on Linnet\'s next kite. That\'s the best any of us can do.
"Dear Sun. Please come back. I will be good. I will be so good." ...No name. No address.
Orla pins it in the very middle of the wall, where everyone will see it.
It doesn\'t need one.
"To Aldo Brannock." Aldo...
You\'ll know him as Brother Cinder. The one at the pulpit, shouting about the Keeper\'s girl. Aldo had a wife called Bett. She never made it to the big rock.
You should give this one to him yourself, love. I don\'t think I could.
Your letter\'s up, Lark. Right next to "Dear Sun."
Come by in the mornings. You never know.
Four letters home. Four more than anybody else has managed this year.
Here — paper, and a stub of charcoal. Everybody writes one, sooner or later. You\'ve been staring at the wall like you\'ve got one in you.
You write for a long time. You cross out most of it. In the end there are only a few lines left.
_I\'m going to find them. All of them. Then I\'m going to figure out what I owe, and pay it._
_I\'m carrying the lamp. You were right. It\'s lighter._
No address?
She knows where I am.
Then this is for the one who brought them all home.
I brought Orla four lost letters. Then I wrote one of my own, to Mom, and pinned it on the Lost Wall.
Brother Cinder
Aldo. Just Aldo, now.
I\'m learning to make soup. Bett would laugh herself sick.
Seven wounds in the sky! Seven! And who opened them? The Choir says it plain: the last stone was GIVEN. Given, by the Keeper\'s daughter of Lanternfall!
Somewhere out there she\'s eating, and sleeping, and breathing our air. Find her! Give her to the abyss, and maybe — maybe — the sky will close!
Brother Cinder. Aldo. This is for you. It was out in the wreckage.
What is— that\'s Bett\'s hand.
He reads it standing up. Then he sits down on the step of his own pulpit, like his strings have been cut.
_Aldo. If I don\'t make it to the big rock, don\'t you dare turn this into anybody\'s fault._
_Not the Keepers\'. Not the Choir\'s. Not God\'s. Not yours._
_Things break. Then you pick up the pieces that are left, and you make soup. — Bett._
She always did make soup out of everything.
I wanted it to be somebody\'s fault. If it\'s somebody\'s fault, then it isn\'t just... the sky. Then you can do something about it. Throw somebody off a rock.
Here. It was Bett\'s. She\'d want it on somebody going somewhere.
I gave Brother Cinder his wife\'s last letter. She told him not to make it anybody\'s fault. He stepped down off his pulpit.
And where are you going, girl?
Nobody goes east. Nobody but fools and the guilty.
Red hair. Lanternfall accent. Came in off the Drift — from the west, where Lanternfall used to be. Fennick\'s "granddaughter," that nobody ever heard of.
The Keeper\'s girl had red hair, they say. Lanternfall red.
People are stopping. Turning. A crowd gathers the way weather gathers — slowly, then all at once.
That\'s enough, Aldo.
Maela. You\'re from Lanternfall. You tell them who she is.
I will.

This is Lark. Lark Tobiasdaughter. I\'ve known her since she was a baby. My Tobias taught her to gut a fish when she was six, and she cried, and he gave her the fish to keep as a pet. It went off in a week.
Pell calls every red-haired girl "Wren" because he misses her. So do I.
Go home, Aldo. Pray at your pillar. Leave my girl be.
I don\'t know what you did up there.
I know what they say. And I know Tobias went back for more boats and didn\'t come back, and I am not losing anybody else from Lanternfall to a lot of shouting.
Thank you, Maela.
Don\'t. Just come back.
Brother Cinder almost had me, at the east gate. Maela told the whole crowd I was Lark Tobiasdaughter. She lied for me. She said, "Just come back."
Sister Ottilie
Wash your hands, Lark. Then wash them again.
The Ember Ward\'s girl says the rot spreads through dirty hands faster than through bad luck.
Careful — don\'t touch the cots. Gloam-rot. It starts as a gray patch on the skin and it doesn\'t stop.
I wore the Choir\'s white for eleven years. I sang the Dawnsong every morning of my life. I don\'t sing anymore.
The only one who\'s ever beaten the rot is a Mender in Aurenne. The Ember Ward. She wrote me, once, by kite. Told me how to keep them alive longer.
Her letter began: "Three things. One: wash your hands. Two: wash them again. Three: nobody is beyond help until they\'re dead, and then they\'re beyond help, so stop crying and go to the next bed."
You know her?
I used to.
A plank nailed to two oars. Notices pinned three deep. MISSING: GOAT, ANSWERS TO "COUNCILOR". WANTED: ANYONE WHO CAN FIX A KITE-WINCH.
And, in Warden Hale\'s blocky capitals:
_BOUNTY — "GLASSBACK." GLASS GOLEM, SALVAGE QUARRY, WEST OF THE NORTH SPOKE. 1,500 GOLD._
_BOUNTY — "THE LIDLESS." ON THE PERCH NORTH OF THE LAST HEARTH. DO NOT LOOK AT IT. 2,000 GOLD._
_PROOF TO THE WARDEN._
Lark! Kite-post\'s open — I can fly you anywhere I\'ve flown before. Costs nothing. Well, costs your stomach.
Take the kite-post?
The old strait between Lanternfall and the mainland. You crossed it once in Tobias\'s boat with your friends, and Bram was sick over the side, and a sea serpent tried to eat you.
Now there is no water in it. Only wreckage, hanging in the air, and the long drop underneath.
Two winches. North spoke, south spoke. Then the bridge. Then Aurenne. Then Ilse.
Turn the salvagers\' winches on the north spoke (the Chainyard) and the south spoke (the wreck of the Gilded Psalm).
The winch is turned and locked. Somewhere east, a chain hangs slack.
A salvagers\' winch, as big as a cart, chained to the rock. The crank is stiff with ash.
The _Gilded Psalm_\'s anchor-winch, rigged by the salvagers to haul the strait chain. The crank is wedged with debris.
Turn the winch?
Turn it
Leave it
The noise carries. Something heavy and glittering hauls itself up over the edge of the island.
The noise carries through the hull. Down in the dark of the hold, something answers, and comes up the ladder.
You put your whole weight on the crank. It gives, all at once. Far off to the east, with a sound like a bell dropped down a well, a chain-lock comes open.
Both winches are turned. Cross the strait bridge east of the hub.
I turned both salvagers\' winches. The strait bridge is open.
A Choir hymnal, warped with damp, wedged under a crate. It falls open by itself at a page that has been opened many times. The song is called _The Vespersong — Draft Thirty-One._
In the margin, in a small, careful hand: _Not yet. The measure is wrong. Lysa would laugh at this line._
I know that handwriting. I have forty letters in that handwriting.
"The measure is wrong." He knew. Some part of him knew it was wrong, and he sang it anyway.
What\'s left of the _Psalm_\'s banner, flapping in the ash-wind.
A Choir banner of white silk, still bright under the soot. The gold sunburst on it is almost the color of the real thing.
A Choir banner of white silk, still bright under the soot. You cut a good wide piece free.
The quarry floor heaves. A shape unfolds out of the glass — like a man, almost, but twice as tall, and so clear you can see the seven wounds of the sky bent through its body.
Glassback shatters. In the middle of the heap, something still glows: a fist-sized core, warm as a hearthstone.
The perch is quiet. Then the dark at the edge of the island opens, and keeps opening, and is an eye.
The Lidless closes, at last. Where it was, a single cold violet orb rolls across the stones and stops against your boot.

Someone made a camp here once — a ring of stones, a cold firepit, a Hearthstone humming to itself. Beyond the next bridge, the ash in the air goes thick and dark, and something very large is moving through it.
You take out your mother\'s lamp and set it on a stone beside you.
Mom. I\'m going to find them. All of them.
And then I\'m going to— I don\'t know yet. Something. I\'m going to fix something.
The little flame doesn\'t answer.
It doesn\'t go out, either.
The island lurches. Up from the abyss below — slowly, the way a whale rises — comes a serpent the length of a street, swimming through the empty air as if it were still the sea.
Its scales are crusted white with old brine. Its eyes are the violet of the Gloam. And across its jaw there\'s a long, ragged scar, the shape of a Dawnguard shield.
You\'re the one from the strait. From the boat. Bram threw up on you.
It does not remember. Or it remembers wrong. It opens its mouth.
Okay. Okay. Last time it took four of us.

Brinefang shudders all down its endless length. Then it stops swimming. It hangs in the air for a moment, as if surprised — and slides, gently, tail first, down off the edge of the island into the dark.
Go on. Go find your sea. It\'s up there somewhere.
Cross the last bridge east, toward Aurenne.
The Unmoored was Brinefang — the serpent from the strait, the one we fought on Tobias\'s boat. It took four of us last time. This time it took one.
Past the last bridge the islands crowd closer together, and then closer still, until they are not islands anymore but the broken edge of a continent.
Far ahead, across a field of floating rubble, the towers of Aurenne stand against the bruised sky. Half of them are gone. Smoke rises from the rest — cookfires, not burning.
And from the top of a broken bell-tower on the east side, someone has hung a white sheet, painted with a red cross.
Okay. Let\'s go.
I crossed the Shattered Sea. Aurenne is ahead — and a hospital flag on the cathedral. I\'m coming, Ilse.
The Mender of Ash
Find the Ember Ward in the ruins of Aurenne.
src/story/ch7.js: The Mender of Ash
A year ago, Aurenne had four hundred bells. Every hour they argued about what time it was.
Now it is always the same time. Always this bruised, burning dusk.
And no bells ring.
The Grand Lantern. It\'s cracked straight down the middle, like an egg somebody dropped.
He stood up there and sang the world to pieces. And I handed him the last piece.
Stop there. Hands.
Palms, then backs. Sleeves up. I\'m looking for violet under the skin.
Clean. Lucky you. Name?
Just Wren?
Just Wren.
Fine, Just Wren. Rules. Water\'s rationed — the well in Ash Square, one bucket a family. Anyone who shows violet goes to the Ward. And nobody goes into the Undercroft.
What\'s in the Undercroft?
Water. And singing.
Who\'s in charge here?
Nobody\'s in charge. The Ward Mother keeps people breathing. These days that\'s the same thing.
Came in off a boat from the west, a year back. Nothing but a Mender\'s Crest and a temper. Sixteen, if she was a day. Name of Marrow.
You know her?
I used to.
The Ember Ward\'s the old Bellwrights\' Hall, east side. If you\'ve got hands that lift, she\'ll use them. If you\'ve got questions, she won\'t.
Find Ilse at the Ember Ward (the old Bellwrights\' Hall, east side of the ruins).
Aurenne is ash. The bells are silent. And Ilse is alive. She runs a hospital here — and I have no idea what I\'m going to say to her.
Forty beds in a hall built for casting bells. Every one of them full.
Wash your hands at the basin. Then tell me where it hurts.
Her hands stop moving. Only for a moment.
Basin\'s by the door.
Ilse, it\'s me. It\'s Wren. I looked for you — after — I didn\'t know if anybody—
I know who it is.
Noll. Bed six needs his dressing changed. Bed nine needs a priest. We haven\'t got one, so she needs you to hold her hand.
Yes, Ward Mother.
Can we talk? Please. Just for a—
Three things.
One. This is a hospital, and you are standing in the only clean aisle. Two. I have forty-one patients, and none of them is you.
And three?
Three is none of your business.
She didn\'t look at me. Not once.
_(whispering)_ She\'s not like that.
I\'m Noll. I\'m the Ward\'s apprentice. Well — I\'m the Ward\'s everything-else.
What\'s wrong with them? All of them?
Gloam-rot. It gets in through cuts. Turns the blood violet, then it turns _you_ violet, and then you get very quiet.
We had sunsalt — the Choir\'s old remedy. Holds the rot back for a season. We\'re down to two phials. Forty-one patients.
Where does sunsalt come from?
The Choir apothecary made it. Under the Cathedral. In the Undercroft.
Then somebody goes down and gets more.
Somebody did. Three somebodies. Their names are on the wall by the door.
If you want to help — really help — we\'re out of water. The well\'s in Ash Square. Sorrel\'s strict, but she won\'t say no to the Ward.
Fetch water for the Ember Ward from the well in Ash Square.
Ilse wouldn\'t look at me. Forty-one patients with Gloam-rot, and the medicine is somewhere under the Cathedral. I can at least carry water.
Noll takes the water. Not me. I\'m busy.
If you\'re not bleeding, you\'re in the way.
Basin. Door. Either one.
Noll knows where everything is. Ask Noll.
Pell\'s asked for his breakfast _twice_. Ward Mother says that\'s the best symptom there is.
Thank you. Both of you. I mean — all of you. Whoever\'s counting.
I can hold the Ward. I can. I\'ve watched her do it for a year.
Just... come back. Both of you. She\'d hate it if I cried in front of the patients.
Water first. And if you\'ve got time after... there\'s Bette. She lost Captain Buttons — her doll — and she won\'t sleep without him.
And Old Aurel in bed eleven wants somebody to read to him. The rot took his eyes, not his ears.
Captain Buttons
Bette, a child in the Ember Ward, lost her rag doll somewhere in the ruins.
The Blind Archivist
Old Aurel in the Ember Ward wants someone to read to him.
The well\'s in the middle of Ash Square. Tell Sorrel it\'s for the Ward.
You lower the bucket. It takes a long time to reach anything.
Bring the water back to Noll at the Ember Ward.
The rationed well. Someone has scratched a tally into the stone: one mark per bucket, a year of marks.
The rationed well. A chain and a bucket, and a long way down to water that tastes faintly of bells.

thank you.
don\'t tell her I said it.
t supposed to tell you that part either.
Ward Mother— _Ward Mother_—!
Pell. Pell, look at me. Breathe. In through the nose—
The boy in bed four is shaking. Violet runs under his skin like ink in water.
Pell. Little Pell from Lanternfall. Who wanted to be a Vanguard when he grew up.
Noll. The phial. The last one.
But that\'s the—
The violet slows. Stops. Retreats, a little, the way the tide retreats: to gather itself.
That buys him a week. Maybe less.
Noll. Get my coat.
Ward Mother, no. You made the rule. Nobody goes down there—
I made the rule. I said nobody _else_.
I\'m coming with you.
You patch, I go first. That\'s how it always worked. The tide caves. The black rocks. Every time.
Every time you went first, Wren, I ended up patching _you_.
Then you know I\'m good at being patched.
Ilse looks at the boy in bed four. At the forty other beds. At the wall of names by the door. At everything in the Ward except Wren.
Not for you.
I\'ll hold the Ward. I can hold the Ward.
You can. Beds two and thirty get water every hour. Don\'t let Old Aurel talk you into reading him the whole hymnal.
The Undercroft gate is in the Bellfounders\' Quarter — the sunken court on the west side. Sorrel bricked it up after the third team didn\'t come back.
Go to the Undercroft gate in the Bellfounders\' Quarter (west side of the ruins).
Pell is here. Pell from home. The rot nearly took him and Ilse used the last of the medicine. We\'re going into the Undercroft — "for the patients, not for you." I\'ll take it.

s getting worse.
Rubble, packed tight under the old arch. Someone has chalked across it in big letters:
NOBODY. NOT EVEN YOU, MARROW.
Ward Mother. You know the rule.
I wrote the rule, Sorrel.
Then you know why I bricked it. Three good people. Mags could carry a door on her back.
And Pell has a week. Move the rubble.
You\'re the only one who knows how to keep them breathing. You know that? If you don\'t come back, nobody does.
Noll does. I taught him.
Noll is thirteen.
So was I, once. It didn\'t last.
You. Just Wren. You go first down there, hear me? She\'s worth ten of anybody in this city.
I know. I\'ve always known.
If you\'re not back by the dark bell—
Descend into the Drowned Undercroft and find the Choir\'s sunsalt stores.
Sorrel opened the Undercroft for Ilse. Not for me. That\'s fair. Everybody here would follow Ilse into the dark. I have to earn it.
Two rules. One: we don\'t split up. Two: if I say we turn back, we turn back.
There isn\'t a three.
There\'s always a three.
Somewhere far below, under the slap of water, something is singing. Not words. Just a note, held and held and held.
Your guard drops when you swing. The left side. It did a year ago, too.
You remember that?
I remember where I had to put the stitches.
A shallow alcove where three people sheltered. They are not here anymore.
An alcove of stacked bones — and, among the old ones, three new packs. A rope. A lantern, long dead. Three tin tags on cords.
_(very quietly)_ Doran. Mags. Little Cobb.
Cobb was fifteen. He wanted to be a Mender. He used to watch me stitch and count the knots out loud.
We\'ll take them home.
They don\'t have homes. That\'s why they were in my Ward.
Three Tin Tags
The third sunsalt team died in the Ossuary. Bring their tags back to Sorrel at the gate.
Cages. Notes. Cauldrons... This was a laboratory.
Sister Mercy\'s. Before the end, people from the Undercroft went missing. Everybody knew. Nobody looked.
We looked. Remember? A year ago. We were so proud of ourselves for stopping her.
We did stop her.
We stopped _her_. We didn\'t stop the man who signed her orders.
I know. I was there.
A ledger in Mercy\'s cramped hand:
"Subject 7 held its shape three days. On the second day it asked for its mother. It did not have one. I wrote one down for it, so it would stop asking."
A loose page, pinned under a scalpel:
"The Gloam keeps everything it is given — every face, every voice. One need only _remember hard enough_ to draw the shape back out. Grief is the needle. Love is the thread."
A letter, unsent:
"Holiness — my work is crude beside yours. You speak of _her_ as though she were already home. Let me see her. Let me see what perfect looks like." There is no reply.
"Her." Who\'s "her"?
A black-haired girl, washed up on the rocks, who didn\'t have a name. Who said: don\'t let him find me.
You\'re lying. You always touch your ear when you lie.
I don\'t _know_, Ilse. I\'m afraid of what I think.
The sluice wheel is turned as far as it will go. Water roars somewhere behind the walls.
A great iron sluice wheel, crusted with rust. A plate reads: NAVE GATE — BOTH WHEELS TO RAISE.
Turn the wheel?
It groans. It shrieks. It turns.
Far off, in the Nave, iron grinds against stone — and the sluice gate rises.
That\'s both. The gate north of the Nave should be open now.
The Nave gate is open. Go north through the Nave.
One. The plate said both wheels. The other one must be across the Nave.
Turn the second sluice wheel to raise the Nave gate.
An iron sluice gate bars the way north. Two chains run from it into the walls — west and east.
Sluice gates have wheels. One west, one east.
The masonry here is newer than the rest — and cracked straight through. Cold air breathes out of the seams.
Put your shoulder into it?
The wall gives way into a forgotten niche. Somebody hid something here, a long time ago.
A little chapel, above the waterline. Dry. Almost warm. The kind of place you only find when you have stopped looking.
We rest here. Five minutes. That\'s an order from your Mender.
Ilse takes something from her coat pocket and turns it over and over in her fingers. A silver gull, missing the tip of one wing.
That\'s Nana\'s brooch.
She pressed it into my hand at the dock. With the sky coming apart over us. I said, "Nana, get in the boat."
She said the Doyle children were still up the hill. And she went back for them.
The square went first. I watched it go.
Ilse. I—
If you say sorry, I\'ll have to decide what to do with it. And I am too tired to decide anything.
She always went back for people. Her whole life. Every sick neighbor, every stray. I thought that was what good people do. Go back. Never keep anything for yourself.
I\'ve been very good for a year, Wren. I\'ve been _so_ good.
Five minutes are up.
Descend the stair below the chapel to find the source of the singing.

Nana Brisa went back up the hill for the Doyle children. Ilse watched the square fall. She still has the gull brooch. She asked me not to say sorry, so I didn\'t. It\'s still there, in my mouth, like a stone.
A cistern the size of a cathedral, flooded to the ribs. Bells — dozens of them — lie half-drowned in the black water.
It\'s... a hymn. I know it. I _know_ it. It\'s the Dawnsong.
No. It\'s the Dawnsong backwards.
Follow the singing to the Choir Loft at the north end of the cistern.
Robed figures stand in a ring at the Choir Loft, waist-deep in nothing, mouths open on a single note. Water runs out of their sleeves. They have been singing for a year.
Drowned Precentor
It\'s over. There isn\'t going to be a noon. The song didn\'t work.
The song _always_ works, child. You simply have not been singing long enough.
Wren. Behind it — the iron door. "APOTHECARIUM." That\'s the vault.
Choir. A new verse. _Together._
The note breaks. For the first time in a year, the cistern is silent — except for water, finding its level.
You can stop now. Nobody needs you to hold it anymore.
You called him "you." Not "it."
He was a patient. He just didn\'t have a bed.
Open the Apothecary Vault east of the Choir Loft.
Shelves. Crates. Racks of little stoppered phials, each one glowing like a coal kept under ash.
That\'s... that\'s enough for a year. For everyone. For _everyone_—
Ilse laughs — once, sharp and bright, like something breaking — and then stops herself, as if she\'s been caught.
You\'re allowed to laugh.
I know what I\'m allowed. Let\'s go. Pell has a week and we\'ve used two days of it.
Bring the sunsalt back to the Ember Ward.
We found the vault. Enough sunsalt for a year. Ilse laughed. It was the best sound I\'ve heard since the world ended.
One phial. Then another, for bed two, and bed thirty, and every bed after. The Ward smells of hot salt and morning.
I\'m here. Don\'t sit up.
Is that... is that _Wren_? Wren Halloway?
Hi, Pell.
Are you still a Vanguard? Did you bring your sword?
Can I hold it?
When you\'re better. Just the handle.
Just the handle.
For the first time since Wren walked into the Ward, Ilse looks at her.
Then she looks away.
Pell asked if he could hold my sword. Just the handle — like he did the day before the Kindling. Ilse looked at me. Just for a second.
Later. The Ward is sleeping — really sleeping, for the first time in months. Ilse sits on the steps with her coat around her knees.
Can I sit?
It\'s a step. I don\'t own it.
Noll asked me what I wanted for my birthday. I\'m seventeen next month.
I didn\'t have an answer. I\'ve had a list for everything my whole life. What to pack. What to say. What Nana needed. What the patients need.
I don\'t have a list for me.
Start one.
One thing. Something you want. Not something somebody needs.
And Pip. And Sable.
There. That\'s a list. Happy?
Fenna — the scrap-trader in Ash Square — says there\'s a sellsword up at Kiteholm. Big. Blond. Drinks like a drain. Terrible at cards.
That\'s either Bram, or a very specific disaster.
And a boy with an eyepatch who runs a gang of orphans. Talks like a pirate.
The Ward ran before you got here, Ward Mother. It can run for a week while you\'re gone.
That\'s not true.
It\'s a kind lie. You taught me those.
I\'m not forgiving you, Wren.
I know.
And I\'m not going to Kiteholm for you.
Write that down somewhere. It might not happen again.
When you are ready, ask Fenna the scrap-trader in Ash Square for passage to Kiteholm.
Ilse said she wants something. For herself. She wants to find Bram and Pip — because she wants to, not because anybody needs her to. I wrote it down, like she said.
Kiteholm, is it? My glider-barge goes up on the next ember-wind. You\'ll hate it. Everyone hates it. Then they never leave.
Leave for Kiteholm now? (You can return to Aurenne later by the world map.)
Let\'s go
Not yet
Wind\'ll keep. Wind always keeps.
Fenna Gale, scrap-and-sundry, out of Kiteholm. I haul sunsalt down when there\'s sunsalt, and bad news up when there isn\'t.
Kiteholm? Shanty town on a wind-shard, held together with kite-string and spite. There\'s a boy up there with one eye runs twenty orphans like a pirate fleet.
And a big blond sellsword guards the Scrap Baron. Drinks like a drain. Loses at cards to children. Cries, sometimes, at the coat rack.
Scrap-trader. Sunsalt when I\'ve got it. Today I haven\'t.
Noll has a list. Sorrel has a list. Pell has the handle of your sword on a promise.
And you?
I have a list too. It has three names on it.
We left Aurenne on Fenna\'s glider-barge, riding the ember-wind up toward Kiteholm. Ilse watched the Ward until it was too small to see.
Children of the Wreck
Explore Kiteholm and look for Pip and Bram.

s been on a big adventure. He won\'t tell me about it. He\'s very brave.
CAPTAIN BUTTONS!
Where was he? Was he scared? Did he cry?
He was in the garden, keeping some old soldiers company. He didn\'t cry once.
He\'s very brave. He gets it from me.
Bette\'s Mother
Here — it\'s not much. My husband wore it. He\'d want it to keep somebody alive.
Captain Buttons is lost.
He has two buttons for eyes but one fell off so he can only see half the way home.
Old Aurel
Come back and read to me again sometime. Not the hymnal. Anything with a happy ending. I\'ve earned one.
Forty years I kept the Choir\'s archive. Now I keep bed eleven. A smaller collection.
A reader! Under the pillow — the hymnal. Page with the ribbon. My favorite. Humor an old man.
_"Of the Seven Lanterns, and the Song that Wakes the Sun."_
_"Seven voices raise the dawn. Should seven voices sing it backward, all at once, the day shall be held — as a breath is held — and never let go."_
_"This the Choir forbids, for a breath held forever is not a breath. It is a drowning."_
Lovely, isn\'t it? I read it to the Hierophant once, when he was a boy. He cried. I thought it was the poetry.
A breath held forever is a drowning. He knew. He heard it as a boy and he knew.
_(quietly)_ Wren. Breathe.
Take this, reader. An archivist\'s workbook. Knowledge is for spending.
Old Aurel had me read the forbidden verse: a breath held forever is a drowning. He read it to Cassian when Cassian was a boy.
Post? For me? Nobody\'s written me in— oh. Oh, it\'s from _me_.
I used to post myself reminders at the Cathedral. "Prune the south roses before the frost." Dated the day before.
Mind the graves, miss. They\'re new. Everything here is new except me.
I was the Cathedral\'s gardener. Forty years of roses. Now there\'s nothing to grow but names.
If I had seeds — anything that\'ll take in ash — I\'d give them flowers. The Choir kept dawnmoss for their medicines. Down below, I\'d wager. Where nobody goes.
Flowers for the Fallen
Hollis the gardener wants seeds that will grow in ash. The Choir kept dawnmoss below the city.
You haven\'t seen a rag doll, have you? Button eyes? One button?
Him? I found him on Corporal Dray\'s grave. Thought he was an offering. Been keeping him out of the ash.
He\'s been good company. Doesn\'t talk back.
Dawnmoss! Oh, you clever thing. It grows in anything — ash, rubble, sorrow. It\'s practically a weed. The best things are.
There. They\'ll be up in a week. Gold, like a little dawn on every grave.
Take these. I won\'t be needing them; I\'ve got all the seed I want now.
Little green shoots already. Don\'t tell anyone. They\'ll want to name them after the Hierophant, and I won\'t have it.
Dawnmoss, from the Undercroft. If you\'re ever down there and the singing doesn\'t get you.
Did you see them? Every face in the city, turned up.
Ring it again tomorrow, I think. And the day after. A city needs to know what time it is, even if the answer is always "dusk."
Four hundred bells. I rang the Bellwrights\' Tenor for thirty-one years. Hear that tower? Still standing. One bell left in it.
Its clapper came loose in the Sundering. Fell clean through the floor of the Quarter, down into the Undercroft. I heard it go — _BONG, bong, bong_ — all the way down.
If anyone ever goes down there and comes back up, bring me my clapper. I\'d like this city to hear a bell before I die.
The Last Bell
Osric the bellringer\'s clapper fell into the depths of the Undercroft. Find it.
The clapper fell all the way down. Past the old halls, past the Nave. Somewhere the water\'s deepest.
That\'s it. That\'s _her_. Bruised, but she\'s whole.
Stand back, girl. Ears covered. I\'ve waited a year for this.
The note rolls out over the ash and the broken towers and the cracked Lantern, and keeps going, out past the edge of the shard, into the abyss.
All over the ruins, people stop. A woman at the well. Sorrel at the gate. A child at the soup pot. Every face in Aurenne turns up toward the sound.
There. Now the city knows what time it is.
What time is it?
Time to get on with it.
Osric rang the last bell in Aurenne. Everybody looked up. I think some of them had forgotten they could.
Mail\'s light today. Mail\'s light every day. But I walk the route.
Somebody has to believe there\'s a tomorrow to deliver to.
All delivered? Then my route\'s done for the first time in a year.
There\'s one more. It\'s been in my bag since the day before. I couldn\'t deliver it. Wrong place, you see. Lanternfall.
It\'s addressed to a "Wren Halloway." Choir seal. Never opened.
I thought it might be. You read like a Halloway. Sorry. It\'s a postwoman\'s instinct.
_My dear restless heart —_
_If this reaches you, the song is sung, and you are reading by a light that never moves. I hope it is a good light. I hope your father is beside you, and that he has not aged a day._
_You will understand, now, why I could not let the good days end. One day you will thank me. Until then — I have kept a place for you._
Burn it.
No. I\'m keeping it.
So I remember what it sounds like when he\'s being kind.
I\'m keeping it. So I remember what it sounds like when he\'s being kind.
And this is for your trouble. A postwoman\'s good-luck coin. It never brought me any, but it might be shy.
Petra had a letter for me — from Cassian, written the day before the Last Sunset. "I have kept a place for you." I\'m keeping it. I need to remember.
Post! Royal Aurenne Post, est. four hundred years ago, disestablished one year ago, still delivering.
I\'ve three letters I can\'t walk to — my knees and the rubble aren\'t on speaking terms. One for Sorrel at the gate. One for old Hollis in the garden. And one for "the Cathedral of Dawn."
The Cathedral\'s a hole now, but leave it at the foot of the Lantern. Somebody up there used to answer.
Dead Letters
Deliver Petra\'s letters: Sorrel at the gate, Hollis in the garden, and the Cathedral (the foot of the Grand Lantern).
You leave Petra\'s letter at the foot of the Grand Lantern, weighted with a stone.
It is addressed: "To Whoever Is Still Listening."
The Grand Lantern of Aurenne. A crack runs from the lamp-room to the foundation, wide enough to put your arm in.
The glass up top is dark, like an eye that has seen something it cannot stop seeing.
People come up here to spit on it. Sorrel stopped them at first. Then she stopped stopping them.
Do you?
I don\'t have time to hate a building, Wren.
A letter? For me? ...It\'s from my sister. Posted the day before.
She says the plums are early this year.
Doran. Mags. Little Cobb.
I bricked up that gate so nobody else would go. And now I\'ve got their tags in my hand, and it doesn\'t feel like I did anything right.
You did. You kept forty people from following them. That\'s the job, Sorrel. It never feels like anything.
I\'ll hang them on the Ward wall. Under their names. Here — Mags would\'ve wanted somebody strong to have this.
The thing in the Reliquary? _Dead?_ The thing that ate the second team\'s mule?
Bounty\'s yours. Every coin of it. The whole city chipped in, and believe me, nobody had coins to chip.
If you two are really going down... the board\'s got one bounty on it. Something nests in the old Reliquary, north-east of the Nave. Tolls like a bell when it breathes.
The second team called it _Old Clapper_. Right before it ate their mule. Kill it and the city pays.
Old Clapper
Something that tolls like a bell nests in the Undercroft\'s north-east Reliquary. Slay it for the city\'s bounty.
The Ward Mother came back. Came back _with_ something, for once.
You go first, she patches. Hm. Maybe you\'re not so "just" after all, Just Wren.
Hands clean, mouths shut, eyes open. That\'s Aurenne now.
And nobody goes in the Undercroft.
Something uncoils in the shallows of the Reliquary — scaled, rust-red, its belly swollen around a shape that is unmistakably a bell.
It breathes in. Deep inside it, something tolls.
It swallowed a bell. It _swallowed a bell_. How is it alive?
Spite, mostly. I can relate.
Old Clapper is slain. Tell Sorrel at the gate.
Old Clapper rolls over in the water with one last, muffled _bong_.
src/story/ch8.js: Children of the Wreck
Kiteholm. A spur of rock torn off the old world, hanging in the wind like a fist that refuses to open.
Shacks of scrap and sailcloth cling to it. And everywhere — on poles, on roofs, on strings tied to children — kites.
It\'s all... string.
Fenna said it\'s held _together_ by kites. Held _up_ by stubbornness.
That\'s not how engineering works.
That\'s not how anything works anymore.
A pebble cracks off the planks between Wren\'s boots.
Toll\'s two silver or one secret. Slingshot says pay up.
We\'re looking for someone. A boy called Pip.
Don\'t know him. Two silver.
Twelve years old. Talks like a pirate. Steals anything that isn\'t nailed down and most things that are.
She didn\'t hear it from anybody, Tansy. Go keep watch.
He is taller. Thinner. A scarf, a scavenged coat — and a patch over his left eye. He looks at Wren for a long time with the other.
Well. Look what the wind dragged in.
Pip. Your eye—
Lost it in a card game. You should see the other guy\'s eye.
Pip. Let me look at it.
It\'s healed, Ilse. Healed ugly, but healed. Like everything.
Thought you were dead, Halloway. Hoped so, some days.
Rules of Kiteholm. One: Kites look after Kites. Two: you ain\'t Kites. Three: the Baron owns the air, so pay your mooring fee and don\'t make trouble.
We came to find you. You and Bram.
Pip laughs. It is not a kid\'s laugh.
Bram\'s at the Rusty Anchor, or the Baron\'s door, or face-down somewhere between \'em. Go find him. He won\'t want to be found. He\'s real good at that.
He\'s twelve.
He\'s twelve going on forty.
That\'s what I said.
Find Bram at the Rusty Anchor (the tavern on Kiteholm\'s west side).
Kiteholm. Pip is twelve now, with one eye and twenty orphans who call him Boss. He said he hoped I was dead, some days. I can\'t blame him.
Hah! Full Lantern! Read \'em and—
That\'s nine silver, is what that is.
Bram looks up. His face does something complicated. Then he picks up his cup and drains it.
No. Nope. I\'m drunk. I\'m seeing ghosts. It\'s the cider. This is mostly cider.
It is mostly not cider, Bram. I can smell it from here.
He stands too fast. The chair goes over. For one second he looks like he\'s going to throw his arms around both of them —
— and then he doesn\'t.
You\'re... alive. Both of you. That\'s— that\'s—
Good. That\'s good. I\'m glad.
I\'m working. Guard duty. The Baron. I have to— I\'m _very_ important to the Baron.
He talks about you. When he\'s far enough gone. "My girls from the island."
Then he cries and tries to fight the coat rack. Loses, mostly.
He ran.
He ran _from us_. That\'s different.
Is it?
Go to the Kite Nest (the red-roofed house by the market) and talk to Pip.
Bram is here. He saw us and ran — said he was "very important to the Baron." Dorran says he cries at the coat rack. I think he\'s been running for a year.
He\'s not here.
Pip? Where is he?
Wick and Moth went scavenging two days ago. Down the Underhang, to the old Choir wreck. Good scrap down there. They didn\'t come back.
Boss went after them. Alone. He told us to stay. He said grown-ups don\'t help, grown-ups just get you counted.
You\'re grown. Sort of.
I\'m seventeen.
Exactly. Will you go after him?
Three things. One, we\'re going. Two, nobody else from this room is coming. Three—
Three, Boss\'ll be furious. I know. I\'ll tell the Kites to move the crates off the ladder.
Follow Pip down the Underhang — the ladder at Kiteholm\'s south edge.
Two of Pip\'s Kites went missing in a crashed Choir ship under the shard. Pip went after them alone. We\'re going down after him.
The Baron. Now. He\'s got guards and walls. Kiteholm\'s got kites.
Kites look after Kites.
When I grow up I\'m going to be the Boss of the Boss.
Don\'t tell him.
ALL FIVE? Even Sprocket? Nobody ever finds Sprocket. _I_ don\'t find Sprocket.
Okay. Okay. You can have it. It\'s the tail off the first kite Boss ever built. It\'s lucky. It makes you fast. That\'s science.
Five of the lookouts are supposed to be on watch. They\'re not on watch. They\'re _hiding_. It\'s a game, but it\'s also a crime.
Burr, Fig, Nettle, Pim, and Sprocket. Find \'em all and I\'ll give you something good. Promise on my slingshot.
Hide and Seek
Find the five Kites hiding around Kiteholm: Burr, Fig, Nettle, Pim and Sprocket. Report to Tansy.
Toll\'s paid. You\'re fine. Don\'t touch the kites. They bite.
Shh! I\'m still hiding. It counts if I keep hiding.
I\'m on watch. Very hard. Go away.
Rope ladders. Ledges no wider than a table. Below them: nothing at all, for as far as the haze lets you see.
For the record, I hate this.
I want it _written down_.
On the roc perch, a boy with a knife in each hand has his back to the cliff — and three gale-shrikes have him pinned.
Come on then! Come _on!_ I\'ve got more knives than you\'ve got eyes!
I had them.
You had them _surrounding you_.
That\'s a strategy. Bram taught me. "Let them come to you."
Bram\'s strategies mostly involve falling over.
Wick and Moth went into the wreck. The _Vigil_. I saw Vesper colors on the hull. Somebody\'s using it.
Then we go in together.
Fine. Kites look after Kites. You\'re temporary Kites. _Very_ temporary.
And nobody calls me "kid." I\'m the Boss.
Descend to the wreck of the Vigil and find Wick and Moth.
Found Pip on a cliff ledge, fighting three shrikes and losing. He let us help. We\'re "temporary Kites." Very temporary.
A dead campfire. A bedroll. A Vesper scout\'s satchel, and a journal with a broken spine:
"Day 9. Counted the shanty. Twenty-two children under fourteen. The Penitent will be pleased. He says children remember the best days best."
"Day 10. A boy with one eye watched me from the kites all afternoon. I think he knows. I think he is waiting for me to come back up."
The rest of the pages are blank.
Huh. He never came back up.
Don\'t look at me like that. I didn\'t do nothing. The wind did. The wind takes care of Kiteholm.
An empty nest of sticks and sailcloth.
Tangled in a shrike\'s nest: a patched blue kite with a painted grin. The string is still tied to a little bone toggle carved like a W.
Wick\'s Kite
A blue kite with a painted grin, rescued from a shrike nest in the Underhang. It belongs to Wick, one of Pip\'s Kites.
That\'s Wick\'s. He\'s been looking for it for a month. Shrikes nick anything shiny. Or blue. Or Wick\'s.
Inside the hull, everything leans. And somewhere ahead, faintly, a music box is playing a lullaby.
That\'s not ours. Kites don\'t do lullabies.
What do Kites do?
Bedtime threats. "Go to sleep or the Baron gets your boots."
The captain\'s desk. Charts of the shards, with Kiteholm circled in violet ink.
Orders, under a paperweight shaped like a sun:

"_By the hand of the Penitent:_ The children of the Underhang shards are to be gathered and kept sleeping until the Hierophant\'s barge arrives. Children remember the best days best. Evernoon has need of them."
"KITEHOLM is next. Twenty children. The Penitent will collect them personally."
A ring of keys hangs from the captain\'s chair. One is stamped BRIG.
"Twenty children."
There\'s twenty-two. He can\'t even count my Kites right.
I\'m fine. I\'m _fine_. Brig\'s south. Move.
Open the brig (south of the gun deck) with the Brig Key.
A heavy door, banded in iron. A sign on it reads BRIG, and under that, in a child\'s hand: LET US OUT.
The key turns. The door swings in on a long, low groan.
Cages, built for livestock. And in every cage, a sleeping child — breathing slow and even, eyes moving under the lids.
Wick! Moth! Up, you lazy— _WICK!_
They can\'t hear you. Pulse is fine. Breathing\'s fine. It\'s like... they\'re dreaming on purpose.
_(asleep)_ ...the cake has... _so many candles_...
_(asleep)_ ...Mum, it\'s still sunny... five more minutes...
The lullaby. It\'s coming from the front of the ship. They\'re being _kept_ like this.
Then we break the music box.
We break it into so many pieces it plays every song at once.
Silence the lullaby at the forecastle (the bow of the Vigil).

In the bow sits a machine like a cathedral organ crossed with a cradle: brass pipes, bellows breathing, and a great drum studded with pins, turning, turning. The lullaby comes out of it, sweet and endless.
Vesper Cantor
Shh. Shh. You\'ll wake them.
That\'s the idea.
Why? They\'re _happy_. They\'re at their birthdays. Every one of them. In the noon they\'ll never have a bad day again.
They\'re in _cages_.
Everyone is in a cage, little boy. Theirs just has a nicer song.
The drum seizes. The pins scream across the comb. The lullaby stops in the middle of a bar — and behind them, down in the brig, a child starts to cry.
That\'s Moth. Moth always cries when she wakes up. Every time. Like it\'s a surprise.
Boss? ...Boss, you came for us?
Course I came. Kites look after Kites.
I dreamed it was my birthday, and Mum was there, and it was sunny, and it was _never going to stop_. Boss, it was so nice.
Pip turns away from them, very fast, so they won\'t see his face. He turns straight into Wren instead.
I wasn\'t going to.
Everyone hold hands. Nobody lets go until we\'re on the ladder. That\'s a rule, not a request.
There was a machine in the wreck singing children to sleep, so they\'d keep dreaming their best days for "Evernoon." We broke it. Wick dreamed it was his birthday forever. He said it was so nice.
The Kite Nest erupts. Kites everywhere — on beds, on crates, on Wick.
You found them! Boss, you found— and _them_, they helped, I _told_ you grown-ups—
Tansy. Quiet. All of you, quiet.
The Vespers are coming. Here. A knight called the Penitent. For you. All of you.
Twenty faces go very still. Nobody cries.
So here\'s what we do. We go to the Baron. He\'s got walls and guards and a big stupid gun on his roof. He keeps the air. He can keep us.
And if he won\'t?
Then he\'ll learn what twenty Kites can do to a man\'s boots.
Warn Baron Dask at the Baron\'s Hall (the north terrace).
Baron Dask
Pipkin Tallow. In my hall. With _guests_. To what do I owe the inconvenience?
Vespers. They\'re coming for my Kites. A knight they call the Penitent. We need your guards on the ladders and your gun on the east cliff.
My guards guard _my_ scrap. My gun guards _my_ air. Your orphans guard themselves; that was always the arrangement.
They\'re children!
And I am a businessman, girl. Children are a _cost_.
By the door, Bram has gone the color of old ash.
Black armor. A mask like a weeping face. He fights with... with his blade held high. Like this.
How d\'you know that?
Everyone in the Dawnguard knows the stories. A knight who... never mind. It\'s stories.
Bram. Will you stand with us?
Course you are.
Prepare Kiteholm for the raid. When ready, talk to Pip at the Kite Nest to keep watch for the night.
Baron Dask won\'t help — "children are a cost." Bram knew what the Penitent looks like before anyone told him. He went gray. He\'s "off duty at midnight."
Kites are on the lines. Slingshots, whistles, and every pot in the Nest for banging. We\'ll hear \'em coming.
Keep watch with Pip through the night? (Kiteholm will be attacked.)
Keep watch
Not yet
Don\'t take long. Night comes when it wants now.
Go on, sleep. I\'ll take first watch. I always take first watch.
A whistle. Then twenty whistles. Then every pot in Kiteholm, banging at once.
_(from the kite-lines)_ EAST CLIFF! BLACK SAILS ON THE EAST CLIFF!
A black sky-barge noses out of the haze, sails like torn mourning-cloth. Figures drop from it on ropes onto the Kite Cliffs.
Kites! Positions! Littles in the Nest, bigs on the lines! _GO!_
More — by the market! Those aren\'t men. Look at them. They\'re _empty_.
He comes down the Baron\'s ramp like a funeral bell: slow, heavy, certain. Black armor. A mask carved into a face that has been weeping for a very long time.
The Penitent
The children. Where are the children.
You\'re not taking them.
I am not _taking_ them. I am taking them _home_. To a summer afternoon that never ends. To mothers who never die. To birthdays.
What do you offer them? This? Kites and ash?
We offer them _knives_, you tin-plated—
Wren! Ilse! I— I heard the pots, I came as fast as—
The Penitent turns. Lifts his greatsword high over his right shoulder, point back, elbow up. Waits.
Nobody uses the Venn Guard. Nobody but— nobody but _him_.
Bram does not move. His sword is in his hand. His feet are on the planks. He does not move at all.
Bram! BRAM!
You froze then, too. At your trial. Do you remember? I stepped in front of the blow.
Nobody will step in front of this one.
TANSY, DOWN—!
The stroke comes down like the end of the world. Tansy is on the planks, unhurt, shoved clear. And a boy with one eye is lying where she was standing.
He\'s breathing. He\'s— Wren, I need _time_, I need him to stop _bleeding_—
No. Not again.
NOT AGAIN!
Steel on steel. The Penitent\'s second stroke stops a hand\'s width from the children — on Bram\'s blade.
I\'m _afraid_. You hear me? I\'m so afraid I can\'t feel my hands.
I\'m doing it anyway.
The Penitent goes down on one knee. The weeping mask cracks clean in two, and falls, and rings on the planks.
Under it is the face of a man in his fifties. Gray beard, a broken nose healed crooked — a kind face. And the eyes are empty. Not dark. _Empty_, like the windows of a house where nobody lives.
Sir... Sir Aldous?
Squire Kestrel. You are late for your trial.
You died. You _died_. I saw you die. You stepped in front of—
In the noon, I don\'t have to. The Hierophant gave me back the day before. I polish my armor. You bring me cider. You say you\'re ready. I say you\'re not. Over. And over.
It is very kind of him.
Evernoon. It\'s _real_?
As real as a summer afternoon, little Keeper. He has filled it with us — the dead. We walk its streets. We wear ourselves like coats.
When he needs a hand out here, he sends one of us. We fit very well. We remember our own swords.
Bram. You froze. You froze again.
I did.
And then I didn\'t.
Something moves in the empty eyes. A flicker — like a candle seen through a window, far back in the house.
Sir Aldous
The armor falls in on itself, full of nothing, and the nothing blows away on the wind.
He used to say that. After drills. Every time. Even when I was terrible.
I was always terrible.

The Penitent was Sir Aldous — or something wearing him. Evernoon is real, and it\'s full of the dead, worn like coats. Bram froze. Then he didn\'t. At the very end, something in Aldous\'s eyes said "good lad."
Morning, if there were mornings. The Nest is full of sleeping children, and one small boy in a hammock, stitched up from collarbone to hip.
He\'s going to live. Two things: he\'s going to have a scar, and he\'s going to be insufferable about it.
_(weakly)_ ...already am.
Did we win? Was that... was that _Bram_? Swinging that big stupid sword?
Go to sleep, Pip.
Make me.
He\'s asleep before she can answer. Ilse doesn\'t let go of his hand.
I froze.
You did. Then you fought.
Sir Aldous used to say courage was a thing you _do_, not a thing you _have_. "You act while you\'re afraid, lad, or you never act at all." I thought he was being nice. He was always being nice.
I spent a year making sure I never had to find out if he was right.
I gave Cassian the Dawnstone, Bram. I\'m the reason any of this happened. I didn\'t freeze. I ran straight at it.
If you\'re a coward, I don\'t know what that makes me.
If you\'ll have a coward.
We\'ll have Bram.
And— you paid the Baron. For my shield. I pawned it the first week. Thought I didn\'t deserve to carry it.
You don\'t have to deserve it. You just have to carry it.
One thing. The Penitent\'s barge went west, toward the Noon Spire. If we\'re going after Evernoon, we need wings.
The Baron\'s been dunning an airship captain for eleven thousand silver. Holed up at a place called Corvin\'s Roost.
_Corvin?_ Corvin\'s alive?
And owes everybody money. So: yes. Definitely Corvin.
When Pip went down, you went straight at that thing. You didn\'t even look back to see if I was behind you.
I didn\'t have to. I knew you were there.
It is not forgiveness. But it is not nothing.
Pip wants to see you at the Kite Cliffs (east of the Nest) when he\'s on his feet.
Bram is with us. "If you\'ll have a coward." We\'ll have Bram. Pip will live — scar and all. And Corvin is alive, hiding from his debts at a place called Corvin\'s Roost.
On the highest point of the Kite Cliffs, where the wind never stops, Pip sits with a kite across his knees. Red and gold. Brand new.
Ilse says I\'m not allowed up here. Ilse says a lot.
That\'s a good kite.
I\'ve built a hundred. For the littles. Best kites on the shard.
Never flown one. Not once.
Why not?
Somebody\'s got to hold the string. Somebody\'s got to watch the ladders. Count heads. Find the food. Know where everybody is. That\'s the Boss.
You can\'t do that and look up.
I\'ll hold it.
The Kites. For a bit. Tansy\'s got the ladders. Ilse\'s got the Nest — nobody\'s getting past Ilse. Bram\'s counting heads, very badly, out loud.
You fly it.
I\'m the _Boss_, I don\'t—
You\'re twelve.
He stands. He holds it up into the wind. The wind takes it — snatches it — and the string sings off the spool, up and up into the bruised sky.
Look at it go— look at it _GO!_ Wren! WREN, LOOK!
I\'m looking.
Pip laughs. Not the hard, old laugh. A kid\'s laugh — too loud, cracking in the middle, completely helpless.
Tell them what?
That I\'m a kid.
Pip. They know.
Boss! Ilse says you have to come down or she\'ll— whoa. Is that _yours?_
Tansy. When we go — and we\'re going — who minds the Kites?
Me. I\'m nine and three-quarters. That\'s basically ten.
Yeah. Yeah, okay. Basically ten.
*Pip* rejoins the party.
Take the Baron\'s skiff from the south-west dock to Corvin\'s Roost when you are ready.
Pip flew a kite. His first one, ever. He laughed like a kid. Tansy will mind the Kites — she\'s "basically ten." Next: Corvin\'s Roost.
Skiff-Hand Rook
Baron\'s skiff. Baron\'s orders. Baron\'s bad mood. Come back with a reason.
Baron says you\'re to have the skiff. Says it\'s "an investment." Said it like it hurt him.
Leave Kiteholm for Corvin\'s Roost? (You can return later by the world map.)
Cast off
Skiff\'ll wait. Baron won\'t, but the skiff will.
Corvin Ashe. Last time I saw him he owed me four silver and a boot.
Last time I saw him I _was_ the four silver.
Three things. One, he\'s a coward. Two, he\'s a liar. Three—
Three, he\'s ours.
We left Kiteholm on the Baron\'s skiff. Twenty Kites on the lines, waving. Tansy saluted. Pip pretended not to see, and then saluted back.
The Halcyon
Find Corvin Ashe at Corvin\'s Roost.

s friends. Charming. Your Kestrel owes me fifteen hundred silver in drink, damages, and one very expensive coat rack.
He pawned me a shield against it his first week. Dawnguard steel. Dented. Sentimental garbage, but garbage is my trade.
Bram\'s Debt
Bram owes Baron Dask 1,500 gold. Paying it will redeem the shield Bram pawned.
Pay it
The debt keeps. Interest is my love language.
Your purse says no. I always listen to purses.
Paid in full. How sweet. Here — take the man\'s shield. It\'s been looking at me.
I own the air. Breathe carefully.
Midnight. I\'m off at midnight.
Don\'t look at me like that. Ilse\'s already looking at me like that. There\'s only so much _that_ a man can take.
I\'m on duty. Can\'t talk. Very important. Guarding.
I\'m good at telling people no. Started with myself.
Gaffer Quill
When you find Ashe, tell him Quill says his port wing still pulls left. He\'ll know. He\'ll pretend he doesn\'t, but he\'ll know.
Airship cogs! Real ones! Oh, she\'ll fly now. Well — she\'ll fall slower. Same thing, up here.
I built wings for the _Halcyon_, you know. Years back. Corvin Ashe\'s ship. If he\'s alive, she\'s rusting at the Roost, and he\'s drinking next to her, telling her it\'s not her fault.
Take this. A wright\'s monocle. You see how things fit together, after a while.
Kite-wright. Glider-wright. Wright of anything that wants to be in the air and shouldn\'t be.
I\'m building a glider big enough to carry the Kites off this rock if it ever cracks. I need three airship cogs. The scrap-golems down in the Underhang have \'em in their bellies — don\'t ask how.
The Kite-Wright
Gaffer Quill needs 3 Scrap Gears (scrap golems in the Underhang and the Vigil carry them) for an escape glider.

s my best thing. A fruit off the Baron\'s roof-tree. He counts them. He\'ll never notice. He\'ll _definitely_ notice.
I\'m teaching it to do loops. It doesn\'t want to. We\'re negotiating.
The gale-shrikes of the Underhang stole Wick\'s blue kite. They nest on the western ledges.
I dreamed it was my birthday forever. It was nice. I don\'t want to go back.
Does that make sense? I don\'t want it even though it was nice.
Also the shrikes took my kite. That\'s a separate sadness.
Rank I — Rustjaw
Rank II — Cog & Sprocket
Rank III — Iron Moll
Champion — the Gale Roc
Madame Ratchet
Welcome to the Scrap Arena, darlings! Kiteholm\'s finest — and only — entertainment, now that the Baron\'s banned singing.
Four ranks. Win and you get prizes. Lose and you get carried out. The crowd enjoys both equally.
The Scrap Arena
Fight through the four ranks of Madame Ratchet\'s Scrap Arena.
Champions! The crowd adores you. The crowd also adored a goat that could count, so don\'t let it go to your heads.
Cold feet? We have braziers for that.
Carried out! The crowd is delighted. Do come again — we patch you for free. It\'s in the ticket price.
THE GALE ROC FALLS! Darlings, you\'re Kiteholm\'s champions! Here — the champion\'s purse. Don\'t spend it on the Baron.
And the crowd goes _moderately_ wild! Your prize, darlings.

    crowd(s, { ilse: [9, 21,
s Roost. A crack in a fallen mountain, too narrow for the wind to find and too ugly for the Choir to bother with.
Kite-lines hum between the canyon walls. Somebody, somewhere, is frying something that used to be a bird.
For the record? I said this was stupid.
Noted. On the kite, off the kite, and twice in the middle when you thought we were going to die.
We *were* going to die.
The man saved our lives in the desert. Several times. Mostly by accident, but a save is a save.
He saved his *ship*. We happened to be standing on it.
Everything left in the world is floating, Pip. We need wings. Corvin\'s the only captain we know.
A year ago Pip followed Corvin around the Halcyon like a gull after a fishing boat. Now he won\'t say his name.
At the head of the canyon, half-buried in ash, lies a ship. Her masts are snapped. Her lift-sail hangs in rags. On her bow, in chipped gold paint: HALCYON.
Oh. Oh, no. Look at her.
That\'s not wings. That\'s a grave.
Three things. One: find Corvin. Two: find out if that can fly. Three: nobody punches anybody until we\'ve done one and two.
Why are you looking at me?
Find Corvin. Someone in the Roost will know where he drinks.
Corvin\'s Roost. The Halcyon is here, broken in the ash. Pip didn\'t want to come. I think he wanted to come more than any of us.
Bar\'s closed.
Bar\'s open.
Bar\'s closed to people who want something. You can tell by the shoes. Hopeful shoes.
It\'s *Sir* Tin— no. No, it isn\'t. Carry on.
Hey, kid.
You got taller.
You got *drunker*.
That\'s fair. That\'s very fair. I worked hard at it.
Three things. One: we need your ship. Two: you\'re going to stop drinking. Three: I wasn\'t asking.
Doc, I missed you. Nobody else in this canyon makes lists at me.
Halcyon\'s dead. Broke her back coming down into this crack the day the sky did. She\'s a very expensive place for spiders to live now.
Then we fix her.
With what? Good intentions? Odessa doesn\'t take those. I\'ve tried.
Who\'s Odessa?
CORVIN ASHE!
Bailiff Crane
By order of the Ledger, your marker has come due. The Ledger Queen sends her regards, and two large men.
Bailiff Pike
Also a dog.
Fellas. Kids. Kids, fellas. I\'m going to finish my drink.
And the children?
*The children* are standing right here.
Well. That was a great deal of my furniture.
Odessa. You look expensive.
I *am* expensive, darling. That\'s rather the point of me.
Odessa Quill. I keep the Ledger. Every crate in the Roost is written in it — every bed, every debt, every drink this man has poured into himself since the sky fell.
Fifty-one thousand, four hundred gold. Plus interest on his charm, which I stopped extending last spring.
Put it on my tab.
You *are* the tab, darling.
At the next Long Bell I take the Halcyon. Grounded, she\'s firewood. But firewood is worth something, in a world without a sun.
Then we\'ll make her fly. And you\'ll get your money.
Red hair. Lanternfall vowels. Halloway, isn\'t it? The Keeper\'s girl.
There\'s a song about you. They sing it on the eastern shards. It isn\'t a nice one.
She\'s heard it.
Fix the ship, little Keeper. If she flies before the Long Bell, we\'ll talk terms. If she doesn\'t, I\'ll sell her for kindling and him for parts.
Which parts?
The charming ones. It won\'t take long.
She likes you.
That was *liking*?
She didn\'t charge you for the conversation.
Mags is up at the wreck. She\'ll tell you what\'s broken. Short version: everything. Long version: everything, slowly.
Come with us.
Sparrow. Look at me. Look real close.
This is what\'s left. You don\'t want it on your ship.
_(quietly)_ Kid\'s still got fast hands.
Talk to Mags, the Halcyon\'s engineer, aboard the grounded ship at the head of the canyon.
Corvin\'s alive. He drinks at a bar called the Last Call, which is the least subtle thing I\'ve ever seen. He owes a woman named Odessa more money than Lanternfall ever had.
Pip unscrews a dented silver flask. He holds it out over the ash, and pours, and does not look away.
That was probably his last one.
He taught me to cheat at cards. On the deck, nights. Said a man should know how to lose on purpose, so he\'d know how to win when it counted.
Then the sky broke and he flew *away*.
I\'m fine. I\'m twelve. I\'ve been fine for a year.
Pip poured out Corvin\'s flask. He said he\'s been fine for a year. He said it the way people say it when they haven\'t.
Stop right there. That plank\'ll hold you, but it won\'t enjoy it.
If you\'re looking for the Captain, try the bottom of a glass. The Last Call. Can\'t miss it; it\'s the building that smells like regret.
All three? Then what are you standing there for? Bring \'em to the plank and let me work.
Coil and sail. Two out of three.
Last one\'s the heart, and the heart\'s in Odessa\'s pocket. Go and charm her at the Ledger House. Or let the redhead do it — the Captain\'s charm is mortgaged.
Ruddock\'s barge will take you to the Benediction. You\'ll find him west, at the Lip.
Bring me stormsilk. And bring *him* back. I\'ve only just got him up the plank.
Hold on to that coil. I\'m not bolting anything in until I\'ve got all three — she\'ll tear herself apart if she lifts half-healed.
The lift\'s on the east wall. Key\'s in your pocket.
Something down there\'s been dragging the good scrap into a pile. Scrappers call it the Foreman.
So you\'re the kids. He talks about you. When he\'s drunk enough, which is always, so: constantly.
Can she fly?
Can she— ha! Girl, she\'s the Halcyon. She was built to fly by people who hated the ground. She *wants* to fly. It\'s the parts that object.
Here\'s the butcher\'s bill.
One. Her lift-coil\'s slag — cracked clean through when we came down. There\'s a dozen wrecks in the Boneyard below the canyon. Sky fell, ships fell with it. Find me a coil that isn\'t cracked.

Two. Her lift-sail\'s rags. I need stormsilk, and the only stormsilk this side of the abyss is on the *Benediction* — a Choir pilgrim galleon stuck in the Squall east of here. The lightning never stops.
Three. Her heart. Sun-ember core, cracked the day the sun did. The only embers big enough are in the Cinderdeep. Odessa\'s mine. Odessa\'s embers. Odessa\'s terms.
So: a graveyard, a haunted ship, and a mine owned by a woman who wants to sell our friend for parts.
The *charming* parts? She told you that one. She\'s proud of that one.
Start with the Boneyard. Lift\'s on the east wall. Here.
Something down there\'s been dragging the good scrap into a pile. The scrappers call it the Foreman. You\'ll know it when it steps on you.
Why are you still here, Mags? If the ship\'s dead, and the captain\'s...
Somebody has to be.
He comes up here, you know. Nights. Never comes aboard. Just stands at the bottom of the plank like a dog that\'s been put out of the house.
Go on. Bring me a coil.
Take the lift on the east wall down to the Boneyard. Find a lift-coil that isn\'t cracked.
Mags needs three things: a lift-coil from the Boneyard, stormsilk from the Benediction, and a sun-ember heart from Odessa\'s mine. A graveyard, a ghost ship and a debt.
It\'s like a graveyard. For ships.
It\'s called the *Boneyard*, Bram.
And they named it *well*.
Stay together. Anything that moves down here is either hungry or sharp.
Or both. It\'s usually both.
