s yard (north) is open.
Not enough. The northern gate is still held shut — there must be another winch.
In the yard, wreckage moves. Hull plates slide together with a sound like teeth. A ship\'s furnace swings up into the place where a heart should be — and lights.
It\'s building something.
It\'s building *itself*.
Can we fight it before it finishes? I\'d like to fight the unfinished version.
The Foreman comes apart like a sentence nobody finishes. In the cradle of its chest, wrapped in copper and still humming, sits a lift-coil. Whole.
It is stamped GILDED GULL — SKYREACH YARDS.
Don\'t count. It\'s bad luck to count.
Is it?
Corvin says it is.
Bring the lift-coil to Mags at the Halcyon.
The thing in the Boneyard was made of fallen ships, with a furnace for a heart. It had a lift-coil in its chest. Now we do. One down.
Well, look who\'s at the bottom of my plank again. And look who\'s behind him.
Sparrow. You... came back.
We came back.
People don\'t, much. From the Boneyard.
People come back, Corvin. It\'s a thing they *do*. You should try it.
Coil. Now. Before the pair of you start crying in my ash.
Wren holds up the coil. Mags squints down at it from the deck.
Gilded Gull. Skyreach yards. Good bones. She\'ll sing on that.
Hold on to it. I\'m not bolting anything in till I\'ve got all three.
Next is the Benediction.
You know it?
I\'ve flown pilgrims. Choir pays in gold and hymns, and only one of those spends.
A galleon like that, broke open in a storm — she\'ll kill you in ways you won\'t find funny. Stairs that go nowhere. Holds full of things that used to pray.
Is that an offer?
It\'s a weather report.
Corvin. Come with us.
I\'m coming for the *ship*, sparrow. Not for—
—any of this. She\'s the only thing I own that doesn\'t owe somebody money.
_(to Wren, quietly)_ That\'s almost word for word what I said to you. In the Ward.
_(quietly)_ I know. I\'m trying very hard not to smile.
Captain. Catch.
Something heavy sails down from the deck. Corvin catches it without looking: a long-barreled hand-cannon, oiled, gleaming.
Cleaned it every week. Didn\'t know who for.
Mags. You beautiful wrench.
You\'re not staying.
I\'m here, ain\'t I?
You were here before, too.
Ask Ruddock the ferryman (the Lip, west of town) to take you to the wreck of the Benediction.
Corvin is coming. "For the ship," he says. Ilse made a face at me like she was remembering something. Pip didn\'t say anything. Then he said the worst possible thing, which was the truth.
Toll Barge. Odessa\'s barge, Odessa\'s toll.
Goes where she says. Today she says nowhere.
The Cinderdeep
Wreck of the Benediction
Nowhere to go but where she says.
Get the Captain up that plank first, then we\'ll talk about where. Odessa wants that ship flying. Says it\'s worth more alive.
Toll\'s two hundred a head.
She said to say yes.
That woman frightens me in ways I\'ve never been frightened.
Where to?
Stay in the Roost
The Toll Barge drops off the Lip on a sigh of hot air and slides out across the dark.
The Squall has not stopped for a year. Rain falls sideways, upward, every way but down.
Pinned to the crag like a moth to a board, the galleon Benediction groans in the wind.
Somewhere aboard, people are singing.
Please tell me that\'s the wind.
That\'s not the wind, tin-can.
Pilgrim hymn. "Rest Ye, Dawn-Bound." They\'d sing it on the approach to Aurenne.
They were flying in to hear the Vespersong. Best seats in the sky.
There\'s a ward of light around the mainmast. It pulses when they sing.
Then we stop the singing. Galleons like her carry two hymn-censers: one on the forecastle, one in the chapel down in the hold.
And kid — the masts on these things are hollow. Something always nests in a hollow mast.
Why would you tell me that.
Silence the two hymn-censers — on the forecastle and in the spilled hold — to break the ward around the mainmast.
The Benediction. A Choir pilgrim galleon, pinned in a storm that hasn\'t stopped for a year. The pilgrims are still singing. They were flying in to hear the Vespersong.
The censer is cold and shut. This part of the hymn is over.
A brass censer, still smoking after a year. The hymn rises out of it like heat off a road.
Close the censer?
As your hand touches the lid, the singing stops. All of it. Then, behind you, every pilgrim on the deck turns its head at once.
You shut the censer. The smoke thins and stops. Half of the hymn goes with it.
The ward around the mainmast cracks like a bell dropped on stone. High above, in the torn mainsail, something enormous unfolds.
The ward is broken. Climb to the mainmast.
One down. The other half\'s still going — hear it?
Along the rail, the pilgrims\' luggage is still strapped down. Name-tags. A child\'s mitten. A letter, folded small, the ink gone blue with rain.
They came to watch. Because of what I did.
Because of what *he* did.
I gave him the stone, Corvin. I climbed into the light and took it out with my own hands.
When the sea went up, the Halcyon was in the air. Engines hot. Close enough to see the light on your mother\'s tower.
I could have come back for you. I did the arithmetic. And I turned her east.
Guilt\'s a bar tab, sparrow. You can drink on it forever, and it never gets any smaller.
Or nothing. That\'s as far as I ever got.
Figured you might work out the rest. You were always the one reading.
Or you pay it down. One piece at a time. And you don\'t get to stop.
Corvin told me he could have come back for us when the sea went up. He did the arithmetic and turned east. He says guilt is a bar tab. I think he wants me to tell him what comes after "or".
The torn mainsail is not a sail. It opens. It has eyes.
Squall drake. They nest in storms. This one\'s been nesting in a hymn.
Is that bad?
It\'s been eating lightning for a year, kid. Everything\'s bad.
Squallmaw falls into the rigging and is still. The wind lets go of the ship.
For the first time in a year, the rain falls _down_.
Tangled in the mainmast hangs a lift-sail of gray stormsilk, scorched at one corner and otherwise whole.
And through a tear in the clouds — far to the north, on a shard brighter than anything left in the sky — stands a needle of white light.
That wasn\'t there last year.
It\'s standing on the biggest shard. Right where the sun broke.
It\'s not noon anywhere. It hasn\'t been noon for a year.
I know.
Take the stormsilk back to the Roost. Ruddock\'s barge waits at the south pier.
We killed the storm drake. The rain fell down. Far away, on the biggest shard of the sun, there\'s a white tower that looks like noon. Two parts.
The captain\'s log, swollen with rain. The last pages are legible.

"Day of the Vespersong. Pilgrims in high spirits. The Hierophant will sing the sun to sleep tonight, and it will never set on us again. The Abbess asks if we may circle the Cathedral twice for the view."
"Later. The sun is wrong. The sun is—"
The rest is water.

m almost impressed.
Don\'t let him near my bar on the way out. He has a tab, and the tab has a tab.
The Long Bell is coming, little Keeper. Bells always do.
Do sit. Debtors stand on the carpet. Guests may sit. You\'ll know which you are by the end.
The Cinderdeep, darling. Ruddock knows the way. Try not to die on my property; it does terrible things to the price of land.
The Long Bell is close. I can feel it in my ledgers.
Go and finish your ship. I\'ll be along to see what it\'s worth.
The Keeper\'s girl and her keeper. Sit. Don\'t touch the ledgers; they bite.
You want into my mine. Everyone wants into my mine. It\'s the only warm place left in the world.
My miners stopped coming up two Bells ago. The ones who did come up talk about a worm made of light, coiled round the biggest ember we ever dug. It\'s eating my embers. And three of my debtors.
We\'ll kill it.
I adore a girl who skips the negotiation.
Kill it, and take one heart-ember for your ship. Bring my three debtors out alive, and I shall be... grateful. I\'m told it\'s a pleasant feeling.
Down in the Deep
Odessa\'s three missing miners — Dagny, Hobb and Ines — are somewhere in the Cinderdeep. Bring them out alive.
Now. Children, out. I need a word with the Captain. Adult business.
I\'m *twelve*.
Then you\'re very nearly a third of the way there.
The Choir came calling, darling. A knight-captain in a white ship. Very polite. Very *armed*.
They want the sparrow.
They want the Keeper\'s daughter, alive and unbruised. The Hierophant misses her, apparently. They\'ll pay enough to clear your marker four times over.
And you said...
I said I\'d think about it. I\'m thinking about it, darling. Are you?
Your little skiff\'s still fueled, I notice. Moored at the Lip. Pointed at open sky.
You always keep a door open, Corvin. It\'s the most honest thing about you.
Is that all?
That\'s all. Mind the step on your way out. People trip on it. It\'s how I like them.

    crowd(s, { pip: [32, 17,
d she want?
To tell me I\'m handsome. She does it every Bell. It\'s in my contract.
You\'re lying. Your left hand does a thing when you\'re lying.
You did.
Ride the Toll Barge to the Cinderdeep. Find the heart-ember — and Odessa\'s three missing miners.
Odessa gave us a permit for her mine. Then she sent us out and kept Corvin. He came out smiling. Pip didn\'t believe the smile. Neither did I.
Heat rolls up the shaft like breath. Somewhere far below, something breathes back.
Why is it always *down*? Why is the worst thing never at the top of a nice hill?
Because people who build on hills charge rent.
Odessa\'s miners will be in the side-galleries if they\'re anywhere. Keep your eyes open.
The valve is open. Steam whistles through the pipes, thin and steady.
A steam valve, its wheel crusted with slag. The pipe runs off into the dark toward the deep galleries.
Open the valve?
Steam screams through the pipes. Far to the east, a river of slag hisses, cools, and cracks into rubble.
Steam roars up a shaft to the north. Somewhere above, molten slag goes gray and breaks apart.
I owe Odessa six hundred gold for a bed I never slept in.
I\'ve been sleeping down here instead. It\'s very warm. That\'s the only good thing about it.
Out? Oh, gods. Yes. Yes please.
Leg\'s gone bad. Fell when the worm came through. Been eating mushrooms and telling myself jokes.
They\'re terrible jokes. I\'ve heard them all.
You\'ll take me up? ...Then here. Found this when I fell. Never had a use for it.
My daughter\'s in the Roost. Nell. She\'s six. She\'ll think I left.
I didn\'t leave. I didn\'t. I just couldn\'t get *up*.
Thank you. Thank you. I\'ll tell her — I\'ll tell her someone came.
All three miners are on their way out. Tell Odessa.
Dagny. Hobb. Ines. All three, walking into my Roost on their own legs, smelling of brimstone and gratitude.
I said I\'d be grateful. Here is the strange part: I am. Name your price, little Keeper.
Forgive their debts.
Five thousand gold.
You walked out of my mine with a fortune in your pocket, and you spend it on three people who can\'t even thank you properly.
Odessa takes three pages out of the Ledger. She looks at them for a long moment. Then she feeds them, one by one, to the lamp.
Don\'t tell anyone. I have a reputation.
Ines asked me to give you this. Her girl made it. It\'s hideous. I\'m told it\'s lucky.
Gold. Sensible. I could almost love you.
The chamber is bright as noon. At its center lies a well of molten light — and coiled around it, drinking, a worm the length of a street, its scales like stained glass with the sun behind them.
Well. That\'s the biggest ember I ever saw.
It\'s *eating* it.
It\'s eating the sun.
Then it can learn to share.
The Sunworm uncoils, slow as a sunset, and goes dark. The well of light settles. At its bottom, cooling from white to gold, sits an ember the size of a heart.
Mags is gonna cry.
I might cry.
You cry at bread, tin-can.
Bread is *moving*.
She still says it. Somewhere. She has to.
Take the heart-ember back to the Halcyon. Mags is waiting.
Three parts. The heart is gold and still warm. Bram said Sable\'s line about bread, and nobody could say anything for a while.
Coil. Sail. Heart.
Mags takes the three parts up the plank as tenderly as if they were newborns.
Give me the time it takes to swear properly, and she\'ll fly.
Mags swears properly. It takes about an hour. Some of it is in languages that no longer have countries.
Across the Roost, the Long Bell tolls. There is no sun to mark the days anymore, so the Roost rings a bell and agrees to believe it.
The Long Bell, darling. I\'ve come for my ship.
Your ship\'s about to leave, Quill.
Then I\'m just in time.
A shadow falls across the canyon. Something white and enormous blots out the sky — a warship, its hull painted with the Choir\'s golden sunburst, lowering itself between the walls on singing engines.
That\'s the *Steadfast*. They used to show it to the squires. To make us proud.
By order of the Hierophant: Wren Halloway, the Keeper\'s daughter. Unharmed.
The rest of you are... optional.
Ashe. Corvin Ashe. They still teach you at the academy, you know. In the lecture on desertion.
Sev. You got old.
You got *drunk*.
And Kestrel. The squire who froze. Aldous Venn died so you could run away — and here you are, running with a deserter. How fitting.
We\'ll see.
_(quietly)_ Your skiff\'s at the Lip, darling. Fueled. Pointed at open sky.
_(quietly)_ Go now, and I\'ll burn your marker myself. Nobody would blame you. Nobody ever expected anything else.
At the canyon\'s lip, Corvin\'s skiff rocks on its mooring line. Small. Fast. Pointed at nothing at all.
_(quietly)_ You\'re good at it.
I am.
Corvin draws, turns, and fires — once — down the whole length of the canyon.
At the Lip, the skiff\'s mooring line parts. The little boat tips, slides, and drops into the dark without a sound.
Always wondered what that would feel like.
How\'s it feel?
Terrible. Get behind me, kid.
Something in Corvin\'s Crest turns over, like a card laid face-up on the table.
Sev. Let\'s play a hand. You win, you get the sparrow. I win, you go home and tell the Hierophant Corvin Ashe says hello.
I don\'t gamble, deserter.
Everybody gambles, Sev. Only some of us admit it.
Marines. Take the girl.
This isn\'t... over, Ashe.
Nothing ever is, Sev. That\'s the trouble with things.
Steadfast! Lift!
The warship\'s engines scream. It claws its way up out of the canyon, scraping stone, and is gone. A sealed letter flutters down where the Knight-Captain stood.
Her orders. That\'s not the Hierophant\'s seal...
"Bring the Keeper\'s daughter to the Noon Spire, unharmed. The vessel grows restless, and asks for her by name. — M."
"M." Mercy.
The vessel...
Sable. That\'s *Sable*. She\'s alive!
The Noon Spire. It stands on the greatest shard, where the sun broke. The Choir ferries supplies in every Bell. Everyone who goes in comes out smiling.
That\'s what frightens me.
You sold us out, Quill.
I never told the Choir a thing, darling. Severine found you all on her own; she\'s very thorough.
I only wanted to see what you\'d do with an open door.
Odessa opens her ledger to a page near the back, worn soft with handling. She tears it out.
Fifty-one thousand, four hundred gold. Paid in full.
Paid with what?
With the look on your face when that skiff went over. I\'ve held your marker nine years, waiting to see it.
Don\'t make me regret the investment. Regret is terrible for business.
I\'m a *banker*.
CAPTAIN! Are we flying, or are we *chatting*?
Take her up.
The Halcyon rises out of Corvin\'s Roost like a held breath let go.
Below, the canyon shrinks to a crack, then a line, then nothing at all. Above, the bruised sky opens its arms.
Coil\'s singing. Sail\'s full. Heart\'s burning hot as a scandal.
She\'s flying, Captain.
_(quietly)_ She\'s flying.
Kid. C\'mere.
Both hands. She doesn\'t like being held loose.
Like this?
Like that. Feel her pull? She wants to go up. Everything does. You just let her, a little at a time.
I\'M FLYING. I\'M FLYING THE—
Ahem. I mean. It\'s fine. It\'s basically a boat.
He\'s beaming. Look at him. He\'s *beaming*.
He\'s twelve.
Wren laughs. It surprises her. It is the first time in a year.
Hey. Sparrow.
Found the "or".
You pay it down. A bit at a time. And you don\'t get to stop.
Figured you did. Took me nine years and a skiff.
Mags. Set a course for the Noon Spire.
The sparrow\'s giving orders on my deck now?
Course for the big shiny tower of certain death. Aye aye.

Round one! From the kennels under the east stand — the SAND HOUNDS! They have not been fed. That is a joke. Mostly.
Round two! Brothers in arms, brothers in debt — KELL THE NET and KELL THE FIST!
The final round! He has eaten three gates and a herald — GRIZZLEMAW!
Silver Cup
Round one! Imported at great expense from the Sunscar — the GLASS SCORPIONS! Do not step on them. They hate that.
Round two! Fastest blade in the Heartland, slowest to pay his tab — SERENO THE SWIFT!
The final round! Forged in the bell foundries from a broken bell and a bad idea — THE IRON BULL!
Gold Cup
Round one! Dredged from the Fens at tremendous personal risk — the MIRE LURKERS!
Round two! One prays, one curses, neither has ever lost — the MASKS OF DAWN AND DUSK!
The final round! Mother of a thousand, mercy for none — THE SCYTHE MATRON!
Sunsteel Cup
Round one! They ride the bells\' own echoes — the STORM KITES!
Round two! Three shields, one wall, no gaps — the PHALANX OF AURENNE!
The championship! Forty-one bouts. Forty-one wins. Your champion, and mine — VALKA THE UNDEFEATED!
Ottavio Brass
The medics have you. The cup waits. It always waits. It is a cup.
Welcome, welcome, WELCOME to the Bellring! Aurenne\'s oldest colosseum! Its loudest! Its only!
I am Ottavio Brass, ringmaster, and I can tell a contender at forty paces. You are contenders. Or very lost.
We\'re contenders. What do contenders win?
Cups! Four of them. Three rounds each, no rest but what my medics give you. Win a cup and the prize is yours — and Bell Tokens, every time you win.
And if we lose?

The Bellring
Win the four cups of Aurenne\'s colosseum: Copper, Silver, Gold — and the Sunsteel Cup, against Valka the Undefeated.
How does it work?
Which cup?
Three rounds a cup. Your wounds come with you from round to round; my medics give back a quarter between bouts.
Lose and the cup resets — no shame, no fee. Win and the prize is yours, plus Bell Tokens. Win again later and the crowd still pays, a little.
Spend Tokens with my clerk. New cups open as your name grows. Which it will. I am never wrong. I am occasionally early.
Go on, then. The bell will wait. The bell is very patient. It is a bell.
Ring the bell!
Not yet
Forty-one and one. ...Good. I was getting bored of winning. Look after that laurel — it has been mine for nine years.
LADIES! GENTLEMEN! THE BELLRING HAS NEW CHAMPIONS!
We won the Sunsteel Cup at the Bellring. Valka the Undefeated is now Valka the Defeated Once. She shook our hands like it was a gift.
Prize Clerk
Tokens are won in the ring, not bought at the counter. Talk to Mr. Brass. Loudly. He prefers it.
Come back richer. In Tokens. Gold doesn\'t count here.

ve the look of Lanternfall, girl. Salt in the eyes.
My gran was a Tidecaller. You\'ll not have heard of it. The Choir struck it from the rolls when the fishing towns stopped paying tithe — said the sea was a heathen thing to sing to.

Struck it out of the books, but they couldn\'t strike it out of the water. Gran said the last Tidecaller\'s crest-glass went down with the last singer, out past the strait. She\'s still out there, singing. I hear her some nights.
If the sea\'s gone, maybe the song is all that\'s left of it. Go and listen. Take it back, if she\'ll let you.
Grandmother Wend in Keelhaven says the last Tidecaller\'s crest-glass lies at the far east end of the Strait That Was, still guarded by its singer.
Past the last bridge, at the very end of the strait. Listen for her.
You found her. I heard it last night — the singing stopped. Thank you for letting her rest.
Sing to the sea sometimes. It\'s still listening, wherever it went.
A slab of crest-glass, crusted white with old salt, wedged in the rock like a figurehead. Something inside it is singing.
Water that is not there rises around the glass — and in it, a drowned woman in a Cantor\'s robe, still singing the boats home.
The song ends on a long, low note, like a tide turning. The crest-glass clears, and in it burns a Crest none of you has ever seen: three waves, each over the last.
The crest-glass is clear and quiet now. If you listen very hard, it still sounds a little like the sea.
At the end of the Strait That Was, the Drowned Cantor sang over a lost Crest. We let her finish her song. The Tidecaller calling is ours to carry now.
Founder Hask
Hask. Last of the founders\' guild. Well — last of anything, these days.
Every bell in this city was poured by Bellwrights. That was a calling once, child — a Crest. Then the Choir decided a bell that could call the faithful could call other things too.
They struck the calling from the rolls and walled the guild\'s crest-glass up in the old foundry under the Undercroft, with the Abbot to watch it. The Abbot is a bell. Don\'t ask.
The flood opened the walls. If you\'re going down there anyway... ring it for me. Once. That\'s all I\'ve ever wanted.
Founder Hask in the ruins of Aurenne says the Bellwrights\' crest-glass is walled up in the far north-east of the drowned Undercroft, watched by the Bronze Abbot.
North-east corner of the drowned Undercroft, past the old reliquary. You\'ll hear it before you see it.
I heard it. All the way up here, through the ash. First time in four hundred years that bell has rung for anyone but the Choir.
Go on, then, Bellwright. Make some noise.
A bell of crest-glass, taller than a man, hangs in a cage of rusted chain. Before it, something bronze stirs on its yoke.
The Bronze Abbot swings down from the dark, ringing with every step it takes.
The Abbot cracks down the middle with a sound like the last bell of evening. The chains fall away. In the glass bell burns a Crest you have never seen: a bell, mid-swing, ringing.
The glass bell hangs free now. Touch it, and it hums.
Under Aurenne we rang the bell the founders hid. Hask heard it. The Bellwright calling is ours now.
Ada Kestrel
Kiteholm flies kites because kites are what we have. But there were folk who flew more than kites, once. Kitewrights.
The Choir struck them out. "Only the sun belongs in the sky." Burned the workshops. One didn\'t burn — it was already too far down to reach.
It\'s in the Underhang. Deep. The south end. With the thing they built to lift it, which never lifted anything but grudges.
If you find their crest-glass, bring the calling back up. Let somebody fly who isn\'t a kite.
Ada Kestrel in Kiteholm says the Kitewrights\' last workshop lies at the far south end of the Underhang, guarded by the Scrap Colossus.
South, as deep as the Underhang goes. Mind the lines.
Look at you. A Kitewright. Gaffer Quill is going to be unbearable about this — he always said they\'d come back.
Go on. Fall upward.
A workshop hangs in the dark, all struts and old canvas, half-swallowed by the rock. At its heart, a slab of crest-glass shaped like a wing.
Something huge unfolds out of the scrap around the glass, rivets screaming.
The Colossus sags, then sits, almost gently, as if it had only ever wanted to be allowed to stop. The wing-shaped glass clears. In it burns a Crest: a kite on a long line.
The wing of crest-glass catches the faint light from above. The Colossus sits beside it, very still, keeping it company.
Deep in the Underhang we found the Kitewrights\' last workshop, and the Colossus they built to lift it. The Kitewright calling flies again.
Sexton Mabry
Every flower here is a last word. I keep the book of names that goes with them. Someone must remember them, or what are they for?
There was a calling for this, once. Mnemonists. Keepers of memory. The Choir struck it out when it decided some things were better forgotten.
The last Mnemonist is buried at the heart of the maze. The Choir set something on her grave — an appetite. It eats names. It has eaten so many.
If you can stand before it and still remember who you are, the calling is yours. I would like someone to remember her.
Sexton Mabry at the Garden\'s gate says the last Mnemonist lies at the heart of the Garden\'s maze, where the Forgetting guards her grave.
The heart of the maze. Hold on to your name.
You came back with your names. All of them? Good.
A plain stone at the heart of the maze. The name on it has been eaten away. Around it the flowers are silent — and something pale is feeding on the quiet.
The Forgetting turns toward you, and for a moment you cannot remember your own name. Then Wren says it out loud, and so does everyone else.

The Forgetting comes apart into a thousand small sounds — names, voices, the last words of everyone it ate, rushing back into the flowers. The name on the stone returns: ISOLDE VANE, MNEMONIST. Crest-glass clears in the stone around a Crest like a knot with no end.
ISOLDE VANE, MNEMONIST. The flowers around her stone are murmuring again.
In the Garden That Remembers we stood before the Forgetting and kept our names. The last Mnemonist has hers back, and the calling is ours.
Touch the crest-glass?
Touch it
Not yet
When you come to, the glass is quiet again. Whatever guards it is waiting for you to come back.

One Crest, mastered all the way down to the bottom. Most people get one in their whole life and never finish it.
Six masteries. You\'re all becoming a great many things. Here: a lamp lit at the Nadir Light. For choosing who you are next.
Twenty-four. The old proverb says one Crest, one life. I\'m crossing it out. Right here in the ledger. Look.
Seventy-two masteries. I don\'t have a word for what you are anymore. Good. Words are edges. Keep a few of yours loose.
Three things. One: it\'s dark. Two: it\'s very dark. Three—
It\'s dark?
Three: something just breathed on my neck.
That was me. I am breathing heroically.
A Hearthstone. Somebody carried that down five flights of nightmare.
Or somebody forgot it, and it fell.
I like my version better, sparrow. Mine has a hero in it.
Streets. Down here.
A city someone forgot. All of it at once.
How does one forget an entire *city*?
Same way you forget anything, big man. A little at a time, then all at once.
These shelves are full of books.
Every page is blank.
Snow. Underground.
It is the first winter. The very first one. Nobody remembers it, so it came here.
Can a winter be lonely?
Everything can.
It\'s... white.
I thought the bottom would be black.
Black is a color. This is from before colors.
I hate it. I hate it in a very specific, educated way.
Is anyone else afraid?
Good. Then we go together. That\'s how it works. I looked it up.
At the lip of the deepest rift in the world, a lighthouse stands with its lamp turned the wrong way.
It does not shine out to sea. It shines *down*.
A Lantern. Out here? There were only ever seven.
There were only ever seven *anyone sang about*.
Six. Six of you. Hold still.
There. You\'re in the Tally now. Congratulations. It\'s mostly moths.
Sir, I must protest. We are not moths. We are an elite fellowship of—
No. Moths have the sense to stay away from the edge. I\'ll make a note.
I like him.
Orrin Vey. Underkeeper of the Nadir Light — the Eighth Lantern. Nobody sings about it because it doesn\'t raise the sun. It holds something *down*.
Something is down there.
It is not angry. It is... unfinished.
Before the Hearthsun there was the First Dark. Not evil. Not anything. The sun gave things *edges* — this is a stone, that is a sea, you are you.
When something is forgotten, it loses its edges and sinks. Down there. Thirty stairs of everything the world ever dropped.
And you just... live here. On the rim of the bottomless pit of forgotten things.
Rent\'s cheap.
Funny thing. The sky\'s got a new light in it. Small. Stubborn. Since it came up, my lamp reaches all the way to the bottom.
If you\'re the ones who lit it... well. The First Dark felt it too. It\'s stirring.
My light reaches ten stairs down. Below that the dark is too thick for an old lamp. It\'ll take a new kind of light.
I\'ll know it when I see it.
Go down if you like. Bring back names. I write them all in the Tally — every creature you put a name to is one less thing the dark gets to keep.
Thirty stairs beneath the Nadir Light. At the bottom, something without edges is waiting.
The Tally
Orrin rewards names (the Bestiary) and mastery (Crests at rank 10). Report to him now and then.
Descend the Gloam Abyss to the thirtieth stair.

The Abyss
The First Dark
Orrin looks up from his ledger.
Thirty stairs. Gloamdeep first — the newest forgettings, still warm. Then a drowned city. Then the first winter. Then... white.

You gave it an edge. Dusk, you said?

There\'s nothing left I can give you. You\'ve out-counted me.
Customers! Real ones, with pulses! Welcome to Sorrel\'s Salvage. Everything here fell out of the world and landed in my net.
Swords nobody remembers forging. Tonics nobody remembers brewing. All perfectly good. Mostly.
How much for the stuff that\'s *perfectly* good?
Double. And I count my fingers after you leave, sweetheart.
Ten stairs! That\'s further than my last three assistants. They\'re fine. They\'re in Kiteholm. They don\'t write.
Twenty! The first winter — did it really snow? Don\'t answer. I want to imagine it. Take this; it helped me see in the drifts.
The bottom. You mapped the *bottom*. I\'m going to frame this. I\'m going to frame *you*. Here — my lucky coin. It\'s done its job.
Hello! Don\'t step on the map. That\'s the map. That\'s also the map. I\'m Quill — I chart the Abyss.
From up here, I mean. Through the telescope. It\'s mostly guesswork and very confident handwriting.
Go down and tell me what\'s there. Every ten stairs you reach, I\'ll pay you for the news.
If you see a little golden light flitting about down there — a Wishing Mote — use magic. Blades go right through it. Catch one and it might leave a Crest Tome.
The chests down there that bite are Hoarder Mimics. They\'ve eaten whole fortunes. Pierce them, shock them, and they cough up the most wonderful fruit.
Every fifth stair has a Hearthstone. Somebody put them there. I would very much like to meet that somebody.
I read it every morning now. Takes me a long while. I stop in the middle and look at the sky.
Thank you. I don\'t say it enough. I\'m saying it.
Tobb. We found something on the third stair.
I threw it in. Thought if I didn\'t have the letter, I wouldn\'t have the — the rest. The missing her.
It didn\'t work. I only missed the letter too.
It doesn\'t work. People keep trying. I\'ve watched them try at the Ward.
You don\'t get to keep someone without the hurting. It\'s one thing, not two.
Here. I brought these to sell to the bookie for a bet I wasn\'t going to make. You have them.
We brought Tobb his daughter\'s letter back up out of the dark. Ilse said the true thing. She usually does.
You lot going down? Then mind the third stair. That\'s about where it\'d land.
A letter. From my girl, Mara, before the Sundering took her. I threw it in. I wanted to forget.
Turns out I\'d rather remember and hurt. Bit late to decide, eh.
The Unsent Letter
Tobb threw his late daughter\'s letter into the rift. It would have landed around the third stair.
Third stair, or thereabouts. A blue envelope. You\'d know it. It\'s the only thing down there anyone ever loved.
I sang in the Choir. In the Vespersong. I stood in the Grand Lantern and sang the sun to pieces because a kind man told me to.
So now I fill this lamp with oil every morning. It does not make anything even. It is just the next right thing.
Take these. Holy water. I blessed it myself — whatever my blessing is worth now.
There is a new sun. A small one. I keep looking up at it to check it\'s still there. It always is. I don\'t know what to do with that.
Orrin says guilt looks backward and the lamp needs looking after. He is very annoying when he is right.
PIP. Pip Tallow! In the flesh! You still owe me four coppers.
You owe ME four coppers.
I owe *everyone* four coppers, that\'s my whole business model.
Dace pays me to run bets. You lot fighting in the Colosseum? I\'m putting my four coppers on you. Everyone\'s four coppers.
You beat YOURSELVES. Dace cried. Not the happy kind — he had money on the hollow ones. I didn\'t. I\'m rich. Four coppers rich.
The Colosseum\'s through that big door. Dace\'ll fight you against anything the Gloam remembers. Everything you ever beat, it remembers.

m fine. Something in my eye. A knight. A whole knight in my eye.
The Lantern-lift now stops at B10.
Descend deeper into the Gloam Abyss.
The tenth stair was guarded by every soldier nobody remembered. Bram gave them one name to keep.
The stairwell is sealed by ice as old as the first winter. Something vast is asleep in it, curled around the way down.
Don\'t. Nobody poke it.
Nobody is going to poke the—
Rime Sovereign
{blue|WHO. REMEMBERS. ME.}
Nobody. That is why you are here.
{blue|THEN I WILL BE REMEMBERED AS THE COLD IN YOUR BONES.}
Okay. Okay. Big lizard. Fire, everybody.
The Sovereign shatters into a snowfall so fine it never lands. Something heavy clinks onto the ice where her head was.
I\'m writing that one down myself. Orrin can copy it.
The Lantern-lift now stops at B20.
Descend to the bottom of the Gloam Abyss.
The twentieth stair had a queen of snow with no kingdom. Wren\'s plan was "fire." It worked.
The marble ends. Beyond it there is no floor, no wall, no color. Only a white so total it has no direction.
In the middle of the white, something without any edges at all turns its attention toward you.
{purple|...you are very loud.}
{purple|all of you. so many edges. doesn\'t it hurt?}
{purple|come back down. no names. no edges. nothing to lose. nothing to be.}
{purple|you will not have to choose anymore. not one crest. not many. none.}
It\'s offering us *nothing*.
It\'s a very sincere nothing. I almost respect it.
I was made from you. A little. I remember being nothing. It was quiet.
Then someone gave me bread. It was warm.
I would rather have bread.
Me too. I\'d rather have bread than be nothing. That\'s not even close.
I would rather be afraid than be nothing. I have given this a great deal of thought.
Edges hurt. That\'s how you know where you stop and someone else starts.
We\'re keeping ours.
{purple|then i will take them off you. gently. one by one.}
The First Dark does not die. There is nothing in it that could.
It shrinks. It folds. The white around it grays, then dims, then — for the first time in all of time — becomes a color:
the deep blue of the sky an hour after sunset.
{purple|...what is this.}
It is called dusk. It is the edge between the day and the night.
You have one now. An edge.
{purple|...it is small.}
They start small.
{purple|...then i will sleep in it. wake me when it is bigger.}
The dark folds itself into the dusk the way a cat folds into a lap, and is still.
Something warm moves out of the stillness and into all six of you: a heat like a forge, and a glow like the hour after the sun.
We did it. We punched the dark in the face.
We gave the dark a bedtime.
Same thing.
Far, far above, a lamp on a chain begins its long swing down to find you.
The First Dark sleeps. Ride the Lantern-lift home — and tell Orrin.
At the bottom of everything was the First Dark. It wanted us to be nothing. Sable gave it dusk instead, and it went to sleep in it like a kid. Two new Crests woke up in all of us.
An old wall, scrawled with chalk: a girl with long black hair and a ribbon, and an arrow pointing down into the rift. Under it, in careful capitals: COUNT TO A HUNDRED. NO PEEKING.
Not yours. Hers.
Lysa. She drew herself. Small. The way children draw themselves when they want to be found.
Chalk doesn\'t last forty years in the open.
Unless someone keeps redrawing it.
Hide and Seek
Someone has been leaving chalk marks in the Gloam Abyss. Find them all: they lead somewhere.
Chalk on the stone in a child\'s hand: a hopscotch grid, and beside it — I\'M HIDING. DON\'T LOOK HERE. (She was not hiding here.)
A chalk arrow, pointing the way she went. Underneath: WARMER!
Chalk, faded but careful: CASSIAN ALWAYS FINDS ME. HE\'S THE BEST AT THIS GAME. Below it, very small: are you cassian?
A chalk door, drawn small, rubbed out, and drawn again bigger. Under it: I GOT TIRED OF WAITING. I\'M SOMEWHERE NICE NOW. THE DOOR IS WHERE IT STARTED.
Hopscotch. Down here. That\'s... that\'s the creepiest nice thing I\'ve ever seen.
She is playing. She thinks this is still a game.
For forty years.
Where it started. The wall by the Abyss Gate — that\'s where the first drawing was.
Lysa\'s chalk marks point back to the wall by the Abyss Gate.
The last chalk mark says the door is "where it started" — the chalk wall at the Abyss Gate.
The chalk door is still there. It is closed now, and someone has drawn a small, smiling sun above it.
Where the drawing of the girl was, there is now a door — drawn in chalk, on a wall that has no door. It is slightly open.
Step through the chalk door?
A summer night in a city that does not exist anymore. Paper lanterns. Bunting. A fountain still warm from the day. Nobody here.
From somewhere far away, a boy\'s voice, counting: "...ninety-eight... ninety-nine..."
"...a hundred! Ready or not!" The voice stops. It never starts again.
Somewhere in the square, someone small giggles.
She is hiding. She has been hiding all this time.
Then let\'s find her.
Search the festival square for Lysa. (Check the hiding places.)
Nobody is hiding here anymore. It\'s just a nice place to sit.
"Warmer! Warmer!"
"Freezing! Brrr!"
You found me!
Nobody EVER finds me. I\'m the best at hiding. Cassian says so.
Yes. I am sorry. I did not choose it.
It looks nice on you. You\'re taller.
Where\'s Cassian? He\'s supposed to be seeking. He\'s *always* seeking.
Since the festival. It got dark all of a sudden — REALLY dark — and I thought: this is the best hiding place ever. Nobody will ever find me in the dark.
And nobody did.
I know.
It\'s my turn to seek now. That\'s the rule! Whoever gets found has to seek!
Ready or not!
Lysa sits down hard on the edge of the fountain, out of breath and grinning.
Okay. Okay, you win. You\'re really good.
Did Cassian grow up?
He did. He got old. He was the most important man in the world.
Cassian? He\'s scared of geese.
Is he, now.
No. He missed you every day. He looked for you for forty years.
He built a whole world to find you in.
Did he stop? Looking?
At the very end. He held my hand. And then he let go.
At the very end. He let go.
That\'s how it\'s supposed to go. You look and you look, and if you can\'t find them you go home for supper. You\'re not supposed to look forever.
Hey. Face-girl. Will you do something for me? Get really old. Get wrinkly. Get gray hair. Do ALL of it.
I will. I promise. I will be very wrinkled.
And — here. For drawing doors. In case you ever need one.
I think I\'ll go home now. I\'ve been out *really* late.
Where she sat there is only a little chalk on the fountain\'s edge, and the warmth of the stone.
I\'m not crying. There\'s chalk in my eye.
There is chalk in ALL of our eyes, Pip.
Lysa went home. Return through the chalk door.
We found Lysa. Forty years of hiding, and she just wanted someone to say "found you." She asked Sable to get old. Sable promised.
Ladies! Gentlemen! And things that used to be gentlemen! Welcome to the ECHO COLOSSEUM!
Kiteholm had a colosseum. Then it had a fire. Now it has a very nice memorial. I brought the betting slips.
Here\'s the trick: the Gloam remembers every fight there ever was. I just... ask it to remember them *here*, where I sell tickets.
Ten ranks. Ten memories. Each one nastier than the last. Prizes for the living!
The Echo Colosseum
Dace runs ten ranks of remembered fights beneath the Abyss Gate. Win them all.
Not today
Dace fans out a hand of fight cards.
The Gloam will remember you tomorrow. It always does.
And they\'re DOWN! Medics! Medics, the expensive ones!
Don\'t worry about it. Losing to a memory is the most natural thing in the world.
A rematch, and a win! The crowd goes mild!
We fought ourselves in the Echo Colosseum — the versions of us the Gloam would have kept. We won. I don\'t know how to feel about that, but Wick made four coppers.
Under the red stall: candied plums, a lost shoe. Nobody.
Behind the blue stall: a stack of paper kites. Nobody.
Inside the yellow stall: a fortune-teller\'s cards, all blank. Nobody.
Behind the barrels: cider, by the smell. Nobody.
Behind the crates: bunting, unpacked. Nobody.
In the hay: a pony\'s hat. No pony. Nobody.
Down the well: your own face, and stars. Nobody.
Around the fountain: coins, a hundred wishes. Nobody.
In the sweet-seller\'s cauldron: cold toffee. Nobody.
The Tide Remembers
Rank One! From the black rocks of Lanternfall, the very first nightmare: the Drowned Hound — as you remember it!
The Hound is down! Prize: one Mossy Bangle. It grows on you. Literally.
Strait Terror
Rank Two! It guarded the strait! It ate a boat! Two boats, the way sailors tell it: BRINEFANG!
Serpent subdued! Take this monocle. Makes you learn faster. Makes you look smarter. Only one of those is guaranteed.
Highway Royalty
Rank Three! Eight feet tall! Undefeated! Never lied once! RED TAM, as told by Red Tam!
Legend deflated! The Thief\'s Glove is yours. Tam left it here. He says.
Undercroft Hymnal
Rank Four! She sings! She saves! She does NOT take requests! SISTER MERCY and her poor, poor beast!
The hymn is over! A Crest Brooch for the choir — learn your Crests twice as fast.
Glass and Sand
Rank Five! From under the Sunscar dunes — when the sand hums, RUN! The GLASSWYRM!
Wyrm wrangled! Quicksilver Anklet — start every fight already running.
The Hollow Knight
Rank Six! Black armour! Hollow mask! THE PENITENT! ...Is it me, or is it colder in here?
The knight kneels for good! Ember Heart — burns brighter, faster.
Rank Seven! Head of the Dawnguard! Sword of the Hierophant! The man himself: GARRICK THORNE!
The Lord-Commander falls! The Champion\'s Belt — you\'ve earned the buckle!
Remnant Chorus
Rank Eight! Three Keepers who became something else, singing in harmony! The REMNANT CHORUS!
The chorus is silenced! An Archmage Ring, for the one doing the thinking.
Rank Nine! The sun stood still for him! Shield your eyes! THE NOON KING!
Noon is OVER! Phoenix Charm — get up again, once, every fight.
Mirror Match
The final rank. The Gloam remembers everyone who ever fought here... including YOU. As you were. At your worst. HOLLOW!
You beat yourselves! The crowd is screaming! I am screaming! The Echo Laurel — CHAMPIONS!

s light to receive a Crest —
the calling they will carry for the rest of their life.
_One Crest. One life._
That is how it has always been.
Wren! The sun\'s been up for an hour!
There you are. I was starting to think the gulls had carried you off.
I was reading.
Until dawn. _Again._ Tomorrow you stand in the Lantern\'s light. You could at least do it with your eyes open.
The Hierophant\'s ship comes in today, doesn\'t it? Ilse says he\'s coming himself. For _our_ Kindling.
Mom. He\'s the _Hierophant_. He wrote back to me. Twice.
I know. I read them.
You read my—
Chores. Tobias needs his net back from Nana Brisa\'s. After that you can go and gawk at the harbor with everyone else.
Some mothers would be proud their daughter writes to the most important man in the world.
Happy Kindling Eve, little bird.
Fetch Fisher Tobias\'s mended net from Nana Brisa\'s house.
The day before the Kindling. The Hierophant himself is coming to Lanternfall. Mom read my letters.
Supper soon. Wash the sea out of your hair first.
The tide caves? ...Of course you are.
Take Ilse. Stay out of the deep pools. And Wren — the tide comes back faster than you think.
Nana Brisa\'s house is the plaster one by the square. Red roof.
And don\'t let Tobias talk you into gutting fish. Not today.
You\'re late.
I\'m _exactly_ on time for someone who was reading.
Wren, dear! Tobias\'s net is by the fire. Mended with my best knots — tell him that.
If only everything mended so easily...
Nana lost her brooch. The silver gull Grandpa gave her.
In the tide caves, years ago. I was gathering sea lavender and it simply... went into the water. I\'ve made my peace with it.
The tide caves? I could get it back.
The tide caves are _full of things that bite_.
Then you\'d better come with me. Bring your bandages.
Three things. One: we deliver the net first. Two: we\'re back before the ship comes in. Three: if you die, I\'m telling your mother.
Nana\'s Silver Gull
Find Nana Brisa\'s lost brooch in the Tide Caves, east of the village.
Give the net to Fisher Tobias by the beach, then search the Tide Caves (east road) for Nana\'s brooch.
Nana Brisa lost her silver gull brooch in the tide caves. Ilse and I are going to find it — after the net.
Tomorrow you\'ll both be grown. Sixteen.
I remember mine. My Crest burned so bright I couldn\'t see for an hour. Mender, same as Ilse will be — you mark my words.
The tide caves are east along the shore road. Mind the pools.
Nana. Close your eyes and hold out your hand.
Oh, my silly gull. Look at you. Still missing your wing tip.
Thank you, my darlings. Here — I was saving these for after the Kindling, but I think you\'ve earned them early.
She\'s going to cry.
I am _not_. Off with you. Supper\'s at your mother\'s tonight, Wren, isn\'t it?
Go home for supper.
We found the brooch. Nana cried. (Nana says she didn\'t.)
Ha! Brisa\'s knots. I\'d know \'em in the dark.
Here — for your trouble. Don\'t tell your mother I\'m paying you in medicine. She\'ll think I\'m sweet on her.
Tide caves, is it? Careful. Tide\'s been strange all week. Pulls out further every morning, like the sea\'s holding its breath.
And take my old rod. A Halloway ought to fish. The dock end\'s good — face the water and give it a try.
Search the Tide Caves (east road) for Nana\'s brooch.
A girl, out of the storm? The sea gives back strange things, Wren. Strange things.
Mornin\', Wren! Big day tomorrow, eh?
Brisa\'s got my net. I\'d fetch it myself but my knees and her stairs are not on speaking terms.
There — in the pool! Something silver.
Wren. The water\'s moving.
A silver gull. Missing the tip of one wing. That\'s it!
Ilse... look at the back of the cave.
Is that... a crystal? It\'s _purple_. Crystals in these caves are blue.
It\'s cold. Colder than the water. Like it\'s breathing.
Don\'t touch it. Wren. _Wren._ Don\'t touch it.
Far away, the harbor bells begin to ring.
The ship! The Hierophant\'s ship is coming in!
And we\'re in a cave. Covered in eel. Wonderful.
Hurry back to Lanternfall\'s docks!
There was a purple crystal deep in the tide caves. Cold, like it was breathing. Ilse made me promise not to touch it.
A white ship with sails like folded wings. The Choir\'s sunburst on every one.
Keeper Ysolde. You haven\'t aged a day.
Hierophant. You have.
And you must be Wren. The girl who writes me about the stars.
I— yes. Hello. Sir. Your Holiness? Your... Holy... sir.
Cassian will do.
In your last letter you asked why the sun sets in the west and never in the east. I\'ve brought you a book that doesn\'t answer that question at all — but asks it beautifully.
Received *The Sunward Atlas*.
_(whispering)_ You\'re glowing.
_(whispering)_ I am _not_.
May we speak tonight, Ysolde? At the Lantern.
Make way! Squire Bram Kestrel of the Dawnguard, reporting for honor-guard du— oh.
He\'s... already here. Of course he is.
Squire Kestrel. Sir Aldous spoke of you.
Did he.
He spoke well of you. Often.
Wren! Ilse! You saw that? He knew my name. The _Hierophant_ knew my name.
You smell like the inn, Bram.
Cider is a breakfast drink on islands. Everyone knows that.
Return the brooch to Nana Brisa.
Hierophant Cassian arrived. He gave me a book! He knew my letters. Mom was... Mom.
He gave you a book.
An atlas. Of the sun. Did you know there are cities in the east where it never quite gets dark in summer—
Wren. What did he say to you?
Nothing! He was _nice_. Is that so strange? That somebody important would be nice to me?
Important people are nice when they want something.
And what could he possibly want from _me_?
After the Kindling... I want to go to Aurenne. Study at the Cathedral. He\'d sponsor me, I know he would—
You didn\'t even let me—
Tomorrow you\'ll be given your Crest. And then you\'ll learn the Lantern. As I did. As my mother did.
Because _you_ never left, nobody can?
Because the last Halloway who sailed east never came back!
Your father would have gone _with_ you.
That night, a storm comes in off the Western Sea.
Wren does not sleep.
Lightning over the black rocks... wait.
There\'s someone down there. On the rocks. In _this_.
Someone is on the black rocks (southeast beach). Go!
Mom and I fought. She said Dad would have gone with me. Then there was someone on the black rocks, in the storm.
A girl! And those— are those _dogs_?
They are shaped like dogs the way smoke is shaped like a fire.
Wren! You saw it too? From my window, the lightning—
Ilse, stay back—
Absolutely not. Who do you think is going to patch you up?
They\'re gone. Like smoke. Wren, what _were_ those?
Something rises out of the surf. Something that was a dog once, long ago, and has been at the bottom of the sea ever since.
We are _not_ leaving her.
HALT, foul— uh— dog-thing! You face Bram Kestrel of the Dawnguard!
I saw your lanterns from the inn. Also I may have been awake for unrelated reasons. Stand behind me!
Did you see that? I was magnificent.
You fell over twice.
She\'s breathing. Cold as the sea, but breathing.
Who? Let _who_ find you?
She\'s fainted. Nana\'s is closest. Bram — carry her.
Carrying. Yes. Very knightly. I am good at carrying.
They carry her up the beach between them. The storm is already blowing itself out, grumbling away east over the strait.
Out past the black rocks the sea goes flat and quiet, as if nothing had ever come out of it at all.
It\'s past midnight, Wren. Happy birthday.
I don\'t think I\'m going to sleep.
The Kindling
We fought shadow-dogs on the black rocks, and something that came out of the sea. Bram helped (he says he saved us). The girl from the storm said: "Don\'t let him find me."
Check on the girl at Nana Brisa\'s house.

The white flower turns toward you and, in a voice that is not a voice:
Antlers over the door. Smoke from the chimney. Somewhere inside, a woman is shouting at a ledger.
Welcome to the Hunters\' Lodge. I\'m Adelind; I keep the board, the books and the peace, in that order.
People post bounties for monsters that are too much for a village. You hunt them, you bring proof, you get paid. Proof is the monster not being there anymore.
Wipe your boots.
Lodge is open. Mostly. The roof\'s over there now.
I was Adelind\'s apprentice. She went down with the north wing when the sky broke. Kept the books dry, though. She\'d want me to say that.
The board still works. Monsters are worse. People need them gone more than ever.
Oh — I know your face. You hunted for her. She used to say you never wiped your boots.
Old Sill
At low tide a causeway rises out of the bay, and at its end a dome — half-sunk, green with weed, older than any Lantern.
That\'s not on any map I\'ve read.
Then we\'re about to read a new one.
The great lens throws a bar of light up the stair. The way is open.
A great lens on a brass arm, crusted with salt. Beyond the gallery, the stairway is sealed by a curtain of pale crystal.
Turn the lens toward the stair?
Turn it
Leave it
Sunlight bends through the glass and strikes the crystal. It sings — one clear note — and shatters.
That note. It is the one the Lanterns sing. But backwards.
The orrery is still now. Seven brass suns, and one empty socket in the middle.
A vast brass orrery fills the dome: seven small suns on seven arms, circling an empty socket.
Carved around the rim: _WHAT IS SUNG FORWARD CAN BE SUNG BACK. WE MEASURED IT. WE CHOSE NOT TO._
"We chose not to." Who\'s we?
The orrery\'s keeper wakes!
In the empty socket you find a book of measurements, written by the very first Keepers.
The last page: _Seven voices hold the sun. Any one of them could stop it. That is why there must always be seven._
There was an observatory under the bay older than the Lanterns. The first Keepers knew the Dawnsong could be sung backwards. They chose not to.
Fort Ashwatch: an old Dawnguard frontier fort, abandoned for twenty years. The banners are rags. The gate is open.
Ashwatch. Sir Aldous held this fort before he was my mentor. He said it was the coldest place he ever loved.
A row of soldiers\' graves, each marked with a Dawnguard sunburst. The newest is twenty years old.
Someone has been leaving wildflowers. Recently.
Sir Aldous\'s old office. The desk is empty now.
A commander\'s office, frozen in the moment it was left. In the desk, an unsent letter, sealed, addressed in a square hand:
_To my squire, whoever he turns out to be._
He wrote it before he ever met me. "Whoever he turns out to be."
_If you are reading this, you are my squire, and you have just frozen in front of something terrible, and you think you are a coward._
_I froze my first time too. In this fort. A man died covering for me. I have never told anyone._
_Courage is not the part where you are not afraid. It is the part after. — A.V._
I\'m fine. There\'s dust. In the fort. It\'s a very dusty fort.
In Fort Ashwatch we found a letter Sir Aldous wrote to his future squire. Bram says the fort is very dusty.
An empty suit of commander\'s armor stands guard over the stairs. As you approach, it draws its sword.

Light the old signal fire?

From the ashes beneath the grate you pull a commander\'s ring, warm as a hand.

A shard of the old world, and beneath it, hanging by its roots like a seed-pod, the bell-tower of the Abbey of Hours — upside-down.
Every few minutes, the bell inside it rings. No one is pulling the rope.
Sexton Orrin
The bell remembers the order now. Go on down to her. Go gently.
You came down the tower? Upside down? Ha. Welcome to the Hollow Bell. I\'m the sexton. I was the sexton. I am still, I think, the sexton.
There are three chimes in this nave. The bell below won\'t let anyone pass until they\'re rung in the old order. The order we rang for weddings.
"Low for the promise, high for the joy, and the middle for every day after."
It\'s quiet. I didn\'t know it could be quiet. Thank you.

I can\'t stop. The bell won\'t let me. It thinks if it stops, everyone will be gone for real.

The bell rings once more — softly, the way you ring a bell at the end of something — and goes still.
Agathe sits down for the first time in a year, and laughs, and cries, and presses something cold into Wren\'s hand.
In the upside-down tower of the Hollow Bell a girl named Agathe had been ringing for a wedding that would never come. We helped the bell be quiet.
After the Sundering, white flowers began to grow on a cemetery shard. When the wind moves them, they speak.
They say the last thing someone said before they died.
The White Gardener
The heart is quiet. Let them grow. Let them say what they need to.
Mind the beds. Everyone in them was loved by someone.
I don\'t plant them. They come up on their own, a flower for every last word nobody was there to hear. I only keep the paths clear.
At the heart there\'s a bloom that won\'t stop growing. It wants to hold every word ever spoken. It\'s strangling the others.
At the heart of the garden, a single bloom the size of a house, petals overlapping like a thousand mouths, all of them whispering at once.
As the great bloom withers, the voices untangle, one by one, into silence.
One small white flower is left at the heart. It turns toward Wren.
_"Grow up well, my little bird."_
Tangled in the roots, where the flower grew: a locket, small and tarnished. Inside, a tiny painting of three people.
In the Garden That Remembers, a flower said Mom\'s last words. I found her locket in its roots. There are three of us in the painting.
Where the Black Star hung there is only sky now — bruised, broken, and yours.
Above the seven wounds, the sky goes the wrong kind of dark.
The Black Star does not shine. It takes. Light bends toward it and does not come back.
The Black Star collapses into a single cold shard, small enough to hold. It hums a note below hearing.

t waste turns re-inflicting an ailment, and once a status bounces off someone they stop trying it. On Story difficulty they think less clearly.

Greer Thackery\'s *Compendium* (in the menu once she gives it to you in Aurenne) records every creature you meet, numbered by chapter, with *???* where something is still out there. It fills in as you learn: weaknesses you strike or Scan, resistances and immunities you run into, moves you see used. Fell three of a kind (one, for a boss) to learn its *tactics*. Q/E turns the sections.

Greer posts *marks* on the Hunter\'s Ledger: named rare beasts that stand where they live, shown in blue. Talk to one to hunt it. Marks hit hard, can\'t be fled and wind up for a big move. Tell Greer when you fell one: she pays for each, gives a keepsake at three, six and ten, and pays as the Compendium grows. Marks you leave alive come through the Sundering.

Open *Arts* in the menu to read every Art a character knows: what kind it is, whom it hits, its power, element and MP, and every effect (ailments, stat changes, cures, piercing, speed). Arts of the primary and secondary Crests can be used in battle; Mastery Arts still to come show when they unlock. The same details appear in the Crest screen and in battle as you pick an Art.

Supports are passive abilities learned from any Crest rank. Once learned they belong to you, whatever Crest you wear. Equip them in *Supports* within your Support Point budget, which grows with level.
Weapons and armor depend on your primary Crest. In *Equipment*, press *F* to Optimize. Accessories fit anyone.

The orb in the lower-left warms from green to red as a random battle approaches. Settings → *Encounter Rate* halves random battles or turns them off (story battles still happen), and *Skip Random Battles* resolves them at once.

Only the first four in your *Formation* fight; the rest wait in reserve and earn half the EXP. Change the order on the menu\'s Formation screen. In battle, *Swap* brings a reserve member in for the one whose turn it is.

Leave a town or region by its edge to reach the *world map*, then pick a place and go: a marker shows where your objective lies, blue ones mark side quests. *Travel* in the menu jumps straight to towns and to every Hearthstone you have touched, from anywhere outside a dungeon.
A card explains each system the first time you meet it, and names the Guide entry with the rest. Each shows once per save. Settings → *Tutorials* turns them off.

Once *Kindle* the Emberhart is with you, press *R* (Ride) on open roads and in the wilds to ride, and again to get down. Kindle runs faster than you can, and nothing from the Gloam catches you while you ride — no random battles. Towns, buildings and dungeons are on foot; talking to someone or opening a chest gets you down. On the world map, Kindle carries you to where you are going.
